A Square and A Cube

Why only square-numbered lockers stay open, the hidden patterns in squares and cubes, and how prime factors and clever estimates help us find their roots.

🟩

🔐 The puzzle of the 100 lockers

Queen Ratnamanjuri's will hides a puzzle. There are 100 lockers, all closed, and 100 people numbered 1 to 100. Person 1 opens every locker. Person 2 toggles every 2nd locker (open → closed, closed → open). Person 3 toggles every 3rd locker, and so on up to person 100. Which lockers are open at the end?

Key idea: person k touches locker n only when k is a factor of n. So locker n is toggled once for each factor of n. Odd number of toggles → open. Even number → closed.

🎬 Watch 20 people play with 20 lockers

Factors come in partner pairs whose product is the number: 12 = 1 × 12 = 2 × 6 = 3 × 4. Pairs make the count even. But in 36 = 6 × 6, the factor 6 is its own partner, so 36 has an odd number of factors (9 of them).

Arcs join partner factors. 36 has 9 factors because 6 pairs with itself → locker 36 stays open.

💡 A number made by multiplying a number by itself (1 × 1, 2 × 2, 3 × 3, …) is a square number. Only squares have an odd number of factors, so the open lockers are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100.
🎯
Try thisThe clue says the passcode is the first five lockers touched exactly twice. Exactly two factors means 1 and itself, so these are the primes: the code is 2-3-5-7-11.

🟩 1.1 Square numbers

Why "square"? A square of side n units holds n rows of n unit squares, so its area is n × n square units.

We write n × n = n², read "n squared". For example 5 × 5 = 5² = 25 and 10² = 100.

Sides need not be whole numbers. A square of side 35 unit has area (35)² = 35 × 35 = 925 sq unit, and a side of 2.5 gives (2.5)² = 6.25 sq units.

💡 The squares of natural numbers, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, …, are called perfect squares.

Memory trickSquaring is not doubling: 7² = 7 × 7 = 49, not 14. The small 2 tells you how many times the number is used as a factor.

🔍 Patterns in perfect squares

Units digits. Look at the table: squares end only in 0 1 4 5 6 9. A square never ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8. Why? The units digit of n² depends only on the units digit of n:

n ends in0123456789
n² ends in0149656941
  • n ends in 1 or 9 → n² ends in 1 (1², 9², 11², 19², 21², 29², 31², 39² …).
  • n ends in 4 or 6 → n² ends in 6. So 34², 46², 56², 74² end in 6, but 38² and 82² do not.

⚠️ The units digit can only say "not a square". 16 and 36 are squares ending in 6, but 26 also ends in 6 and is not a square.

Zeros. 10² = 100, 20² = 400, 100² = 10000, 700² = 490000. Each zero at the end of n gives two zeros in n². A number ending in 3 zeros has a square ending in 6 zeros. So a square always ends in an even number of zeros: 1000 or 250 can never be squares.

Parity. Even × even is even and odd × odd is odd, so the square of an even number is even and the square of an odd number is odd.

🧠
Memory trick"2, 3, 7, 8 — never a square, mate!" Use it as a quick first test before any calculation.

🧱 Perfect squares and odd numbers

Differences of consecutive squares: 4 − 1 = 3, 9 − 4 = 5, 16 − 9 = 7, 25 − 16 = 9, … the odd numbers! So adding odd numbers from 1 builds the squares: 1 = 1, 1 + 3 = 4, 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 …

🎬 Grow a square with L-shaped layers

The picture is a proof without words: to grow an n × n square into the next one, you add an L-shape with n + n + 1 = 2n + 1 tiles, always an odd number. So the sum of the first n odd numbers is n².

Using it: the n-th odd number is 2n − 1. Given 35² = 1225, the 36th odd number is 2 × 36 − 1 = 71, so 36² = 1225 + 71 = 1296.

Square test: keep subtracting 1, 3, 5, … If you land exactly on 0, the number is a perfect square, and the count of subtractions is its square root. If you jump below 0, it is not a square.

🎬 Subtract odd numbers: do we hit 0?
🤩
Did you know?In mathematics, a picture can be a complete argument by itself. The L-shaped layers are a famous "proof without words".

📏 Between squares, and triangular numbers

How many numbers lie between consecutive squares? From n² to (n + 1)² the jump is 2n + 1, so 2n numbers lie strictly between them. Between 4² = 16 and 5² = 25 there are 8 numbers (17 to 24). The gaps keep growing, so squares get rarer:

Block1–100101–200201–300301–400401–500501–600601–700701–800801–900901–1000
Squares10433222221

The largest square below 1000 is 961 = 31² (32² = 1024 is too big).

Triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, … are dots stacked in a triangle. Put two consecutive triangles together and they make a square! (Blue = one triangle, orange = the next one turned around.)

1 + 3 = 4 = 2², 3 + 6 = 9 = 3², 6 + 10 = 16 = 4², and the next term is 10 + 15 = 25 = 5².

√ Square roots

A square has area 49 sq cm. Its side is 7 cm because 7 × 7 = 49. We call 7 the square root of 49. In general, if y = x², then x is a square root of y. Finding the square root undoes squaring.

But (−8) × (−8) = 64 too! So 64 has two square roots, +8 and −8, written √64 = ±8. In this chapter we use only the positive root, so √64 = 8, √100 = 10.

Is 576 a perfect square, and what is its root? The units digit (6) allows it, but cannot prove it. Three ways:

  1. List the squares: 20² = 400, 21² = 441, 22² = 484, 23² = 529, 24² = 576 ✓. Slow for large numbers.
  2. Subtract odd numbers until you reach 0. 81 − 1 − 3 − 5 − … − 17 = 0 in 9 steps, so √81 = 9. Works, but long for 729.
  3. Prime factorisation: if the prime factors split into two identical groups, the product of one group is the square root.
🎬 Pair up the primes

324 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = (2 × 3 × 3) × (2 × 3 × 3) = 18², so √324 = 18

156 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 13 → 3 and 13 have no partner → not a square

🎯
Try this1156 = 2 × 2 × 17 × 17 = (2 × 17)², so √1156 = 34. 2800 = 2⁴ × 5² × 7: the 7 is alone, so 2800 is not a perfect square.

🎯 Estimating square roots

For a big perfect square we can narrow down the root instead of factorising. Example: √1936.

  1. 40² = 1600 and 50² = 2500, so 40 < √1936 < 50.
  2. 1936 ends in 6, so the root ends in 4 or 6: it is 44 or 46.
  3. 45² = (40 + 5)² = 1600 + 400 + 25 = 2025. Since 1936 < 2025, the root is below 45.
  4. So √1936 = 44. Check: 44 × 44 = 1936 ✓
🎬 Squeeze the root, then halve the interval

Not a perfect square? Aribam says 250. 15² = 225 and 16² = 256, so 15 < √250 < 16. 250 is much closer to 256, so √250 ≈ 16 (a little less).

🌍
Real lifeAkhil's square cloth has area 125 cm². A 15 cm handkerchief needs 225 cm², too big. Since 11² = 121 ≤ 125 < 144 = 12², the largest whole-number side is 11 cm.

🧊 1.2 Cubic numbers

A cube is a solid whose edges are all equal and meet at right angles. A cube of edge 2 cm needs 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 small 1 cm cubes; edge 3 cm needs 27; edge 4 needs 4 layers of 4 × 4 = 64.

🎬 Build a cube layer by layer

So 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, … are perfect cubes: n × n × n = n³ ("n cubed"). 9 is not a cube: 2³ = 8 and 3³ = 27, and nothing in between works (10 to 26 are not cubes either).

n12345678910
n³1827641252163435127291000
n11121314151617181920
n³1331172821972744337540964913583268598000
  • Last digits: cubes can end in any digit 0–9, and different units digits give different endings (2 → 8, 8 → 2, 3 → 7, 7 → 3, others stay the same).
  • How many cubes? 1-digit: 1, 8 (two). 2-digit: 27, 64 (two). 3-digit: 125, 216, 343, 512, 729 (five).
  • Zeros: each zero in n gives three zeros in n³ (10³ = 1000), so a cube can never end in exactly two zeros.
  • Fractions, decimals and negatives can be cubed too: (46)³ = 64216, (13.08)³ = 2237.810112, (−6)³ = −216.
🤩
Did you know? Taxicab numbers 🚕When G. H. Hardy visited Srinivasa Ramanujan in hospital, he said his taxi number 1729 was rather dull. Ramanujan at once replied that it is the smallest number that is a sum of two cubes in two different ways: 1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³. Such numbers are now called taxicab numbers. The next two are 4104 = 2³ + 16³ = 9³ + 15³ and 13832 = 2³ + 24³ = 18³ + 20³. His colleague Littlewood said every positive integer was one of Ramanujan's personal friends.

🌈 Cubes and consecutive odd numbers

Odd numbers build cubes too! Cut the list of odd numbers into groups of 1, 2, 3, 4, … numbers:

🎬 Group the odd numbers and watch cubes appear

1 = 1³ · 3 + 5 = 2³ · 7 + 9 + 11 = 3³ · 13 + 15 + 17 + 19 = 4³ · …

Why does it work? The n numbers in group n are centred on n² (e.g. 7, 9, 11 average 9 = 3²). So their sum is n × n² = n³.

🎯
Try this91 + 93 + 95 + … + 109 has 10 numbers, so it is group 10 and the sum is 10³ = 1000, without adding!

∛ Cube roots

Since 8 = 2³, we call 2 the cube root of 8 and write ∛8 = 2. In general, if y = x³ then x = ∛y. So ∛27 = 3, ∛1000 = 10, and ∛(n³) = n.

Is a number a perfect cube? Use prime factorisation again, but now we need three identical groups (or, equally, every prime in triplets).

🎬 Group the primes in threes

3375 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 5 × 5 = (3 × 5) × (3 × 5) × (3 × 5) = 15³, so ∛3375 = 15

500 = 2 × 2 × 5 × 5 × 5 → the 2s are only a pair → not a cube

NumberIts cube, in primes
4 = 2 × 264 = 2³ × 2³
6 = 2 × 3216 = 2³ × 3³
15 = 3 × 53375 = 3³ × 5³
12 = 2 × 2 × 31728 = 2³ × 2³ × 3³
💡 Each prime factor of a number appears three times in its cube. Squares → pairs; cubes → triplets.
🎯
Try this∛64 = 4, ∛512 = 8 (2⁹ = three groups of 2³), ∛729 = 9 (3⁶ = three groups of 3²).

🪜 Successive differences

Take differences of the squares, then differences of those: after two levels everything is 2. Do the same for cubes and you need three levels before all the differences are equal (all 6).

🎬 Differences of differences of cubes
Cubes182764125216
Level 1719376191

Level 3666
🧠
Memory trickPower 2 → constant at level 2. Power 3 → constant at level 3. The gaps between cubes grow much faster than the gaps between squares.

📜 1.3 A pinch of history

🏺 ~1700 BCEBabylonians wrote lists of squares and cubes on clay tablets, to look up roots quickly for land measurement and building.
🟩 vargaSanskrit for both the square figure (and its area) and the square power. The 4th power was varga-varga.
🧊 ghanaSanskrit for both the solid cube and a number multiplied by itself three times.
🌱 mula"Root of a plant". varga-mula = square root, ghana-mula = cube root (used from at least the 1st century BCE).
📖 Aryabhata, 499 CECalled a four-sided equal figure and the number for its area varga, and also the product of two equal quantities.
📖 Brahmagupta, 628 CEUsed pada (foot, basis): the root of a square is that of which it is the square.
🤩
Did you know?That is why we say "root"! The Indian word mula was copied by Arabic (jidhr) and Latin (radix), both meaning the root of a plant. The word "radical" for √ comes from radix.

🔐 The locker room

Choose how many lockers, then slide how many people have had their turn. Tap a locker to see its factors and partner pairs. When everyone has played, which lockers are open?

🔍 Root detective

Type a number and choose square root or cube root. See its primes grouped into pairs or triplets, whether it is perfect, the smallest multiplier that makes it perfect, and an estimate.

🧩 Square pairs puzzle

The end-of-chapter puzzle: arrange the numbers so that every two neighbours add up to a square. Green-bordered numbers fit next. Try a row of 1–17, then a circle of 1–32.

📘 Think & Math Talk questions in the text pages 2–15

aDoes every number have an even number of factors? Which numbers have an odd number of factors?
Show solution

No. Factors come in partner pairs, but when a number is a square one factor pairs with itself (9 = 3 × 3), so it is counted once. 1 (factor 1), 4 (1, 2, 4), 9 (1, 3, 9) and 36 (nine factors) all have an odd number.

Answer: No — exactly the square numbers have an odd number of factors
bWrite the locker numbers that remain open (100 lockers).
Show solution

Open lockers are toggled an odd number of times, i.e. their numbers are squares up to 100.

Answer: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100
cWhich of these have 6 in the units place: 38², 34², 46², 56², 74², 82²?
Show solution

Only the units digit matters. 4² = 16 and 6² = 36 end in 6; 8² = 64 and 2² = 4 end in 4.

Answer: 34², 46², 56², 74²
dIf a number ends in 3 zeros, how many zeros does its square end in? Can a square end in an odd number of zeros? What about the parity of a number and its square?
Show solution

Each zero is a factor 10; squaring uses it twice, so the zeros double: 3 → 6. The number of zeros in a square is always double, so always even. Even² is even and odd² is odd, so a number and its square have the same parity.

Answer: 6 zeros; no, always an even number; same parity
eHow many numbers lie between two consecutive squares? Count the squares in each block of 100 up to 1000. What is the largest square below 1000?
Show solution

Between n² and (n + 1)² there are (n + 1)² − n² − 1 = 2n numbers. Counting from the table of squares: 10, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1 squares in the blocks 1–100, 101–200, …, 901–1000.

Answer: 2n numbers; largest square below 1000 is 961 = 31²
fDraw the next term of the triangular-number pattern 1 + 3 = 2², 3 + 6 = 3², 6 + 10 = 4².
Show solution

Put the triangle of 10 dots and the triangle of 15 dots together: they fill a 5 × 5 square.

Answer: 10 + 15 = 25 = 5²
gUse prime factorisation to decide whether 1156 and 2800 are perfect squares.
Show solution

1156 = 2 × 2 × 17 × 17 = (2 × 17) × (2 × 17), so it is 34². 2800 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 × 5 × 7: the 7 has no partner.

Answer: 1156 = 34² is a square; 2800 is not
hWhat are the possible last digits of cubes? How many cubes have 1, 2 and 3 digits? Can a cube end in exactly two zeros?
Show solution

The cubes 1³ … 10³ end in 1, 8, 7, 4, 5, 6, 3, 2, 9, 0, so every digit is possible. 1-digit cubes: 1, 8; 2-digit: 27, 64; 3-digit: 125, 216, 343, 512, 729. A number ending in k zeros has a cube ending in 3k zeros (0, 3, 6, …), never exactly 2.

Answer: all digits 0–9; 2, 2 and 5 cubes; no
iWrite 4104 and 13832 as sums of two positive cubes in two ways.
Show solution

Try subtracting cubes and check whether the rest is a cube: 4104 − 16³ = 4104 − 4096 = 8 = 2³ and 4104 − 15³ = 4104 − 3375 = 729 = 9³. 13832 − 24³ = 13832 − 13824 = 8 = 2³ and 13832 − 20³ = 13832 − 8000 = 5832 = 18³.

Answer: 4104 = 2³ + 16³ = 9³ + 15³; 13832 = 2³ + 24³ = 18³ + 20³
jFind 91 + 93 + 95 + … + 109 without adding.
Show solution

There are (109 − 91) ÷ 2 + 1 = 10 numbers, so this is the 10th group in the pattern 1 = 1³, 3 + 5 = 2³, 7 + 9 + 11 = 3³, …

Answer: 10³ = 1000
kFind ∛64, ∛512 and ∛729. Then compute successive differences of the cubes 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216.
Show solution

64 = 2⁶ = (2 × 2)³; 512 = 2⁹ = (2 × 2 × 2)³; 729 = 3⁶ = (3 × 3)³. Differences: 7, 19, 37, 61, 91 → 12, 18, 24, 30 → 6, 6, 6.

Answer: 4, 8, 9; the third level is constant (all 6)

📘 Figure it Out · 1.1 Square numbers pages 10–11

1Which of these are not perfect squares? (i) 2032 (ii) 2048 (iii) 1027 (iv) 1089
Show solution

(i) 2032 ends in 2 and (iii) 1027 ends in 7: never squares. (ii) 2048 ends in 8: not a square. (iv) 1089: 33² = 1089, so it is a square.

Answer: (i), (ii) and (iii)
2Which of 64², 108², 292², 36² has last digit 4?
Show solution

Look only at units digits: 4² = 16 → 6; 8² = 64 → 4; 2² = 4 → 4; 6² = 36 → 6.

Answer: 108² and 292²
3Given 125² = 15625, which is 126²? (i) 15625 + 126 (ii) 15625 + 262 (iii) 15625 + 253 (iv) 15625 + 251 (v) 15625 + 512
Show solution

The next square is the previous one plus the next odd number. The 126th odd number is 2 × 126 − 1 = 251 (or: 125 + 126 = 251). So 126² = 15625 + 251 = 15876.

Answer: (iv) 15625 + 251
4Find the side of a square whose area is 441 m².
Show solution

Side = √441. 441 = 3 × 3 × 7 × 7 = (3 × 7)², so √441 = 21.

Answer: 21 m
5Find the smallest square number divisible by each of 4, 9 and 10.
Show solution

It must be a multiple of LCM(4, 9, 10) = 180 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5. The 5 has no partner, so multiply by 5: 180 × 5 = 900 = 30².

Answer: 900
6Find the smallest number by which 9408 must be multiplied to get a perfect square. Find the square root of the product.
Show solution

9408 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 × 7. All primes pair up except 3. Multiply by 3: 9408 × 3 = 28224 = (2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 7)² = 168².

Answer: 3; √28224 = 168
7How many numbers lie between the squares of (i) 16 and 17 (ii) 99 and 100?
Show solution

Between n² and (n + 1)² there are 2n numbers. (i) 16² = 256, 17² = 289: 2 × 16 = 32 numbers (257 to 288). (ii) 2 × 99 = 198 numbers.

Answer: (i) 32 (ii) 198
8Fill in: 1² + 2² + 2² = 3², 2² + 3² + 6² = 7², 3² + 4² + 12² = 13², 4² + 5² + 20² = (__)², 9² + 10² + (__)² = (__)²
Show solution

The third number is the product of the first two (1 × 2, 2 × 3, 3 × 4, 4 × 5); the right side is one more than it. So 4² + 5² + 20² = 21² (16 + 25 + 400 = 441 ✓) and 9² + 10² + 90² = 91² (81 + 100 + 8100 = 8281 ✓).

Answer: 21; 90 and 91
9How many tiny squares are in the picture? Write the prime factorisation of that number.
Show solution

The picture is a 9 × 9 arrangement of 81 tiles (tilted and straight, taking turns). Each tile is a 5 × 5 grid of 25 tiny squares. Total = 81 × 25 = 2025 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 5 = 3⁴ × 5². Notice 2025 = 45² is itself a perfect square, as it must be: 81 = 9² and 25 = 5².

Answer: 2025 = 3⁴ × 5²

📘 Figure it Out · 1.2 Cubic numbers pages 16–17

1Find the cube roots of 27000 and 10648.
Show solution

27000 = 2³ × 3³ × 5³ = (2 × 3 × 5)³ = 30³. 10648 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 11 × 11 × 11 = (2 × 11)³ = 22³.

Answer: ∛27000 = 30, ∛10648 = 22
2What number will you multiply 1323 by to make it a cube number?
Show solution

1323 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 7 × 7. The 3s form a triplet; the 7s need one more 7. 1323 × 7 = 9261 = 21³.

Answer: 7
3True or false? Explain. (i) The cube of any odd number is even. (ii) No perfect cube ends with 8. (iii) The cube of a 2-digit number may be a 3-digit number. (iv) The cube of a 2-digit number may have seven or more digits. (v) Cube numbers have an odd number of factors.
Show solution
  1. False. Odd × odd × odd is odd: 3³ = 27.
  2. False. 2³ = 8 and 12³ = 1728 end in 8.
  3. False. The smallest 2-digit number is 10 and 10³ = 1000 already has 4 digits.
  4. False. The largest 2-digit number is 99 and 99³ = 970299 has only 6 digits.
  5. False. 8 = 2³ has factors 1, 2, 4, 8 (four, even). Only cubes that are also squares, like 1 and 64, have an odd number.
Answer: all five are false
41331 is a perfect cube. Guess its cube root without factorising. Similarly guess the cube roots of 4913, 12167 and 32768.
Show solution

Strategy: the last digit of the cube fixes the last digit of the root (1→1, 3→7, 7→3, 8→2); the part before the last three digits fixes the tens digit.
1331: ends in 1 → …1; front 1 → 1³ = 1 → root 11.
4913: ends in 3 → …7; front 4 is between 1³ and 2³ → root 17.
12167: ends in 7 → …3; front 12 is between 2³ = 8 and 3³ = 27 → root 23.
32768: ends in 8 → …2; front 32 is between 3³ = 27 and 4³ = 64 → root 32.

Answer: 11, 17, 23, 32
5Which is the greatest? (i) 67³ − 66³ (ii) 43³ − 42³ (iii) 67² − 66² (iv) 43² − 42²
Show solution

Gaps between consecutive squares are odd numbers: 67² − 66² = 133, 43² − 42² = 85. Gaps between consecutive cubes are much bigger and keep growing (7, 19, 37, 61, …), so the cube gap with the larger numbers wins: 67³ − 66³ = 13267, while 43³ − 42³ = 5419.

Answer: (i) 67³ − 66³

🧩 Puzzle · Square Pairs! page 18

1Arrange 1 to 17 in a row so that every two neighbours add up to a square. Is there more than one way?
Show solution

16 can only sit next to 9 (16 + 9 = 25) and 17 only next to 8 (17 + 8 = 25), so 16 and 17 must be the two ends. From 16 each next step is forced:

16, 9, 7, 2, 14, 11, 5, 4, 12, 13, 3, 6, 10, 15, 1, 8, 17

Sums: 25, 16, 9, 16, 25, 16, 9, 16, 25, 16, 9, 16, 25, 16, 9, 25 — all squares.

Answer: only this row (and its reverse)
2Arrange 1 to 32 in a circle so that every two neighbours add up to a square.
Show solution

One solution (going round, and the last joins back to the first):

1, 8, 28, 21, 4, 32, 17, 19, 30, 6, 3, 13, 12, 24, 25, 11, 5, 31, 18, 7, 29, 20, 16, 9, 27, 22, 14, 2, 23, 26, 10, 15 (→ back to 1)

Every neighbouring sum is 9, 16, 25, 36 or 49, and 15 + 1 = 16 closes the circle. Try it in the 🧩 Lab!

Answer: possible — one circle is shown above

✗ 9² = 18 and 4³ = 12

✓ 9² = 9 × 9 = 81 and 4³ = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. The small number counts factors, it does not multiply.

6️⃣

✗ "26 ends in 6, so it is a square"

✓ 26 is not a square. The units digit can only rule a number out (2, 3, 7, 8). To show a number IS a square, find its root: 2116 = 46².

🔟

✗ "1000 is a square because it ends in 0"

✓ A square ends in an even number of zeros. 1000 has three, so it is not a square (but it is 10³).

🔐

✗ "Locker 12 is touched 3 times (by 2, 3, 4)"

✓ Count every factor, including 1 and 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 → 6 times → closed.

📏

✗ "Between 16² and 17² there are 33 numbers"

✓ The difference is 289 − 256 = 33, but the numbers strictly between are 257 … 288: 32 = 2 × 16.

🧩

✗ 500 = 2 × 2 × 5 × 5 × 5, so ∛500 = 2 × 5

✓ The 2s are only a pair, not a triplet. 500 is not a perfect cube (multiply by 2 to get 1000 = 10³).

➕

✗ √(9 + 16) = √9 + √16 = 7

✓ √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. You cannot split a root over a plus sign.

🔄

✗ "32768 ends in 8, so its cube root ends in 8"

✓ 8³ ends in 2, but 2³ = 8. A cube ending in 8 has a root ending in 2: ∛32768 = 32. (2 ↔ 8, 3 ↔ 7 swap.)

Power Play

When you multiply again and again, numbers explode. Learn the shorthand (exponents), the rules that make them easy, what 2⁰ and 2⁻³ mean, how to write giant numbers neatly, and how to get a feel for them.

⚡

📄 2.1 Fold a paper … to the Moon?

Take a sheet of paper and fold it in half, again and again. Each fold puts one stack on top of another equal stack, so the thickness doubles every time. Try it: most paper refuses after about 7 folds!

Now imagine we could keep going. Start with a sheet 0.001 cm thick:

26≈ 670 malmost the Burj Khalifa (830 m) 🏢
30≈ 10.7 kmwhere planes fly ✈️; nearly as deep as the Mariana Trench (11 km), the deepest point in the oceans
46≈ 7,03,687 kmfar past the Moon (3,84,400 km) 🌙
🎬 Fold the paper again and again

Why so fast? Look at any stretch of folds. After any 3 folds the thickness becomes 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 times. After any 10 folds it becomes 2 multiplied by itself 10 times = 1024 times: from 0 to 10 folds, 10 to 20, 20 to 30… always ×1024.

💡 Growth by multiplying again and again is called multiplicative or exponential growth. It starts slowly and then shoots up.

⚡ 2.2 Exponential notation

Writing 0.001 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 is tiring. We write the repeated factor once and put a small number on top to say how many times it is used:

0.001 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 0.001 × 27 = 0.128 cm

na means n multiplied by itself a times. Read 54 as "5 raised to the power 4", "5 to the power 4" or "the 4th power of 5". 54 is the exponential form of 625. n2 is "n squared", n3 is "n cubed". The numbers 51, 52, 53, … are the powers of 5.

  • After 10 folds the thickness is 210 × v (v = the starting thickness), because v is doubled 10 times. 210 = 1024.
  • Letters work too: a × a × a × b × b = a3b2 ("a cubed b squared").
  • Negative bases: (−4)3 = (−4) × (−4) × (−4) = −64. An even power of a negative number is positive, an odd power is negative. So (−1)5 = −1 but (−1)56 = 1, and (−2)4 = 16.
  • 02 = 0, 05 = 0, and 0n = 0 for any counting number n.
🧠
Don't mix them up4 + 4 + 4 = 3 × 4 = 12 (repeated addition), but 4 × 4 × 4 = 43 = 64 (repeated multiplication).

Prime factors in exponential form. Divide by primes again and again, then count each prime:

÷ by2222553333
left3240016200810040502025405812793 → 1

32400 = 24 × 52 × 34

💎 The Stones that Shine: multiplying powers

A king has 3 daughters. Each gets 3 baskets, each basket has 3 keys, each key opens 3 rooms, each room has 3 tables, each table has 3 necklaces, each necklace has 3 diamonds. How many diamonds?

🎬 Count the branches of the tree

Rooms = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 34 = 81. Diamonds = 3 multiplied 7 times = 37. We need not start again: split the seven 3s into a group of four and a group of three:

37 = (3 × 3 × 3 × 3) × (3 × 3 × 3) = 34 × 33 = 81 × 27 = 2187

We could split them as 2 + 5 too: 37 = 32 × 35. With letters, p4 × p6 = (four p's) × (six p's) = p10.

💡 na × nb = na + b: same base, multiplying → add the exponents (you are just counting all the factors).
🎯
Try this29 = 24 × 25 = 16 × 32 = 512.   57 = 53 × 54 = 125 × 625 = 78,125.

🧱 Power of a power

46 is six 4s multiplied. Group them in two different ways:

Two groups of 43: 43 × 43 = 64 × 64 = 4096, which is the square of 43, written (43)2. Three groups of 42: 16 × 16 × 16 = 4096, the cube of 42, written (42)3. Likewise 210 = (22)5 = (25)2.

💡 (na)b = (nb)a = na × b: b groups of a factors each → multiply the exponents.
🎬 See the laws with factor chips
🎯
Two ways each86 = (82)3 = (83)2; and since 8 = 23, 86 = 218.   914 = (92)7 = (32)14 = 328.

🪷 The Magical Pond: same exponent, different bases

In a magic pond the number of lotuses doubles every day, and the pond is full on day 30. When was it half full? Not day 15! Since it doubles each day, it was half full just one day earlier, on day 29. Starting from 1 lotus: full = 230, half = 229.

🎬 Watch a small pond fill up

Damayanti puts 1 lotus in the doubling pond; after 4 days she moves them all to a tripling pond for 4 more days: 1 × 24 × 34 lotuses. Swapping the ponds gives 34 × 24, the same. Regroup the eight factors into pairs:

24 × 34 = (2 × 3) × (2 × 3) × (2 × 3) × (2 × 3) = 64 = 1296

💡 ma × na = (mn)a and mana = (mn)a (n ≠ 0). This works only when the exponents are the same.
🎯
Quick ones25 × 55 = 105 = 1,00,000.   104 ÷ 54 = 24 = 16.

👕 How many combinations?

Estu has 4 dresses and 3 caps. For each cap there are 4 dresses: 4 + 4 + 4 = 4 × 3 = 12 outfits.

Roxie has 7 dresses, 2 hats and 3 pairs of shoes: 7 × 2 × 3 = 42 ways. Every new choice multiplies the count.

A 5-digit lock. If a problem is hard, try a simpler version first. A 2-digit lock: 10 choices for the first digit, and for each, 10 for the second → 10 × 10 = 100 (00 to 99). A 3-digit lock: 100 × 10 = 1000. So a 5-digit lock has 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 105 = 1,00,000 passwords (00000 to 99999).

A lock with 6 slots of letters A–Z has 266 = 30,89,15,776 passwords: far safer!

🌍
Real lifePIN codes (6 digits, like 464001 for Vidisha and 796017 for Zemabawk), mobile numbers and vehicle numbers are all built this way. Find out how they are given out!

✂️ 2.3 The other side of powers: dividing, zero and negative exponents

Take a line 16 = 24 units long and keep erasing half of it.

🎬 Halve a line again and again, even past 1

Halving three times: 24 ÷ 23 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 22 × 2 × 2 = 2 = 24 − 3. Matching factors cancel, so:

💡 na ÷ nb = na − b (n ≠ 0): same base, dividing → subtract. Example: 2100 ÷ 225 = 275. (n cannot be 0 because we can never divide by 0.)

Zero exponent. What should 20 be? Let the rule decide: 20 = 24 − 4 = 24 ÷ 24 = 1. In the same way x0 = 1 for every x ≠ 0.

Negative exponents. Halve 24 five times: 24 ÷ 25 = 12, and the rule says 24 − 5 = 2−1. So 2−1 = 12. Halve it 10 times: 24 ÷ 210 = 2−6 = 126 = 164.

💡 n−a = 1na and na = 1n−a (n ≠ 0). For example 10−3 = 1103 and 103 = 110−3.
RuleExample
na × nb = na + b2−4 × 27 = 23
(na)b = (nb)a = nab(13−2)−3 = 136
na ÷ nb = na − b9−7 ÷ 94 = 9−11
n0 = 1,  n−a = 1 ÷ na(−5)−3 = 1(−5)3 = −1125

These rules were found for counting numbers, but they stay true when a and b are any integers.

🧠
Memory trickA negative exponent does not make the number negative. It means "1 over": 2−3 = 18, not −8.

🪜 Power lines

Put the powers of 4 on a vertical line. Going up one step multiplies by 4; going down one step divides by 4. Below 40 = 1 we reach the fractions 14 = 4−1 and 116 = 4−2.

16384 (47) is 16 (42) times 1024 (45), because 47 ÷ 45 = 42: two steps up. And 42 is 42 − (−2) = 44 = 256 times 4−2: four steps up.

🧠
Memory trickOn a power line, multiplying = climbing (add exponents), dividing = going down (subtract). The number of steps between two powers is the difference of their exponents.

🔟 2.4 Powers of 10 and scientific notation

Place values are powers of 10: 47561 = 4 × 104 + 7 × 103 + 5 × 102 + 6 × 101 + 1 × 100. After the decimal point the powers become negative:

561.903 = 5 × 102 + 6 × 101 + 1 × 100 + 9 × 10−1 + 0 × 10−2 + 3 × 10−3

Taming giant numbers. The mass of the Earth is 59,76,00,00,00,00,00,00,00,00,00,000 kg. Too many zeros: it is easy to miscount (like getting ₹5,000 instead of ₹50,000). Any number can be written as a number between 1 and 10 times a power of 10:

5900 = 59 × 102 = 5.9 × 103   20800 = 2.08 × 104   80,00,000 = 8 × 106

💡 Scientific notation (standard form): x × 10y, where 1 ≤ x < 10 is the coefficient and the exponent y is an integer. The exponent tells you how many digits; it matters most.
🎬 Watch the decimal point hop
  • The exponent matters most. Mumbai's 2 crore people = 2 × 107. Change the 2 to 3 and it grows by half (3 crore). Change the 7 to 8 and it becomes 10 times bigger (20 crore)!
  • Digits show how sure we are. Writing Kohima's population as 1,42,395 claims we know it to the last person. If we only know "about 1 lakh 42 thousand", write 1.42 × 105; if only "about 1 lakh 40 thousand", write 1.4 × 105.
  • Like the guide who says a skeleton is "70 million and 15 years old" because he started work 15 years ago 🦖: the "15" is silly precision. Big measurements are rounded estimates.

Comparing. Sun–Saturn 1.4335 × 1012 m, Saturn–Uranus 1.439 × 1012 m, Sun–Earth 1.496 × 1011 m. Look at the exponents first: Sun–Earth has the smallest exponent, so it is the smallest distance, only about 110 of the Sun–Saturn distance.

🤔 2.5 Did you ever wonder? Guess, then estimate

In Tulābhāra, people offer goods equal to someone's weight. If Roxie (13 years) weighs about 45 kg and jaggery costs ₹70 a kg, the jaggery is worth 45 × 70 = ₹3150. If Estu weighs 50 kg and wheat costs ₹50 a kg: 50 × 50 = ₹2500.

For "how many…?" questions with missing information, follow these steps:

  1. Guess first, by instinct: hundreds? thousands? lakhs? crores?
  2. Describe the relationship between the quantities (worth = weight × price per kg).
  3. Assume sensible values for what you don't know.
  4. Compute, then see how close your guess was.
🎯
Roxie in 1-rupee coinsGuess first! Assume a ₹1 coin weighs about 4 g. Coins = 45 kg ÷ 4 g = 45000 g ÷ 4 g ≈ 11,000 coins (thousands, about ₹11,000). Different assumptions give somewhat different answers, and that is fine.

Linear vs exponential growth. How many steps would a ladder to the Moon (3,84,400 km) have, with 20 cm between steps? 3,84,400 km = 3,84,40,00,000 cm, and 3,84,40,00,000 ÷ 20 = 1,92,20,00,000 steps (192 crore 20 lakh). Paper folding needs just 46 folds!

💡 Linear growth is additive (+20, +20, +20, …). Exponential growth is multiplicative (×2, ×2, ×2, …). The Stones that Shine, the Magical Pond and the combination locks are all exponential.
🌍
PādayātraPilgrims who walked 400 km: at about 30 km a day, they set out roughly 13 days (about 2 weeks) earlier. Pilgrimages like Pandharpur Wari, Sabarimala Yatra and the Ajmer Sharif Ziyarat continue this old tradition of walking.

🐜 Getting a sense of large numbers (and long times)

A lakh is 105, a crore 107, an arab 109; a million is 106, a billion 109. Powers of 10 let us line up living things by how many there are:

PowerHow many in the world (estimates)
1002 northern white rhinos (2 × 100) 🦏
102–103242 kakapo parrots (≈ 2 × 102); fewer than 3000 Komodo dragons (≈ 3 × 103)
105about 4.15 lakh African elephants (≈ 4 × 105) 🐘
1073.5 crore camels (3.5 × 107), 5.8 crore horses 🐪
1091.3 arab starlings (1.3 × 109); 8.2 arab people (8.2 × 109)
10123 trillion trees (3 × 1012) 🌳
101620 quadrillion ants (2 × 1016) 🐜, heavier than all wild birds and mammals together
1021–10251021 sand grains; 2 × 1023 stars; 2 × 1025 drops of water on Earth

Dividing is easy in this form: 8 × 109 people ÷ 4 × 105 elephants = 2 × 104 = 20,000 people per African elephant.

A different way to say your age. Roxie is 4840 days old: that is 4840 × 24 = 1,16,160 hours, or about 69,69,600 minutes! Time also lines up nicely in seconds:

Seconds≈Something that long
1021.6 minlight from the Sun reaches us in about 8 min (≈ 5 × 102 s) ☀️
1042.7 hoursan adult mayfly lives about a day (≈ 9 × 104 s)
10611.6 daysa million seconds is less than two weeks
1073.8 monthsMangalyaan took 298 days to reach Mars (≈ 2.57 × 107 s) 🚀

1010317 yearsthe Chola dynasty ruled over 900 years (≈ 3 × 1010 s)
10153.17 crore yearsdinosaurs died out 6.6 crore years ago (≈ 2 × 1015 s) 🦖
10173.17 billion yearsthe Earth is 4.5 billion years old; 1018 s ago the universe did not exist!
💡 106 seconds is under a fortnight, but 109 seconds is about 31 years. That jump of three powers is a jump of 1000 times.

📜 A pinch of history, and a game

🤩
Did you know?The Lalitavistara (a Buddhist text, 1st century BCE) names odd powers of ten up to 1053 (tallakshana) in a dialogue between the mathematician Arjuna and Prince Gautama. Mahāvīrāchārya lists 24 names (up to 1023) in his Ganita-sāra-sangraha, a Jaina text names every power up to 1096, and a Pali grammar of Kāccāyana goes up to 10140 (asaṅkhyeya)!
Indian system (×100 each step)International system (×1000 each step)
hundred thousand = lakh: 102 × 103 = 105thousand thousand = million: 103 × 103 = 106
hundred lakh = crore: 107thousand million = billion: 109
hundred crore = arab: 109thousand billion = trillion: 1012
kharab 1011, neel 1013, padma 1015, shankh 1017, maha shankh 1019quadrillion 1015, quintillion 1018, sextillion 1021, …, decillion 1033

The first part of each international name counts the extra groups of a thousand: million = 1000 × 1000 (1 extra), billion (2), trillion (3), quadrillion (4)… A googol is 10100, more than the number of atoms in the universe (1078 to 1082), and a googolplex is 10googol!

🌍
Real lifeIndia's biggest note today is ₹2000. Hungary printed a 1 sextillion (1021) pengő note in 1946 (never issued), and Zimbabwe printed a 100 trillion (1014) dollar note in 2009, worth only about 30 US dollars then.

🎲 Tremendous in Ten! In 10 seconds, each player writes a number or expression with digits and operations; the bigger one wins. 10000000000000 (= 1013) beats 999999 × 999999, which is less than (106)2 = 1012. And 101000 + 101000 + 101000 + 101000 = 4 × 101000 loses badly to 101000000 × 9000. Play with rules like "only addition" or "exponents allowed".

💡 Exponents capture enormous quantities in a few symbols. Comparing them with familiar things (folds, ladders, seconds, ants) gives a feel for how big they really are.

📄 Paper-folding race

Slide the number of folds. The scale is a power-of-10 ruler: each mark is 10 times the one before. Watch the stack pass a building, a mountain, the Moon… and compare with a ladder that grows by 20 cm a step.

🪜 Power-line explorer

Pick a base, then choose where to start and where to end on the power line. See why jumping between powers multiplies or divides by a power of the base.

🔭 Big-number studio

Type a large number to see it in scientific notation with its Indian and international name. Then climb the powers-of-ten ladder of living things and of time.

🤔 In-text questions · 2.1–2.2 pages 20–22

aComplete the folding table (start 0.001 cm) for folds 21 to 45.
Show solution

Each fold doubles the previous thickness (0.001 × 2n cm):

Fold≈ ThicknessFold≈ ThicknessFold≈ Thickness
2121 m295.4 km382,749 km
2242 m3010.7 km395,498 km
2384 m3121.5 km4010,995 km
24168 m3243 km4121,990 km
25336 m3386 km4243,980 km
26671 m34172 km4387,961 km
271.3 km35–36344 km, 687 km441,75,922 km
282.7 km371,374 km453,51,844 km
Answer: after 46 folds ≈ 7,03,687 km, more than the distance to the Moon
bStarting thickness v. Which expression gives the thickness after 10 folds: 10v, 10 + v, 2 × 10 × v, 210, 210v, 102v?
Show solution

Each fold multiplies by 2, so 10 folds multiply v by 2 ten times: v × 210. (210 alone forgets v; 10v and 2 × 10 × v are repeated addition.)

Answer: (v) 210v
cWhat is (−1)5? Positive or negative? What about (−1)56? Is (−2)4 = 16? What are 02, 05, 0n?
Show solution

(−1) × (−1) = 1, so pairs of (−1) give 1. With 5 factors one is left over: −1. With 56 factors all pair up: 1. (−2)4 = (−2)(−2)(−2)(−2) = 4 × 4 = 16 ✓. Any product with factor 0 is 0.

Answer: (−1)5 = −1 (negative); (−1)56 = 1; yes (−2)4 = 16; 02 = 05 = 0n = 0

📘 Figure it Out · 2.2 Exponential notation pages 22–23

1Write in exponential form: (i) 6×6×6×6 (ii) y×y (iii) b×b×b×b (iv) 5×5×7×7×7 (v) 2×2×a×a (vi) a×a×a×c×c×c×c×d
Show solution

Count how many times each factor repeats; that count is its exponent.

Answer: (i) 64 (ii) y2 (iii) b4 (iv) 52 × 73 (v) 22 × a2 (or (2a)2) (vi) a3c4d
2Write as a product of powers of prime factors: (i) 648 (ii) 405 (iii) 540 (iv) 3600
Show solution
  1. 648 = 2 × 324 = 2 × 2 × 162 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 81 = 23 × 34
  2. 405 = 5 × 81 = 34 × 5
  3. 540 = 4 × 135 = 22 × 27 × 5 = 22 × 33 × 5
  4. 3600 = 36 × 100 = (22 × 32) × (22 × 52) = 24 × 32 × 52
Answer: 23 × 34; 34 × 5; 22 × 33 × 5; 24 × 32 × 52
3Find the value: (i) 2 × 103 (ii) 72 × 23 (iii) 3 × 44 (iv) (−3)2 × (−5)2 (v) 32 × 104 (vi) (−2)5 × (−10)6
Show solution
  1. 2 × 1000 = 2000
  2. 49 × 8 = 392
  3. 3 × 256 = 768
  4. 9 × 25 = 225 (even powers are positive)
  5. 9 × 10000 = 90,000
  6. (−2)5 = −32 (odd power), (−10)6 = 10,00,000 (even power), so −32 × 10,00,000 = −3,20,00,000
Answer: 2000; 392; 768; 225; 90,000; −3,20,00,000

🤔 In-text questions · Stones, ponds and combinations pages 23–27

aHow many rooms were there? How many diamonds? Why is 37 also 32 × 35?
Show solution

Rooms: 3 daughters × 3 baskets × 3 keys × 3 rooms = 34 = 81. Each room adds ×3 tables ×3 necklaces ×3 diamonds = ×33, so diamonds = 34 × 33 = 81 × 27 = 2187. The seven 3s can be grouped as (3 × 3) × (3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3) = 32 × 35.

Answer: 81 rooms; 37 = 2187 diamonds
bUsing na × nb = na+b, compute (i) 29 (ii) 57 (iii) 46
Show solution
  1. 29 = 24 × 25 = 16 × 32 = 512
  2. 57 = 53 × 54 = 125 × 625 = 78,125
  3. 46 = 43 × 43 = 64 × 64 = 4096
Answer: 512; 78,125; 4096
cWrite as a power of a power in at least two ways: (i) 86 (ii) 715 (iii) 914 (iv) 58
Show solution

Split the exponent into two factors (and you may also change the base).

  1. 86 = (82)3 = (83)2; also (23)6 = 218
  2. 715 = (73)5 = (75)3
  3. 914 = (92)7 = (97)2; also (32)14 = 328
  4. 58 = (52)4 = (54)2
Answer: e.g. (8²)³, (7³)⁵, (9²)⁷, (5²)⁴ and the swapped forms
dMagical pond (starting with 1 lotus): number of lotuses when it is (i) fully covered (day 30) (ii) half covered.
Show solution

Doubling for 30 days: 1 × 230. The day before it was half as many: 229 (on day 29).

Answer: (i) 230 (ii) 229
eCompute 25 × 55. Simplify 104 ÷ 54 in exponential form.
Show solution

Same exponents: 25 × 55 = (2 × 5)5 = 105 = 1,00,000. And 104 ÷ 54 = (10 ÷ 5)4 = 24 = 16.

Answer: 1,00,000; 24 (= 16)
fRoxie has 7 dresses, 2 hats and 3 pairs of shoes. How many ways can she dress up?
Show solution

7 dresses × 2 hats = 14 pairs; each with 3 pairs of shoes: 14 × 3.

Answer: 7 × 2 × 3 = 42 ways
gHow many passwords for a 5-digit lock (digits 0–9)? For a 6-slot lock with letters A–Z?
Show solution

Every slot multiplies the count by its number of choices. Digits: 105. Letters: 26 × 26 × 26 × 26 × 26 × 26 = 266.

Answer: 105 = 1,00,000; 266 = 30,89,15,776

🤔 In-text questions · 2.3 The other side of powers pages 27–30

aWhat is 2100 ÷ 225 in powers of 2? Why can't n be 0 in na ÷ nb?
Show solution

Subtract the exponents: 100 − 25 = 75. If n = 0, we would be dividing by 0b = 0, and division by 0 is not defined.

Answer: 275; division by zero is not defined
bDo the three rules still hold when a and b are any integers?
Show solution

Yes. Check one: 2−4 × 27 = 116 × 128 = 8 = 23 = 2−4 + 7 ✓. Negative exponents were defined exactly so that the rules keep working.

Answer: Yes
cWrite equivalent forms: (i) 2−4 (ii) 10−5 (iii) (−7)−2 (iv) (−5)−3 (v) 10−100
Show solution

Use n−a = 1 ÷ na.

Answer: (i) 124 = 116 (ii) 1105 (iii) 1(−7)2 = 149 (iv) 1(−5)3 = −1125 (v) 110100
dSimplify in exponential form: (i) 2−4 × 27 (ii) 32 × 3−5 × 36 (iii) p3 × p−10 (iv) 24 × (−4)−2 (v) 8p × 8q
Show solution
  1. 2−4 + 7 = 23
  2. 32 − 5 + 6 = 33
  3. p3 − 10 = p−7
  4. (−4)−2 = 1(−4)2 = 116 = 2−4, so 24 × 2−4 = 20 = 1
  5. 8p + q
Answer: 23; 33; p−7; 1 (= 20); 8p+q
eOn the power line of 4: how many times larger than 4−2 is 42?
Show solution

42 ÷ 4−2 = 42 − (−2) = 44: four steps up the line. (Check: 16 ÷ 116 = 256.)

Answer: 44 = 256 times
fUse the power line of 7 (7−4 … 77): 2401 × 49, 493, 343 × 2401, 16807 ÷ 49, 7 ÷ 343, 16807 ÷ 823543, 117649 × 1343, 1343 × 1343.
Show solution

Read each number as a power of 7 (49 = 72, 343 = 73, 2401 = 74, 16807 = 75, 117649 = 76, 823543 = 77), then add or subtract exponents.

  1. 74 × 72 = 76 = 1,17,649
  2. (72)3 = 76
  3. 73 × 74 = 77
  4. 75 ÷ 72 = 73 = 343
  5. 71 ÷ 73 = 7−2 = 149
  6. 75 ÷ 77 = 7−2
  7. 76 × 7−3 = 73
  8. 7−3 × 7−3 = 7−6
Answer: 7⁶, 7⁶, 7⁷, 7³, 7⁻², 7⁻², 7³, 7⁻⁶

🤔 In-text questions · 2.4 Powers of 10 pages 30–32

aWrite using powers of 10: (i) 172 (ii) 5642 (iii) 6374
Show solution

Each digit times the power of 10 for its place.

Answer: (i) 1 × 102 + 7 × 101 + 2 × 100 (ii) 5 × 103 + 6 × 102 + 4 × 101 + 2 × 100 (iii) 6 × 103 + 3 × 102 + 7 × 101 + 4 × 100
bWrite the large facts in scientific form: Sun to the centre of the galaxy 30,00,00,00,00,00,00,00,00,000 m; stars in our galaxy 1,00,00,00,00,000; mass of the Earth 59,76,00,00,00,00,00,00,00,00,00,000 kg.
Show solution

Count the digits after the first one. The first number is 3 followed by 20 zeros; the second is 1 followed by 11 zeros; the third has 25 digits, so after the first digit there are 24.

Answer: 3 × 1020 m; 1 × 1011; 5.976 × 1024 kg
cWhich is smallest: Sun–Saturn 1.4335 × 1012 m, Saturn–Uranus 1.439 × 1012 m, Sun–Earth 1.496 × 1011 m? Mark the Earth on a Sun–Saturn number line.
Show solution

Compare exponents first: 11 < 12, so Sun–Earth is smallest even though 1.496 looks bigger. Position: 1.496 × 1011 ÷ 1.4335 × 1012 ≈ 0.104, so the Earth sits about one-tenth of the way from the Sun.

Answer: Sun–Earth; Earth at about 1/10 of the line
dExpress in standard form: (i) 59,853 (ii) 65,950 (iii) 34,30,000 (iv) 70,04,00,00,000
Show solution

Put the point after the first digit, drop end zeros after the point, and count the places moved.

Answer: (i) 5.9853 × 104 (ii) 6.595 × 104 (iii) 3.43 × 106 (iv) 7.004 × 1010

🤔 In-text questions · 2.5 Did you ever wonder? pages 33–43

aHow many 1-rupee coins balance Roxie's weight? With ₹5 coins or ₹10 notes, how much money?
Show solution

Assumptions (yours may differ): Roxie 45 kg; ₹1 coin ≈ 4 g; ₹5 coin ≈ 6 g; ₹10 note ≈ 1 g. Coins = 45000 g ÷ 4 g ≈ 11,250 → about ₹11,000. ₹5 coins: 45000 ÷ 6 = 7500 coins → ₹37,500. ₹10 notes: 45000 notes → ₹4,50,000.

Answer (estimate): about 104 coins; roughly ₹37,500 in ₹5 coins; about ₹4.5 lakh in ₹10 notes
bPilgrims walked about 400 km. How long ago did they start? How many times could a person walk around the Earth (40,000 km) in a lifetime, walking non-stop?
Show solution

Assume about 30 km a day: 400 ÷ 30 ≈ 13 days. Non-stop walking at 5 km/h for 70 years: 5 × 24 × 365 × 70 = 30,66,000 km; 30,66,000 ÷ 40,000 ≈ 77.

Answer (estimate): about 2 weeks ago; about 75–80 times round the Earth
cLadder to the Moon (3,84,400 km) with steps 20 cm apart: how many steps?
Show solution

3,84,400 km = 3,84,400 × 1,00,000 cm = 3.844 × 1010 cm. Divide by 20 cm: 1.922 × 109. This is linear growth; folding paper gets there in 46 steps.

Answer: 1,92,20,00,000 steps (≈ 1.9 × 109)
dWith 8 × 109 people and 4 × 105 African elephants, are there nearly 20,000 people per elephant? Fill in: starlings 1.3 arab = ___; mosquitoes 110 trillion = ___.
Show solution

(8 ÷ 4) × 109 − 5 = 2 × 104 = 20,000 ✓. 1.3 arab = 1.3 × 109; 110 trillion = 110 × 1012 = 1.1 × 1014.

Answer: Yes; 1.3 × 109; 1.1 × 1014
eIn scientific notation: (i) ants per human (ii) flocks of 10,000 starlings (iii) leaves if each tree has 104 (iv) sheets of paper (0.001 cm) to reach the Moon.
Show solution
  1. 2 × 1016 ÷ 8 × 109 = 0.25 × 107 = 2.5 × 106 (using 8.2 × 109 people gives ≈ 2.4 × 106)
  2. 1.3 × 109 ÷ 104 = 1.3 × 105 flocks
  3. 3 × 1012 × 104 = 3 × 1016 leaves
  4. 3.844 × 1010 cm ÷ 10−3 cm = 3.844 × 1013 sheets
Answer: 2.5 × 106; 1.3 × 105; 3 × 1016; 3.844 × 1013
fRoxie is 4840 days old: how many hours? What could "69,70,710" mean? Estu is 4070 days old: find his birth date. How old is someone who has lived a million seconds?
Show solution

4840 × 24 = 1,16,160 hours. 4840 days × 1440 = 69,69,600 minutes, so 69,70,710 is Roxie's age in minutes (a little later in the day). 4070 days ≈ 11 years (4015 days + 2 or 3 leap days) and about 52 more days: count back 11 years and about 7½ weeks from today. 106 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 11.6 days.

Answer: 1,16,160 hours; minutes; about 11 years 52 days before today; about 12 days old
gFill the blanks in seconds: terror bird fossil 15 million years ago; land plants 47 crore years ago. Also suggest events of about 105 s and 106 s.
Show solution

1 year ≈ 3.15 × 107 s. 1.5 × 107 × 3.15 × 107 ≈ 4.7 × 1014 s. 4.7 × 108 × 3.15 × 107 ≈ 1.5 × 1016 s. Ideas: a 2-day weekend trip ≈ 1.7 × 105 s; a 2-week holiday ≈ 1.2 × 106 s.

Answer: ≈ 4.7 × 1014 s; ≈ 1.5 × 1016 s
h(i) Counting one star (of 2 × 1023) per second, how long? (ii) Drinking a 200 ml glass every 10 s, how long to finish all Earth's water (2 × 1025 drops, 16 drops per ml)?
Show solution

(i) One per second: 2 × 1023 s. (ii) Volume = 2 × 1025 ÷ 16 = 1.25 × 1024 ml. Glasses = 1.25 × 1024 ÷ 200 = 6.25 × 1021. Time = 6.25 × 1021 × 10 = 6.25 × 1022 s.

Answer: (i) 2 × 1023 s (ii) 6.25 × 1022 s
iWhat does the first part of the names million, billion, trillion, quadrillion … denote?
Show solution

mi(1), bi(2), tri(3), quadri(4), quinti(5), sexti(6)…: how many times we multiply 1000 by a further 1000. Billion = 1000 × 10002 = 109; in general the k-th name is 103k + 3.

Answer: the number of extra thousands multiplied onto 1000
jTremendous in Ten, Round 2: which is greater, 101000 + 101000 + 101000 + 101000 or 101000000 × 9000?
Show solution

The first is only 4 × 101000 (adding does not increase the exponent). The second is 9 × 101000003, whose exponent is far larger.

Answer: 101000000 × 9000 (Estu's)

📘 Figure it Out · end of chapter pages 44–45

1Find the units digit of 2224 ÷ 432. [Hint: 4 = 22]
Show solution

432 = (22)32 = 264, so the quotient is 2224 − 64 = 2160. Units digits of 21, 22, 23, 24, … repeat as 2, 4, 8, 6. 160 is a multiple of 4, so 2160 ends like 24 = 16.

Answer: 6
2There are 5 bottles in a container. Every day a new container is brought in. How many bottles after 40 days?
Show solution

Each day adds one more container of 5 bottles: this is linear (additive) growth, not doubling. 40 days × 5 bottles = 200. (If you also count a container that was there at the start, it is 41 × 5 = 205.)

Answer: 200 = 2 × 102 bottles
3Write as a product of two or more powers in three different ways: (i) 643 (ii) 1928 (iii) 32−5
Show solution

Change to a prime base, then split the exponent. (i) 643 = 218. (ii) 192 = 26 × 3, so 1928 = 248 × 38. (iii) 32−5 = (25)−5 = 2−25.

Answer (some ways): (i) 210 × 28, 45 × 44, 83 × 83 (ii) 248 × 38, 240 × 68, 648 × 38 (iii) 2−10 × 2−15, 2−5 × 2−20, 4−12 × 2−1
4Always, sometimes or never true? (i) Cube numbers are also square numbers. (ii) Fourth powers are also square numbers. (iii) The fifth power of a number is divisible by its cube. (iv) The product of two cube numbers is a cube number. (v) q46 is both a 4th power and a 6th power (q prime).
Show solution
  1. Sometimes: 64 = 43 = 82 is both, but 8 = 23 is not a square. Cubes that are squares are exactly the 6th powers.
  2. Always: n4 = (n2)2.
  3. Always (for n ≠ 0): n5 ÷ n3 = n2, a whole number.
  4. Always: a3 × b3 = (ab)3.
  5. Never: a 4th power of a whole number would make q's exponent a multiple of 4, a 6th power a multiple of 6; 46 is neither.
Answer: Sometimes; Always; Always; Always; Never
5Simplify in exponential form: (i) 10−2 × 10−5 (ii) 57 ÷ 54 (iii) 9−7 ÷ 94 (iv) (13−2)−3 (v) m5n12(mn)9
Show solution
  1. 10−2 + (−5) = 10−7
  2. 57 − 4 = 53
  3. 9−7 − 4 = 9−11
  4. 13(−2) × (−3) = 136
  5. (mn)9 = m9n9, so m5 + 9n12 + 9 = m14n21
Answer: 10−7; 53; 9−11; 136; m14n21
6If 122 = 144, find (i) (1.2)2 (ii) (0.12)2 (iii) (0.012)2 (iv) 1202
Show solution

1.2 = 12 × 10−1, so (1.2)2 = 144 × 10−2. Similarly (0.12)2 = 144 × 10−4, (0.012)2 = 144 × 10−6, and 1202 = 144 × 102. Decimal places double when you square.

Answer: 1.44; 0.0144; 0.000144; 14,400
7Which are the same? 24 × 36, 64 × 32, 610, 182 × 62, 624
Show solution

Write each with primes 2 and 3: 24 × 36; 64 × 32 = 2434 × 32 = 2436; 182 × 62 = (2 × 32)2 × 2232 = 2436. But 610 = 210310 and 624 = 224324 differ. (All three equal 11,664.)

Answer: 24 × 36, 64 × 32 and 182 × 62
8Which is greater? (i) 43 or 34 (ii) 28 or 82 (iii) 1002 or 2100
Show solution

(i) 64 vs 81. (ii) 256 vs 64. (iii) 1002 = 10,000 = 104, while 2100 = (210)10 = 102410 > (103)10 = 1030.

Answer: 34; 28; 2100
9A dairy will make 8.5 billion milk packets a year, each with a unique code of digits 0–9. How many digits should the code have?
Show solution

With n digits there are 10n codes. 8.5 billion = 8.5 × 109. 109 is too few; 1010 is enough.

Answer: 10 digits
1064 is a square (82) and a cube (43). Are there other numbers that are both? Describe them in general.
Show solution

Yes, infinitely many: the 6th powers n6 = (n3)2 = (n2)3. Examples: 16 = 1, 26 = 64, 36 = 729, 46 = 4096, 56 = 15,625.

Answer: yes; exactly the sixth powers n6
11A locker passcode has 5 characters, each a digit or a letter (e.g. G89P0, 003AZ). How many codes are possible?
Show solution

Choices per character: 10 digits + 26 letters = 36. Five characters: 36 × 36 × 36 × 36 × 36.

Answer: 365 = 6,04,66,176
12Sheep ≈ 109 and goats ≈ 109. Total? Options: 209, 1011, 1010, 1018, 2 × 109, 109 + 109
Show solution

Adding two equal numbers doubles it: 109 + 109 = 2 × 109. Adding does not add the exponents (1018 is 109 × 109). The answer key lists (vi); option (v) 2 × 109 is the same number, so it is correct too.

Answer: 109 + 109 = 2 × 109 (options v and vi)
13In scientific notation: (i) clothes if each person (8.2 × 109) has 30 (ii) bees in 100 million colonies of 50,000 (iii) bacteria in all humans at 38 trillion each (iv) seconds spent eating in a lifetime.
Show solution
  1. 8.2 × 109 × 3 × 101 = 24.6 × 1010 = 2.46 × 1011
  2. 108 × 5 × 104 = 5 × 1012
  3. 3.8 × 1013 × 8.2 × 109 = 31.16 × 1022 = 3.116 × 1023
  4. Assume 1 hour a day for 70 years: 3600 × 365 × 70 = 9,19,80,000 ≈ 9.2 × 107 s
Answer: 2.46 × 1011; 5 × 1012; 3.116 × 1023; ≈ 9.2 × 107 s
14What was the date 1 arab (1 billion) seconds ago?
Show solution

109 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 11,574 days ≈ 31.7 years. Count back 31 years and about 8 months from today. For example, from 15 October 2026 it lands on about 5 February 1995.

Answer: about 31 years 8 months before today (e.g. ≈ 5 Feb 1995 from 15 Oct 2026)

XII060∩IV•—1729Part I · Chapter 3

A Story of Numbers

How people across the world learnt to count and write numbers — from sticks and notches to landmark numbers, bases, place value and the Indian zero.

📜

📜 Where do our numbers come from?

Reema finds an old paper covered with strange marks. Her father says they are numbers, written the way people in Mesopotamia (around present-day Iraq) wrote them about 4000 years ago. 🤯 So people have not always written 25 as "25"!

Humans needed to count even in the Stone Age: food, animals in the herd, goods traded, offerings, and the days until the next full moon or the next season.

The numbers we use today grew up in India:

Sanskrit name (Yajurveda Samhita)ekadashashatasahasraāyuta…
Number110100100010 000up to 1012 and beyond
c. 3rd century CEBakhshali manuscript: ten digits, with zero written as a dot
499 CEAryabhata explains and computes with the 10-symbol system
c. 800–830 CEReaches the Arab world: Al-Khwārizmī and Al-Kindi write on "Hindu numerals"
c. 1100–1200 CEReaches Europe; Fibonacci argues for it
by 1600sReplaces Roman numerals in Europe, then spreads worldwide
🤩
Did you know?The word algorithm comes from the name Al-Khwārizmī. Europeans learnt the digits from Arab scholars and called them "Arabic numerals", but the Arab scholars themselves called them Hindu numerals. Today the usual names are Hindu numerals, Indian numerals or Hindu-Arabic numerals. "Hindu" here means the land and people of India, not a religion.
🌍
A great scientist agreesThe French mathematician Laplace (1749–1827) said that writing every number with just ten symbols, each having a place value, was so simple that people forget how brilliant and important it is.
💡 This chapter follows the big ideas (not the dates) that led to our number system: counting → grouping → landmark numbers → a base → place value → zero.

🐄 How do we count without numbers?

Imagine you live 10 000 years ago with a herd of cows and no number names. How do you check that all cows came back? Do you have fewer cows than your neighbour? How many more would you need?

🎬 Count a herd with sticks: one stick for each cow
  • Method 1 — objects: keep one stick (or pebble) for each cow. Pairing each cow with its own stick, with no two cows sharing a stick, is called a one-to-one mapping.
  • Method 2 — sounds or names: point to each object and say the letters a, b, c, … in order. The last letter says how many. But with 26 letters you cannot count past 26.
  • Method 3 — written symbols: a fixed list like I, II, III, IV, V, VI, … X, … XX (the Roman way).
MethodNever runs out?Easy for big collections?
Sticks✅ yes❌ you need as many sticks as objects
Letters a–z❌ stops at 26✅ quick to say
Roman symbols❌ needs new symbols for bigger numbers✅ fairly compact
💡 A number system is a standard sequence of objects, names or written symbols in a fixed order. To count a collection, we map it one-to-one onto the sequence, in order. The written symbols of a number system are called numerals (like 0, 1, 5, 36, 193).
🎯
Try thisWith sticks you can still compare: put your sticks and your friend’s sticks side by side in pairs. The unpaired sticks tell who has more, and how many more.

✋ Early number systems: body parts, bones and twos

Body parts. A group of people in Papua New Guinea count by touching points on the body in a fixed order: fingers, wrist, elbow, shoulder, ear, eye, nose, and on down the other side. The body itself is the standard sequence!

Tally marks. One of the oldest methods: cut one notch on a bone or a cave wall for each object. It is just like the stick method, but with marks. The Lebombo bone (South Africa, about 44 000 years old) has 29 notches, perhaps a lunar calendar. The Ishango bone (Democratic Republic of Congo, 20 000–35 000 years old) has notches in columns.

Counting in twos. The Gumulgal people of Australia had only two basic words and built the rest from them:

NumberGumulgal (Australia)Bakairi (South America)Bushmen (South Africa)
1urapontokalexa
2ukasarahaget'oa
3ukasar-uraponahage tokale'quo
4ukasar-ukasarahage ahage tokale*t'oa-t'oa
5ukasar-ukasar-uraponahage ahage ahage*t'oa-t'oa-t'a
6ukasar-ukasar-ukasar—t'oa-t'oa-t'oa

* Bakairi words as listed on the book’s map (3 could also be "ahawao"). Old word lists are not perfectly regular, but all three systems are built from words for 1 and 2.

So 3 = 2 + 1, 4 = 2 + 2, 5 = 2 + 2 + 1, 6 = 2 + 2 + 2. Anything above 6 was just called ras ("many"). Three groups living far apart, with no known contact, built the same system — maybe from common ancestors.

Why group at all? Look at these boxes. Up to about 4 objects you see the number at a glance; for 5 or more you have to count.

💡 Big idea 1: count in groups of a fixed size (2, 5, 10 or 20 were popular) and give the group its own word or symbol. Counting in 2s is already much shorter than tally marks.
🧠
Think about itCounting only in 5s, the number 1345 would need 269 fives! One group size is not enough for big numbers.

🏛️ Roman numerals and landmark numbers

Up to 39, the Romans grouped a number into as many 10s (X) as possible, then 5s (V), then 1s (I): 27 = 10 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1 = XXVII. Bigger numbers got new symbols. Numbers with their own basic symbol are called landmark numbers:

SymbolIVXLCDM
Value1510501005001000

To write a number, take as many of the biggest landmark number as you can, then the next one, and so on:

2367 = 1000 + 1000 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 50 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1 = MMCCCLXVII

🎬 Build a Roman numeral, biggest landmark first

Small before big means subtract: IV = 5 − 1 = 4, IX = 9, XL = 50 − 10 = 40, XC = 90, CD = 400, CM = 900. The Romans were not always consistent — 40 was sometimes written XXXX.

💡 Big idea 2: group a number using a whole sequence of group sizes — the landmark numbers — not just one size. That makes Roman numerals far shorter than tally marks.

Adding works by pooling symbols and regrouping. Example: CCXXXII + CCCCXIII → pool: 6 C, 4 X, 5 I. Five I make V; five C make D. Sum = DCXXXXV = DCXLV (645).

Multiplying is hard, because the product of two landmark numbers is usually not a landmark number: V × L = 250 = CCL, V × D = 2500 = MMD, L × D = 25 000 = twenty-five Ms! That is why only specially trained people calculated, using a tool called the abacus.

🤩
Did you know?The Roman system probably grew out of the ancient Greek system around the 8th century BCE and spread across Europe with the Roman empire. You still see it on clock faces and in chapter numbers.

🏺 The Egyptian system: the idea of a base

Around 3000 BCE the Egyptians chose their landmark numbers in a very special way. Start with 1. Group 10 ones → 10. Group 10 tens → 100. Group 10 hundreds → 1000, and so on. Each landmark number is 10 times the one before, so they are all powers of 10:

1
stroke10
heel bone100
coil of rope1000
lotus104
finger105
tadpole106
kneeling man107
sun

A number is grouped exactly as in Roman: biggest landmark first. 324 = 100 + 100 + 100 + 10 + 10 + 4 is written

Variation — base 5. What if we group 5 collections each time instead of 10? Landmark numbers: 1, 5, 5 × 5 = 25, 5 × 25 = 125, … We give them our own shapes:

50 = 1
triangle51 = 5
square52 = 25
hexagon53 = 125
circle54 = 625
wave55 = 3125
arrow

143 = 125 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1 is written

💡 Big idea 3: a number system whose landmark numbers are 1, n, n2, n3, … (start at 1 and keep multiplying by a fixed number n) is a base-n number system. Egyptian is base 10 (a decimal system); our shape system is base 5.
🧠
Memory trickBase 7 → landmarks 1, 7, 49, 343, 2401, … Base 2 → 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, … Always start at 1 = n0.

➕ Why a base makes calculation easy

Adding. Pool the symbols and regroup. Since every landmark is 10 times the one before, the swap is always 10 for 1:

🎬 Add 87 + 78 in Egyptian numerals

That is exactly our "carry"! In 47 + 56: 7 + 6 = 13 ones = 1 ten + 3 ones. In Roman numerals, the swap keeps changing (5 I → V, but 2 V → X), so you must be careful.

Multiplying. Since landmark numbers are powers of 10, the product of two landmark numbers is another landmark number:

× = 10 × 100 = 1000 =    × = 106 =

So to multiply by (10), use the distributive property: (100 + 100) × 10 = 1000 + 1000. Every symbol simply becomes the next symbol up:

× =   and   × =

💡 Because 10a × 10b = 10a+b, a system with a base is good for writing numbers and for calculating. The same is true in base 5 (multiplying by 5, the square, turns every shape into the next shape) or any base. Our Hindu numerals are built on this idea.

🧮 The abacus, and the weak spot of Egyptian numerals

From about the 11th century, even people writing Roman numerals calculated on an abacus built on base 10: a board with lines for 1, 10, 100, 1000. Put as many counters on each line as that power of 10 occurs. A counter in the space above a line is worth 5 of that line.

3426 = 3 × 1000 + 4 × 100 + 2 × 10 + 6 (6 ones = one counter above the line + one on it)

To add 2907 + 43, put both numbers on the board and slide the counters of each line together. 7 ones + 3 ones = 10 ones → remove them and add 1 counter to the 10s line: 2950.

The weak spot. Egyptian numerals had symbols only up to 107 (one crore). To write bigger and bigger numbers you would need to invent new symbols for ever — the same old problem in a new form!

🎯
Try thisIn Egyptian numerals, no symbol is ever needed 10 or more times: 10 copies would be replaced by the next symbol. (Except the biggest symbol, which has nothing above it!)

🌙 Mesopotamia: base 60 and place value

Later Mesopotamians used a base-60 (sexagesimal) system. Why 60? Nobody knows for sure: perhaps their 30-day lunar month, the Sun’s yearly path, easy fractions, or their old landmarks 1, 10, 60, 600, 3600 slimmed down to powers of 60. We still use it: 1 hour = 60 minutes, 1 minute = 60 seconds ⏰.

They used just two wedge marks: for 1 and for 10. With these, 1 to 59 can be written:

1234567891011122030405059

Give the landmark numbers 60, 3600 = 602, … our own diamond symbols ◇1, ◇2, …. Then 640 = (10) × 60 + 40 → and 7530 = (2) × 3600 + (5) × 60 + 30 → .

🎬 Drop the landmark symbols: place value is born

No power of 60 is ever needed 60 or more times: (1) × 3600 + (70) × 60 + 2 = (2) × 3600 + (10) × 60 + 2. The Mesopotamians then dropped the landmark symbols: the rightmost group counts 1s, the next 60s, the next 3600s. A missing power was a blank space.

💡 Big idea 4: a base system where the position of a symbol tells which landmark it counts is a positional or place value system. Now a few symbols can write every number — no endless new symbols!

But there was a problem. Spacing was uneven, so blanks were hard to see:

NumberWith clear spacingAs actually written
1
60
3600
12
602 = 10 × 60 + 2
36002 = 10 × 3600 + 2

Later Mesopotamians invented a placeholder sign for an empty place — the job our 0 does. But they used it only in the middle of numbers, never at the end, so 1 and 3600 still looked alike.

🌽 The Mayan system: dots, bars and a shell

In Central America the Maya (3rd–10th centuries CE) built their own place value system, completely independently, with a seashell for zero. A dot is 1 and a bar is 5, giving 0 to 19:

012345678910111213141516171819

Landmark numbers: 1, 20, 360 (= 18 × 20), 7200 (= 20 × 360), 144 000, … The groups are written one above the other: the bottom level counts 1s, the next 20s, the next 360s.

🎬 Build a Mayan numeral level by level

  = (4) × 360 + (11) × 20 + (0) × 1 = 1660

Strange! The third landmark is 360, not 20 × 20 = 400 — perhaps because of their calendar. So it is only almost base 20, and loses some of the easy arithmetic of a true base. Still, place value and a zero symbol were a big step.

🌍
Base 20 todaySome European languages still count in 20s: in French, 80 is quatre-vingts = "four twenties".

🥢 Chinese rod numerals

The Chinese had a written system for records and rod numerals for calculating (from at least the 3rd century CE to the 17th century). Rod numerals are base 10 with place value. Each digit 1–9 has two forms:

123456789
Zong
Heng

Zong (upright) rods are used for units, hundreds, ten-thousands; heng (lying) rods for tens, thousands, lakhs. A rod across the top stands for 5. The two forms alternate, so neighbouring places are easy to tell apart.

Digit2 (heng)6 (zong)3 (heng)4 (zong)
Landmark103102101

= (2) × 103 + (6) × 102 + (3) × 10 + (4) × 1 = 2634

An empty place was left blank. Since the digit symbols are all about the same size, blanks were easier to spot than in Mesopotamia. With a symbol for zero, this would be a complete place value system — very close to ours!

🇮🇳 The Hindu number system: place value with zero

Our system is base 10, uses ten symbols 0, 1, 2, …, 9, and is a place value system:

Numeral 375375
Landmark102101

375 = (3) × 102 + (7) × 10 + (5) × 1

India had a symbol for 0 at least as early as 200 BCE. With 0 as a digit and exactly one digit in each place, a numeral can never be read in two ways: 36002 and 3602 look different.

Indian mathematicians went further and treated 0 as a number: Aryabhata (Āryabhaṭīya, 499 CE) used rules like "0 + a = a" and "0 × a = 0"; Brahmagupta (Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta, 628 CE) set out arithmetic with 0 and with negative numbers. Such a set, closed under +, − and ×, is what mathematicians now call a ring — a foundation of algebra.

#Big idea in writing numbersExample
1Count in groups of one sizeukasar-ukasar-urapon
2Group with landmark numbersI V X L C D M
3Landmarks = powers of one number (a base)1, 10, 102, 103, …
4Position shows the landmark (place value)1729
50 as a positional digit and as a number2026, 0 + 7 = 7

Other bases with Hindu-style digits. With 8 fingers we might count in base 8, using digits 0–7. 25 = (3) × 8 + (1) × 1 → 31 in base 8. In base 5: 25 = (1) × 25 + 0 + 0 → 100. In base 2: 25 = 16 + 8 + 1 → 11001.

💡 Place value + a symbol for zero + a base lets us write every number with just a few symbols and calculate quickly. It is one of the greatest inventions in human history — used in shops, banks, phones and computers every day.

🔤 Number translator

Pick any number from 1 to 3999 and see it written in every system of the chapter. Notice which systems stay short as the number grows, and where place value helps.

🔷 Base explorer

Choose a base and a number. See its landmark numbers, how many of each it needs, and the numeral you get. Press +1 to watch carrying, and × base to see every count shift one place left.

🧮 Line abacus

Put counters on the lines (1, 10, 100, 1000). A counter above a line is worth 5 of that line. Press Tidy to regroup 5 counters into one above, and 10 into the next line. Try the target challenge!

📘 Figure it Out · 3.1 Reema’s Curiosity page 54

1Using only sticks (no number names, no Hindu numerals), give a way to add, subtract, multiply and divide two collections of sticks.
Show solution

Add: push the two piles together into one pile.

Subtract: pair each stick of the smaller pile with a stick of the bigger pile (one-to-one) and remove the pairs; the unpaired sticks of the bigger pile are the difference.

Multiply A × B: for every stick in pile B, lay out a fresh copy of pile A (matched stick for stick). Pool all the copies.

Divide A ÷ B: keep removing groups that match pile B one-to-one from pile A. Put aside one marker stick for each group removed. The marker sticks give the quotient; the sticks left over (fewer than B) are the remainder.

Answer: Pool to add; pair off and remove to subtract; repeated copies to multiply; repeated removal of equal groups to divide.
2Method 2 uses letters a–z for 1–26. Using strings like “aa” for 27, extend it so that it can represent every number.
Show solution

There are many ways. One simple way: after z, use doubled letters aa, bb, cc, …, zz for 27–52, then aaa, bbb, …, zzz for 53–78, and so on. This never runs out.

A smarter way (like place value): after z come aa, ab, ac, …, az, ba, …, zz (26 × 26 = 676 two-letter strings), then aaa, aab, … Each length gives many more numbers, so names stay short.

Answer: e.g. a, …, z, aa, bb, …, zz, aaa, … (or aa, ab, …, az, ba, …, zz, aaa, …)
3Try making your own number system.
Show solution

Model answer: choose • for 1 and ▲ for a group of 5 •, and ■ for a group of 5 ▲ (= 25). Then 13 = ▲▲•••, 31 = ■▲•. To count, map objects one-to-one with •, and swap every 5 • for one ▲ and every 5 ▲ for one ■.

Answer: Any system with a fixed order of symbols works; grouping makes it shorter.

📘 In the text · Roman arithmetic pages 59–60

(b)Add without converting to Hindu numerals: LXXXVII + LXXVIII.
Show solution

Pool the symbols: L L, X X X X X, V V, I I I I I.

5 I → V, so now 3 V. 2 V → X, so now 6 X and 1 V. 5 X → L, so now 3 L and 1 X. 2 L → C, so now 1 C and 1 L.

Result: C L X V. (Check: 87 + 78 = 165.)

Answer: CLXV
TryFind the products of landmark numbers: V × L, L × D, V × D, VII × IX.
Show solution

V × L = 5 × 50 = 250 = CCL. L × D = 50 × 500 = 25 000 = twenty-five Ms (MMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMM). V × D = 2500 = MMD. VII × IX = 7 × 9 = 63 = LXIII.

None of these products is a single landmark symbol — that is why Roman multiplication is hard.

Answer: CCL; MMM…M (25 Ms); MMD; LXIII
FunThe cartoon asks: multiply CCXXXI by MDCCCLII.
Show solution

231 × 1852 = 427 812. Writing this in Roman needs 427 Ms and more — ordinary Roman numerals get very long for such numbers.

Answer: 427 812

📘 Figure it Out · 3.2 Roman numerals page 59

1Write in Roman numerals: (i) 1222 (ii) 2999 (iii) 302 (iv) 715
Show solution

(i) 1222 = 1000 + 100 + 100 + 10 + 10 + 1 + 1 → M CC XX II.

(ii) 2999 = 1000 + 1000 + 900 + 90 + 9 → MM CM XC IX.

(iii) 302 = 100 + 100 + 100 + 1 + 1 → CCC II.

(iv) 715 = 500 + 100 + 100 + 10 + 5 → D CC X V.

Answer: (i) MCCXXII (ii) MMCMXCIX (iii) CCCII (iv) DCCXV

📘 Figure it Out · 3.2 Early number systems pages 60–61

1Some Pacific islanders use different sequences of number names for different kinds of objects. Why might they do this?
Show solution

For them a number was tied to the kind of thing being counted (fish, canoes, days, coconuts…), not yet an idea on its own. Some goods may also be counted in natural bunches or pairs (like pairs of shoes or bunches of bananas), so a separate sequence fits each trade. (We still do something similar: a dozen eggs, a pair of socks, a ream of paper.)

Answer: Counting was linked to the type of object and its usual grouping.
2Extend Gumulgal counting in 2s (urapon = 1, ukasar = 2). Evaluate without Hindu numerals: (i) (ukasar ×4 -urapon) + (ukasar ×3 -urapon) (ii) (ukasar ×4 -urapon) − (ukasar ×3) (iii) (ukasar ×4 -urapon) × (ukasar-ukasar) (iv) (ukasar ×8) ÷ (ukasar-ukasar)
Show solution

Methods: + pool all words, and two urapons make an ukasar. − remove matching words (break an ukasar into two urapons if needed). × repeat the first collection once for every 1 in the second. ÷ see how many copies of the second collection can be taken from the first.

(i) 4 ukasar + 3 ukasar = 7 ukasar; urapon + urapon = 1 ukasar → 8 ukasar (= 16).

(ii) Remove 3 ukasar from 4 ukasar-urapon → ukasar-urapon (= 3).

(iii) ukasar-ukasar is 4 ones, so take 4 copies of (4 ukasar + urapon): 16 ukasar + 4 urapon = 16 ukasar + 2 ukasar → 18 ukasar (= 36).

(iv) Take ukasar-ukasar out of 8 ukasar again and again: it fits 4 times → 4 = ukasar-ukasar.

Answer: (i) ukasar ×8 (ii) ukasar-urapon (iii) ukasar ×18 (iv) ukasar-ukasar
3Which features make the Hindu number system more efficient than the Roman one?
Show solution

1. Place value: the same digit means different amounts in different places, so ten symbols are enough for every number. Roman needs new symbols for bigger numbers.

2. Zero as a digit: empty places are shown clearly. Roman has no zero.

3. A base (powers of 10): carrying is always 10 for 1, and products of place values are place values, so + − × ÷ are easy. Roman arithmetic is very hard, especially × and ÷.

4. Numerals are short: 3888 is MMMDCCCLXXXVIII in Roman.

Answer: Place value, zero, a base of 10 and compact numerals.
4Refine the number system you made earlier using these ideas.
Show solution

Model answer: start from the system with • = 1, ▲ = 5, ■ = 25. Make every landmark 5 times the previous one (a base). Then drop the shapes and use positions: write how many ■, ▲, • in places, with a 0 for an empty place — 31 becomes 111, and 50 becomes 200. That is base-5 place value.

Answer: Use a base, then place value, then a zero.

📘 Figure it Out · 3.3 Egyptian numerals page 62
