Check✓ Correct! (−q)² = q², 2 × (−q) × 2 = −4q, 2² = 4.

Check✗ Distributivity is for a bracket with + or −. Inside is a product, so just multiply: 3a × 6bc = 18abc.

Check✓ Correct! Both terms were halved, then −3 + 3 = 0.

Check✗ a²b and ab² are unlike terms. Correct: 5a³ + 6a²b + 6ab².

Check✓ Correct! A neat use of distributing (x + 2) as one block.

Check✗ Only "first × first" and "last × last". Correct: ab + 4a + 2b + 8.

Check✓ Correct! Expand to check: ab × b + ab × a + ab × ab = ab² + a²b + a²b².

🛤️ 6.4 This way or that way, all ways lead to the bay

Look at this pattern of circles. How many circles are in Step k?

There are many ways to see it:

Way of seeing Step kExpressionSimplified
(k + 1) × (k + 1) square, one circle missing(k + 1)² − 1k² + 2k + 1 − 1 = k² + 2k
k × k square + a column of k + a row of kk² + 2 × kk² + 2k
k × (k + 1) rectangle + a row of kk(k + 1) + kk² + k + k = k² + 2k
k rows of (k + 2)k(k + 2)k² + 2k
🎬 One pattern, four ways of counting
💡 Different correct methods always simplify to the same expression. Step 15 has 15² + 2 × 15 = 255 circles.

Square tiles. In this pattern, Step n is an (n + 2) × (n + 2) square with an n × n hole:

Tiles in Step n = (n + 2)² − n² = 4n + 4. Step 1: 8, Step 2: 12, Step 3: 16, Step 4: 20, Step 10: 44. Another way: 4 rows of n tiles along the sides plus 4 corners, 4n + 4 again!

🌍
Real lifeFinding more than one method is how mathematicians check their work. If two honest methods disagree, there is a mistake somewhere!

📐 Areas in more than one way

Four equal rectangles (m by n) around a square. Area of the inner square?

Tadang: big square minus four rectangles = (m + n)² − 4mn.
Yusuf: the inner square has side n − m, so (n − m)².

Check: (m + n)² − 4mn = m² + 2mn + n² − 4mn = m² − 2mn + n² = (n − m)² ✓

Three equal rectangles (x by y) make an I-shape. Area of the hatched region?

Anusha: square x² minus the middle bar xy → x² − xy.
Vaishnavi: whole rectangle x(x + 2y) minus 3 bars → x(x + 2y) − 3xy = x² − xy.
Aditya: two pieces, each x by x − y2 → 2x × x − y2 = x(x − y) = x² − xy.

All three agree. With x = 8, y = 3: 64 − 24 = 40.

The hatched region sits in a rectangle s wide and p tall, with an L-shaped strip of width r.

Way 1: it is a rectangle (s − r) by (p − r): (s − r)(p − r) = ps − pr − rs + r².
Way 2: ps − rs − r(p − r) = ps − rs − pr + r². Same!

With p = 6, r = 3.5, s = 9: 5.5 × 2.5 = 13.75 square units.

💡 One idea runs through the whole chapter: multiply every term by every term. The identities are just short-cuts for special cases, and the area pictures show why they are true.

🧱 How does a product change?

Pick two numbers a and b, and the changes m and n (negative means decrease). Green squares are gained, red squares are lost. Compare the count with mb + an + mn. Can you find changes that leave the product the same?

Type any number and choose ×11, ×101, ×1001, ×99 or ×999. See how splitting the multiplier (distributivity) turns it into one easy addition or subtraction.

1In the 10 × 10 multiplication grid, a 3 × 3 frame has the middle number pq (row p, column q). Write expressions for the other eight numbers in the frame.
3 × 53 × 63 × 7
4 × 54 × 64 × 7
5 × 55 × 65 × 7
Show solution

Moving up a row makes the row number one less (p − 1); down makes it p + 1. Moving left makes the column number q − 1; right makes it q + 1.

(p − 1)(q − 1)(p − 1)q(p − 1)(q + 1)
p(q − 1)pqp(q + 1)
(p + 1)(q − 1)(p + 1)q(p + 1)(q + 1)

Expanded, for example: (p − 1)(q − 1) = pq − p − q + 1 and (p + 1)(q + 1) = pq + p + q + 1.

Answer: the table above
2Expand: (i) (3 + u)(v − 3)  (ii) 23(15 + 6a)  (iii) (10a + b)(10c + d)  (iv) (3 − x)(x − 6)  (v) (−5a + b)(c + d)  (vi) (5 + z)(y + 9)
Show solution

Multiply each term of the first bracket by each term of the second.

  1. 3v − 9 + uv − 3u
  2. 23 × 15 + 23 × 6a = 10 + 4a
  3. 100ac + 10ad + 10bc + bd
  4. 3x − 18 − x² + 6x = −x² + 9x − 18
  5. −5ac − 5ad + bc + bd
  6. 5y + 45 + yz + 9z
Answer: (i) uv + 3v − 3u − 9 (ii) 10 + 4a (iii) 100ac + 10ad + 10bc + bd (iv) −x² + 9x − 18 (v) −5ac − 5ad + bc + bd (vi) yz + 5y + 9z + 45
3Find 3 examples where the product of two numbers does not change when one number is increased by 2 and the other is decreased by 4.
Show solution

Let the numbers be a and b. We want (a + 2)(b − 4) = ab.

(a + 2)(b − 4) = ab − 4a + 2b − 8. For this to equal ab we need −4a + 2b − 8 = 0, that is b = 2a + 4.

a = 1, b = 6: 1 × 6 = 6 and 3 × 2 = 6 ✓ · a = 2, b = 8: 16 and 4 × 4 = 16 ✓ · a = 3, b = 10: 30 and 5 × 6 = 30 ✓

Answer: e.g. 1 × 6, 2 × 8, 3 × 10 (any b = 2a + 4)
4Expand (i) (a + ab − 3b²)(4 + b)  (ii) (4y + 7)(y + 11z − 3).
Show solution

(i) 4(a + ab − 3b²) + b(a + ab − 3b²) = 4a + 4ab − 12b² + ab + ab² − 3b³. Like terms: 4ab + ab = 5ab.

(ii) 4y(y + 11z − 3) + 7(y + 11z − 3) = 4y² + 44yz − 12y + 7y + 77z − 21. Like terms: −12y + 7y = −5y.

Answer: (i) 4a + 5ab + ab² − 12b² − 3b³  (ii) 4y² + 44yz − 5y + 77z − 21
5Expand (i) (a − b)(a + b) (ii) (a − b)(a² + ab + b²) (iii) (a − b)(a³ + a²b + ab² + b³). What pattern do you see? What is the next identity?
Show solution

(i) a² + ab − ba − b² = a² − b².

(ii) a³ + a²b + ab² − a²b − ab² − b³ = a³ − b³ (the middle terms cancel in pairs).

(iii) a⁴ + a³b + a²b² + ab³ − a³b − a²b² − ab³ − b⁴ = a⁴ − b⁴.

Pattern: (a − b) × (all the terms aⁿ⁻¹, aⁿ⁻²b, …, bⁿ⁻¹) = aⁿ − bⁿ. Next: (a − b)(a⁴ + a³b + a²b² + ab³ + b⁴) = a⁵ − b⁵. Expanding shows every middle term appears once with + and once with −.

Answer: a² − b², a³ − b³, a⁴ − b⁴; next a⁵ − b⁵

📘 Figure it Out · 6.2 Special cases of the distributive property page 149

1Which is greater: (a − b)² or (b − a)²? Justify.
Show solution

(a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b² and (b − a)² = b² − 2ba + a². These are the same. Another way: b − a = −(a − b), and a number and its negative have the same square.

Answer: they are always equal
2Express 100 as the difference of two squares.
Show solution

a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b) = 100. Choose two factors of 100 that are both even (so a and b are whole numbers): 50 × 2. Then a + b = 50, a − b = 2, so a = 26, b = 24.

Check: 676 − 576 = 100 ✓. (Also 10 × 10 gives 10² − 0², if 0 is allowed.)

Answer: 100 = 26² − 24²
3Find 406², 72², 145², 1097² and 124² using the identities.
Show solution
  • 406² = (400 + 6)² = 160000 + 4800 + 36 = 164836
  • 72² = (70 + 2)² = 4900 + 280 + 4 = 5184
  • 145² = (140 + 5)² = 19600 + 1400 + 25 = 21025 (or 150 × 140 + 5² by Śrīdharācārya)
  • 1097² = (1100 − 3)² = 1210000 − 6600 + 9 = 1203409
  • 124² = (120 + 4)² = 14400 + 960 + 16 = 15376
Answer: 164836, 5184, 21025, 1203409, 15376
4Do Patterns 1 and 2 hold only for counting numbers? What about negative integers and fractions? Justify.
Show solution

They hold for all these numbers. We proved them using only the distributive property and the sign rules, which are true for integers and fractions too.

Check Pattern 1 with a = −3, b = 2: 2(9 + 4) = 26 and (−1)² + (−5)² = 1 + 25 = 26 ✓. Pattern 2 with a = 12, b = 13: 14 − 19 = 536 and 56 × 16 = 536 ✓.

Answer: yes, they hold for negative integers and fractions as well

📘 Figure it Out · end of chapter pages 154–156

1Compute using the suggested identity: (i) 46² with 1A (ii) 397 × 403 with 1C (iii) 91² with 1B (iv) 43 × 45 with 1C.
Show solution
  1. (40 + 6)² = 1600 + 480 + 36 = 2116
  2. (400 − 3)(400 + 3) = 160000 − 9 = 159991
  3. (100 − 9)² = 10000 − 1800 + 81 = 8281
  4. (44 − 1)(44 + 1) = 1936 − 1 = 1935
Answer: 2116, 159991, 8281, 1935
2Find: (i) (p − 1)(p + 11) (ii) (3a − 9b)(3a + 9b) (iii) −(2y + 5)(3y + 4) (iv) (6x + 5y)² (v) (2x − 12)² (vi) (7p) × (3r) × (p + 2)
Show solution
  1. p² + 11p − p − 11 = p² + 10p − 11
  2. Identity 1C: (3a)² − (9b)² = 9a² − 81b²
  3. (2y + 5)(3y + 4) = 6y² + 8y + 15y + 20 = 6y² + 23y + 20; with the minus sign: −6y² − 23y − 20
  4. Identity 1A: 36x² + 60xy + 25y²
  5. Identity 1B: 4x² − 2 × 2x × 12 + 14 = 4x² − 2x + 14
  6. 7p × 3r = 21pr; 21pr(p + 2) = 21p²r + 42pr
Answer: (i) p² + 10p − 11 (ii) 9a² − 81b² (iii) −6y² − 23y − 20 (iv) 36x² + 60xy + 25y² (v) 4x² − 2x + ¼ (vi) 21p²r + 42pr
3Pick the right expression(s). (i) Two more than a square number: 2 + s, (s + 2)², s² + 2, s² + 4, 2s², 2²s. (ii) The sum of the squares of two consecutive numbers: m² + n², (m + n)², m² + 1, m² + (m + 1)², m² + (m − 1)², (m + (m + 1))², (2m)² + (2m + 1)².
Show solution

(i) A square number is s²; two more is s² + 2.

(ii) Two consecutive numbers are m and m + 1, so m² + (m + 1)². Note that m − 1 and m are also consecutive, so m² + (m − 1)² describes it too. (2m)² + (2m + 1)² only covers pairs starting with an even number, and (m + (m + 1))² squares the sum instead of adding the squares.

Answer: (i) s² + 2  (ii) m² + (m + 1)² (and also m² + (m − 1)²)
4In any 2 × 2 square of dates on a calendar, multiply the numbers on each diagonal (for example 4 × 12 = 48 and 5 × 11 = 55). What do you notice? Explain.
aa + 1
a + 7a + 8
Show solution

Try 10, 11, 17, 18: 10 × 18 = 180 and 11 × 17 = 187. The difference is always 7.

Why: the date below is 7 more. Label the square a, a + 1, a + 7, a + 8. Then (a + 1)(a + 7) − a(a + 8) = a² + 8a + 7 − a² − 8a = 7.

Answer: the two diagonal products always differ by 7
5True or false? (i) (k + 1)(k + 2) − (k + 3) is always 2. (ii) (2q + 1)(2q − 3) is a multiple of 4. (iii) Squares of even numbers are multiples of 4, and squares of odd numbers are 1 more than multiples of 8. (iv) (6n + 2)² − (4n + 3)² is 5 less than a square number.
Show solution
  1. k² + 3k + 2 − k − 3 = k² + 2k − 1. For k = 2 this is 7, not 2. False (it is 2 only when k = 1).
  2. 4q² − 6q + 2q − 3 = 4q² − 4q − 3 = 4(q² − q) − 3. It is odd, so never a multiple of 4. False
  3. (2n)² = 4n², a multiple of 4. (2n + 1)² = 4n² + 4n + 1 = 4n(n + 1) + 1; n(n + 1) is a product of consecutive numbers, so it is even, and 4n(n + 1) is a multiple of 8. True
  4. 36n² + 24n + 4 − (16n² + 24n + 9) = 20n² − 5. This is 5 less than 20n², which is not a square (e.g. n = 1 gives 20). False
Answer: (i) False (ii) False (iii) True (iv) False
6One number leaves remainder 3 when divided by 7; another leaves remainder 5. Find the remainders of their sum, difference and product when divided by 7.
Show solution

Write the numbers as 7a + 3 and 7b + 5.

Sum: 7(a + b) + 8 = 7(a + b + 1) + 1 → remainder 1.

Difference: (7b + 5) − (7a + 3) = 7(b − a) + 2 → remainder 2. (If the first number is the larger one, (7a + 3) − (7b + 5) = 7(a − b − 1) + 5 → remainder 5.)

Product: 49ab + 35a + 21b + 15 = 7(7ab + 5a + 3b + 2) + 1 → remainder 1.

Example: 10 and 12: 22 = 21 + 1, 12 − 10 = 2, 120 = 119 + 1 ✓

Answer: sum 1, difference 2 (or 5 the other way round), product 1
7Take three consecutive numbers. Square the middle one and subtract the product of the other two. What do you notice? Write it in algebra and prove it.
Show solution

5, 6, 7: 36 − 35 = 1. 11, 12, 13: 144 − 143 = 1. Always 1!

Let the numbers be n − 1, n, n + 1. Then n² − (n − 1)(n + 1) = n² − (n² − 1) = 1 (Identity 1C).

Answer: always 1; n² − (n − 1)(n + 1) = 1
8Add two numbers, then multiply the sum by half of the sum. Write this as an expression and show it equals half the square of the sum.
Show solution

Let the numbers be a and b. Sum = a + b; half the sum = a + b2.

(a + b) × a + b2 = (a + b)²2 = 12(a² + 2ab + b²).

Answer: (a + b) × ½(a + b) = ½(a + b)²
9Which is larger, without fully computing? (i) 14 × 26 or 16 × 24 (ii) 25 × 75 or 26 × 74
Show solution

(i) 14 × 26 = (16 − 2)(24 + 2) = 16 × 24 + 32 − 48 − 4 = 16 × 24 − 20. So 16 × 24 is larger (by 20).

(ii) 25 × 75 = (26 − 1)(74 + 1) = 26 × 74 + 26 − 74 − 1 = 26 × 74 − 49. So 26 × 74 is larger (by 49).

Also 1C: 14 × 26 = 20² − 6², 16 × 24 = 20² − 4²; the closer the two numbers, the bigger the product.

Answer: (i) 16 × 24 (ii) 26 × 74
10A tiny park in Dhauli has two square lawns, each of area g² sq. ft. The rest is a path w ft wide (around the lawns, and 2w between them) that must be tiled. Write an expression for the tiled area.
Show solution

Length of the park = w + g + 2w + g + w = 2g + 4w. Breadth = w + g + w = g + 2w.

Area of park = (2g + 4w)(g + 2w) = 2g² + 4gw + 4gw + 8w² = 2g² + 8gw + 8w².

Tiled area = park − two lawns = 2g² + 8gw + 8w² − 2g² = 8gw + 8w².

Answer: 8gw + 8w² = 8w(g + w) sq. ft.
11For each pattern: (i) draw the next figure, (ii) find the number of units in Step 10, (iii) write an expression for Step y.

(a)

(b)

Show solution

(a) Step y is a block of y rows of (y + 2) squares, with an arm of (y + 2) squares going up on the right and another going down on the left. Total = y(y + 2) + 2(y + 2) = (y + 2)(y + 2) = (y + 2)². Steps 1, 2, 3 have 9, 16, 25.

Step 4: 6² = 36. Step 10: 12² = 144.

Note: in the printed figure the arms of Step 3 look one square longer (6 instead of 5). Following the rule of Steps 1 and 2 (and the book's answer), each arm has y + 2 squares.

(b) Step y is a (y + 1) × (y + 1) square with a row of y below it: (y + 1)² + y. Steps 1, 2, 3 have 5, 11, 19.

Step 4: 25 + 4 = 29. Step 10: 11² + 10 = 131.

Answer: (a) 144; (y + 2)²  (b) 131; (y + 1)² + y = y² + 3y + 1

🧩 Puzzle Time · Coin Conjoin page 158

★Turn a triangle of 10 coins upside down by moving one coin at a time. What is the least number of moves? What about 15 coins, and bigger triangles?
Show solution

Keep as many coins as possible in place: the coins of a central "hexagon-like" block stay, and only the corner coins move. For 3 coins: 1 move; 6 coins: 2 moves.

10 coins (rows 1, 2, 3, 4): move the top coin to below the bottom row (under the middle), and move the two end coins of the bottom row up beside row 2. That is 3 moves.

15 coins: 5 moves. 21 coins: 7 moves. In general the minimum is the number of coins divided by 3, ignoring the remainder.

Answer: 10 coins → 3 moves, 15 → 5, 21 → 7; in general ⌊T ÷ 3⌋ moves for T coins

✓ (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b². The two ab rectangles are part of the square. Test: (2 + 3)² = 25, but 4 + 9 = 13.

✂️

✓ The outside number multiplies every term: 2(x − 1) = 2x − 2.

✓ (−b) × (−b) = +b², so (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b².

3 : 2::×½a : bad = bcHCFm : nPart I · Chapter 7

Proportional Reasoning-1

When things grow or shrink by the same factor, they keep their shape and their taste. Ratios help us spot this, and the Rule of Three helps us find a missing quantity.

⚖️

🐯 7.1 Same shape, different size

You resize photos on a phone all the time. Sometimes the picture still looks right, and sometimes the tiger looks stretched or squashed. Why?

ImageWidth (mm)Height (mm)Change from A
A6040—
B4020both − 20 ❌
C3020both × ½ ✅
D9060both × 1½ ✅
E6060width same, height × 1½ ❌

The secret is multiplication, not subtraction. In C, the width became half and the height became half. In D, both became 1½ times. When width and height change by the same factor, the picture keeps its shape. We say the changes are proportional.

In B, both sides lost 20 mm. Same difference, but the height became half (40 → 20) while the width became only 23 (60 → 40). Different factors, so the tiger gets stretched.

🎬 Resize a picture: multiply both sides, or subtract from both?
💡 Same shape ⇔ both measurements are multiplied by the same number.

⚖️ 7.2 Ratios

We write the width-to-height of image A as the ratio 60 : 40 (read "60 is to 40"). The numbers 60 and 40 are the terms of the ratio.

🧠
What a : b means"For every a units of the first quantity, there are b units of the second." In image A: for every 60 mm of width there are 40 mm of height.

Order matters! Width : height = 60 : 40, but height : width = 40 : 60.

Two ratios are proportional when you can get one from the other by multiplying both terms by the same factor:

🎯
Try thisBy what factor do you multiply 60 : 40 to get 90 : 60? (90 ÷ 60 = 1.5 and 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5. Same factor ✓)

✂️ 7.3 Ratios in their simplest form

Finding the factor every time is slow. A neater test: bring each ratio to its simplest form by dividing both terms by their HCF. If the simplest forms match, the ratios are proportional.

  • Image A: 60 : 40. HCF = 20. 60 ÷ 20 : 40 ÷ 20 = 3 : 2
  • Image D: 90 : 60. HCF = 30. → 3 : 2 ✅ same as A
  • Image B: 40 : 20 → 2 : 1 ❌   Image E: 60 : 60 → 1 : 1 ❌
🎬 Cut both terms into equal blocks of the HCF

When two ratios have the same simplest form, we join them with the sign :: ("is proportional to"):

60 : 40 :: 30 : 20
a : b :: c : d

🧠
Why dividing by the HCF worksDividing both terms by the same number is just multiplying both by the same factor (like × 120). So the simplest form is always proportional to the original. It is exactly like simplifying the fraction 6040 to 32.

🍋 7.4 Solving problems with proportional reasoning

Are 3 : 4 and 72 : 96 proportional? HCF of 72 and 96 is 24, so 72 : 96 = 3 : 4. Same simplest form → yes.

Lemonade: Kesang uses 10 spoons of sugar for 6 glasses. To make 18 glasses just as sweet, how much sugar?

The first term grew from 6 to 18: the factor of change is 18 ÷ 6 = 3. The second term must change by the same factor: 10 × 3 = 30 spoons. So 6 : 10 :: 18 : 30.

Compound wall: Nitin built 60 ft with 3 bags of cement; Hari built 40 ft with 2 bags. Is Hari's wall weaker? Compare length : bags. 60 : 3 = 20 : 1 and 40 : 2 = 20 : 1. Same! Both walls got the same cement per foot, so they are equally strong 💪.

🌍
Real lifeCount the teachers and students in your school and write teachers : students. Is it proportional to 5 : 170 (= 1 : 34)? Measure your classroom blackboard and draw a small rectangle in the same width : height ratio.

🎂 Adding the same number breaks the ratio

Neelima is 3 and her mother is 10 times older: 30. Ages ratio = 3 : 30 = 1 : 10.

9 years later, Neelima is 12 and her mother is 39. Ratio = 12 : 39 = 4 : 13. Not 1 : 10 any more!

💡 Multiplying (or dividing) both terms by the same number keeps a ratio proportional. Adding (or subtracting) the same number usually does not.

🔢 Filling in missing terms

Find ratios proportional to 14 : 21:

  • __ : 42   42 = 21 × 2, so the first term is 14 × 2 = 28 → 28 : 42
  • 6 : __   What turns 14 into 6? The factor y with 14 × y = 6, so y = 614 = 37. Then 21 × 37 = 9 → 6 : 9
  • 2 : __   14 ÷ 7 = 2 (7 is the HCF), and 21 ÷ 7 = 3 → 2 : 3
🧠
The factor can be a fractionThe factor of change does not have to be a whole number. Shrinking is multiplying by a fraction smaller than 1.

☕ Filter coffee: stronger or lighter?

Manjunath's regular cup: 15 mL decoction with 35 mL milk (15 : 35 = 3 : 7). Every cup holds 50 mL.

The strong cup has more decoction for every mL of milk: 20 : 30 = 2 : 3, while regular is 3 : 7. A neat way to compare: what fraction of the cup is decoction? Regular 1550 = 30%, strong 40%, light 20%.

DecoctionMilkSimplestDecoction shareCoffee
3006001 : 2300/900 ≈ 33%Strong
1505003 : 10150/650 ≈ 23%Light
2004001 : 2≈ 33%Strong
24563 : 724/80 = 30%Regular
1003001 : 3100/400 = 25%Light
🎯
Try thisTo compare 1 : 2 with 3 : 7, write them as fractions of decoction per milk: 12 = 0.5 and 37 ≈ 0.43. Bigger means stronger.

🔺 Trairāśika: the Rule of Three

Mid-day meal: 15 kg of rice feeds 120 students. Only 80 come on a rainy day. How much rice?

120 : 15 :: 80 : ?   Factor of change = 80120 = 23. Rice = 15 × 23 = 10 kg.

Here four quantities are linked; three are known and we want the fourth. Let us find a rule that always works. If a : b :: c : d, then c and d come from a and b by the same factor f:

c = f × a and d = f × b  ⇒  f = ca = db

Multiply both sides by ab and the denominators cancel: a × d = b × c. This is cross multiplication. So the missing term is d = b × ca.

🎬 Cross-multiply to find the missing term
🤩
Did you know?Āryabhaṭa (born 476 CE) and other Indian mathematicians called these Rule of Three problems. The three known numbers were the pramāṇa (measure, our a), the phala (fruit, b) and the ichchhā (requisition, c). The answer, ichchhāphala (d), is found by "multiplying the phala by the ichchhā and dividing by the pramāṇa": d = b × ca.

📏 Same units first! (and when the Rule of Three fails)

Car: 90 km in 150 minutes. How far in 4 hours? Writing 150 : 90 :: 4 : ? mixes minutes with hours ❌. Change 4 hours to 240 minutes:

150 : 90 :: 240 : x ⇒ 150 × x = 240 × 90 ⇒ x = 21600150 = 144 km

Another way: 150 min → 90 km, so 30 min → 18 km (÷ 5), and 240 min = 8 × 30 min → 8 × 18 = 144 km. Many roads, same answer!

Tea: Himachal: 200 g for ₹200. Meghalaya: 1 kg for ₹800. Write the Meghalaya weight in grams too: 1000 : 800 = 5 : 4, while Himachal is 200 : 200 = 1 : 1. Not proportional. Which is costlier? Compare the price of the same weight: 1 kg = 5 × 200 g, so Himachal tea costs 5 × ₹200 = ₹1,000 per kg vs ₹800. Himachal tea is more expensive.

🧠
Not everything is proportional!Puneeth's father rides from Lucknow to Kanpur in 2 h at 50 km/h. At 75 km/h, does the time go up like the speed? No! Going faster means less time. So 50 : 2 :: 75 : ? is the wrong model. (Distance = 100 km, so it takes 100 ÷ 75 = 1⅓ h.)
🌍
Real life: shampooSachet 6 mL for ₹2, bottle 180 mL for ₹154. Volumes 6 : 180 = 1 : 30 but prices 2 : 154 = 1 : 77. Not proportional! Prices depend on packing, transport and offers. Check rice or atta packs in a shop near you.

🪙 7.5 Sharing, but not equally!

Share 12 counters with a friend. Equal shares give 6 : 6 = 1 : 1. If your partner gets 5, you get 7: ratio 5 : 7.

Share 12 in the ratio 3 : 1: deal in rounds. Each round, your partner takes 3 and you take 1 (4 counters per round). After 3 rounds all 12 are gone: 9 and 3.

🎬 Deal the counters round by round, then in groups

Share 42 in the ratio 4 : 3: that is 4 + 3 = 7 groups. Each group has 42 ÷ 7 = 6. Partner: 4 × 6 = 24, you: 3 × 6 = 18. Check: 24 + 18 = 42 and 24 : 18 = 4 : 3 ✓

💡 To divide x in the ratio m : n: there are m + n groups, each of size xm + n. The parts are m × xm + n and n × xm + n.

🛒 Sharing profit and fixing a mixture

Food cart: Prashanti puts in ₹75,000 and Bhuvan ₹25,000. They share a profit of ₹4,000 in the ratio of their money.

  1. 75000 : 25000 = 3 : 1 (HCF 25000)
  2. 3 + 1 = 4 groups; ₹4,000 ÷ 4 = ₹1,000 per group
  3. Prashanti ₹3,000, Bhuvan ₹1,000 ✓

Sand and cement: 40 kg of mix has sand : cement = 3 : 1. How much cement must be added to make it 5 : 2?

  1. Sand = 34 × 40 = 30 kg, cement = 14 × 40 = 10 kg.
  2. Sand does not change. New ratio 5 : 2 :: 30 : ?. Cement is 25 of sand: 25 × 30 = 12 kg.
  3. Add 12 − 10 = 2 kg of cement.
🧠
Find what stays fixedWhen something is added to a mixture, the other ingredient stays the same. Start from it.

🔄 7.6 Unit conversions

Proportion problems often need the units to match. Keep this table handy:

MeasureConversion
Length1 metre = 3.281 feet
Area1 square metre = 10.764 square feet
1 acre = 43,560 square feet
1 hectare = 10,000 square metres = 2.471 acres
Volume1 mL = 1 cubic centimetre (cc)
1 litre = 1,000 mL = 1,000 cc
Temperature°F = 95 × °C + 32    °C = 59 × (°F − 32)

Example: 25 °C = 95 × 25 + 32 = 45 + 32 = 77 °F.

🧠
Temperature is specialLength, area and volume conversions are proportional (double the metres, double the feet). Temperature is not: 0 °C is 32 °F, not 0 °F, because of that "+ 32".
🌍
Real lifeLand in India is often sold in acres or square feet. 2,400 sq ft is about 240043560 ≈ 0.055 acre.

🖼️ Picture resizer

Change the width and height of image A (60 mm × 40 mm). Try "multiply both" and "add to both". Watch the simplest-form ratio: the tiger keeps its shape only when it stays 3 : 2.

🔺 Rule of Three machine

Type three numbers of a proportion a : b :: c : ? and see the factor of change and the cross multiplication that gives the fourth.

🪙 Counter sharer

Pick a total and a ratio m : n. The counters are dealt in groups of m + n. If the total is not a multiple of m + n, see what is left over.

📘 Figure it Out · 7.4 Ratios and proportion pages 165–167

1Which statements of proportion are true? (i) 4 : 7 :: 12 : 21  (ii) 8 : 3 :: 24 : 6  (iii) 7 : 12 :: 12 : 7  (iv) 21 : 6 :: 35 : 10  (v) 12 : 18 :: 28 : 12  (vi) 24 : 8 :: 9 : 3
Show solution

Reduce both sides to simplest form (or cross-multiply: a × d must equal b × c).

  • (i) 12 : 21 = 4 : 7 ✓ (4 × 21 = 84 = 7 × 12)
  • (ii) 24 : 6 = 4 : 1, but 8 : 3 is already simplest ✗
  • (iii) 7 : 12 and 12 : 7 are different (order matters) ✗
  • (iv) 21 : 6 = 7 : 2 and 35 : 10 = 7 : 2 ✓
  • (v) 12 : 18 = 2 : 3 but 28 : 12 = 7 : 3 ✗
  • (vi) 24 : 8 = 3 : 1 and 9 : 3 = 3 : 1 ✓
Answer: (i), (iv) and (vi) are true
2Give 3 ratios proportional to 4 : 9.
Show solution

Multiply both terms by the same number: × 2, × 3, × 4.

Answer: 8 : 18, 12 : 27, 16 : 36 (many more are possible)
3Fill in the missing terms so that each ratio is proportional to 18 : 24:  3 : __,  12 : __,  20 : __,  27 : __
Show solution

First simplify: HCF of 18 and 24 is 6, so 18 : 24 = 3 : 4. The second term is always 43 of the first.

  • 3 : 4
  • 12 × 43 = 16 → 12 : 16
  • 20 × 43 = 803 = 26⅔ → 20 : 803 (a fraction is fine!)
  • 27 × 43 = 36 → 27 : 36
Answer: 4, 16, 80/3 (= 26⅔), 36
4Five rectangles A–E are drawn (some tilted). Which are similar to each other? Measure width and height and compare ratios.
Show solution

Measuring the book's figure with a ruler (long side : short side), we get roughly:

  • A ≈ 3 : 1  (tall and thin)
  • B ≈ 3 : 2
  • C ≈ 5 : 2
  • D ≈ 3 : 1
  • E ≈ 5 : 2

Turning a rectangle does not change its shape, so only the ratio matters. Your measurements may differ by a millimetre, so the simplest forms will be close, not exact.

Answer: A and D are similar (≈ 3 : 1); C and E are similar (≈ 5 : 2); B (≈ 3 : 2) matches none
5Draw a smaller and a bigger rectangle with the same width : height ratio as the given rectangle (about 3 cm by 2 cm). Are all classmates' drawings the same?
Show solution

Measure the rectangle: it is about 3 : 2. Multiply both sides by the same factor: × ½ gives 1.5 cm × 1 cm; × 2 gives 6 cm × 4 cm.

Classmates may draw different sizes (2 × 3 = 6 cm × 4 cm, or 4.5 cm × 3 cm, …). They are all correct if width : height is still 3 : 2. They have the same shape but different sizes. A drawing is wrong only if the ratio changed (for example, adding 2 cm to both sides).

Answer: e.g. 1.5 cm × 1 cm and 6 cm × 4 cm; sizes differ, shape is the same
6Brick wall patterns repeat along the wall. Find the ratio grey bricks : coloured bricks in simplest form for walls (a) and (b).
Show solution

Because the pattern repeats, count bricks in one repeating block; the whole wall has the same ratio.

(a) In one block the three rows have 2, 3, 4 grey bricks and 3, 2, 1 coloured bricks. Grey = 9, coloured = 6. 9 : 6 = 3 : 2.

(b) One block has 28 bricks: 16 grey and 12 coloured. 16 : 12 = 4 : 3 (HCF 4).

Answer: (a) 3 : 2   (b) 4 : 3
7Measure a friend's head, torso, arms and legs. Write head : torso, torso : arms, torso : legs, then draw a figure using the same ratios. Does it look more realistic?
Show solution

This is a measuring activity, so answers vary. Sample measurements: head 22 cm, torso 55 cm, arms 66 cm, legs 88 cm. Ratios: head : torso = 22 : 55 = 2 : 5; torso : arms = 55 : 66 = 5 : 6; torso : legs = 55 : 88 = 5 : 8.

To draw, pick a scale, e.g. torso = 5 cm. Then head = 2 cm, arms = 6 cm, legs = 8 cm. The drawing looks realistic because every part is the real length multiplied by the same factor. If you made the head as long as the torso, it would look like a cartoon!

Answer: depends on your measurements; keep all the ratios when drawing

📘 Figure it Out · Rule of Three pages 170–171

1The Earth travels about 940 million km around the Sun in a year. How far does it travel in a week?
Show solution

A year has 52 weeks (and 1 day). Distance : time is proportional, so 940,000,000 : 52 :: x : 1.

x = 940,000,000 ÷ 52 ≈ 18,076,923 km.

(If you use 365 days: 940,000,000 × 7 ÷ 365 ≈ 18,027,397 km. Both are about 18 million km.)

Answer: about 18,076,923 km (≈ 18 million km) per week
2A house has the plan shown (all walls the same height and thickness). A 10-ft wall needs about 1450 bricks. How many bricks for all the outer walls and the inner wall?
Show solution

Add up the lengths of all walls:

  • Left room (9 ft × 12 ft): left wall 12, top 9, bottom 9
  • Inner wall: 12
  • Right room (15 ft × 12 ft): top 15, right 12, bottom 15
  • Small room below: two sides 9 + 9, bottom 6

Total = 12 + 9 + 9 + 12 + 15 + 12 + 15 + 9 + 9 + 6 = 108 ft.

Rule of Three: 10 : 1450 :: 108 : x ⇒ x = 1450 × 10810 = 15,660.

Answer: about 15,660 bricks

📘 Figure it Out · 7.5 Dividing in a ratio page 175

1Divide ₹4,500 into two parts in the ratio 2 : 3.
Show solution

2 + 3 = 5 groups. Each group = 4500 ÷ 5 = ₹900. Parts: 2 × 900 = ₹1,800 and 3 × 900 = ₹2,700.

Answer: ₹1,800 and ₹2,700
2Acid : water = 1 : 5. How much acid and water are in 240 mL of the solution?
Show solution

1 + 5 = 6 groups of 240 ÷ 6 = 40 mL. Acid = 1 × 40 = 40 mL, water = 5 × 40 = 200 mL.

Answer: 40 mL acid, 200 mL water
3Blue : yellow = 3 : 5 makes green. How much of each for 40 mL of green? Then 20 mL of yellow is added. What is the new ratio?
Show solution

3 + 5 = 8 groups of 40 ÷ 8 = 5 mL. Blue = 15 mL, yellow = 25 mL.

After adding 20 mL yellow: yellow = 45 mL, blue still 15 mL. 15 : 45 = 1 : 3 (HCF 15).

Answer: 15 mL blue, 25 mL yellow; new ratio 1 : 3
4Rice : urad dal = 2 : 1 for soft idlis. How many cups of each for 6 cups of mixture?
Show solution

2 + 1 = 3 groups of 6 ÷ 3 = 2 cups. Rice = 2 × 2 = 4 cups, urad dal = 1 × 2 = 2 cups.

Answer: 4 cups rice, 2 cups urad dal
5A bucket of orange paint is red : yellow = 3 : 5. A whole bucket of yellow is added. New ratio of red to yellow?
Show solution

Think of a bucket as 8 equal parts: 3 parts red and 5 parts yellow. The new bucket of yellow is another 8 parts.

Red = 3 parts, yellow = 5 + 8 = 13 parts. (Same as 38 : 138 of a bucket.)

Answer: 3 : 13

📘 Figure it Out · End of chapter pages 176–177

1Anagh mixes 600 mL orange juice with 900 mL apple juice. Ratio orange : apple in simplest form?
Show solution

HCF of 600 and 900 is 300. 600 ÷ 300 : 900 ÷ 300 = 2 : 3.

Answer: 2 : 3
2Last year 3 full buses carried 162 people. This year 204 are going. How many buses? Will all be full?
Show solution

One bus holds 162 ÷ 3 = 54 people. 3 : 162 :: x : 204 gives x = 3 × 204162 = 349 ≈ 3.78 buses.

We can't hire part of a bus, so we need 4 buses. They have 4 × 54 = 216 seats, so 216 − 204 = 12 seats stay empty. Not all buses will be full.

Answer: 4 buses; 12 seats will be empty
3Delhi: area 1,484 sq km, population about 30 million. Mumbai: area 550 sq km, population about 20 million. Which city is more crowded?
Show solution

Compare people per sq km (same area for both):

  • Delhi: 30,000,000 ÷ 1484 ≈ 20,216 people per sq km
  • Mumbai: 20,000,000 ÷ 550 ≈ 36,364 people per sq km

Delhi has more people in total, but Mumbai squeezes them into a much smaller area.

Answer: Mumbai is more crowded (≈ 36,364 vs ≈ 20,216 people per sq km)
4A crane 155 cm tall has neck : rest of body = 4 : 6. If your body had the same ratio, how long would your neck be?
Show solution

4 + 6 = 10 parts, and the neck is 4 parts, i.e. 410 = 25 of the height. (For the crane: 25 × 155 = 62 cm.)

For you: neck = 25 × your height. If you are 150 cm tall, your neck would be 60 cm! 🦒

Answer: neck = 2/5 of your height (e.g. 60 cm for a 150 cm student)
5From Līlāvatī: 2½ palas of saffron cost 37 niṣka. How much saffron can be bought for 9 niṣkas?
Show solution

Money : saffron is proportional: 37 : 2½ :: 9 : x.

Cross multiply: 37 × x = 2½ × 9 = 22½. So x = 22½ × 73 = 22.5 × 7 ÷ 3 = 52.5.

(Āryabhaṭa's way: phala × ichchhā ÷ pramāṇa = 2½ × 9 ÷ 37.)

Answer: 52½ palas
6Harmain is 1 year old and her brother is 5. How old will Harmain be when their ages are in the ratio 1 : 2?
Show solution

The age difference is always 4 years. In the ratio 1 : 2, the brother is twice Harmain's age, so the difference equals Harmain's age. Hence Harmain = 4.

Check with algebra: after x years, (1 + x) : (5 + x) = 1 : 2 ⇒ 2(1 + x) = 5 + x ⇒ x = 3. Harmain is 1 + 3 = 4, brother is 8. 4 : 8 = 1 : 2 ✓

Answer: 4 years (after 3 years)
7Equal volumes of gold and water have masses in the ratio 37 : 2. 1 litre of water has mass 1 kg. Mass of 1 litre of gold?
Show solution

37 : 2 :: x : 1 ⇒ 2x = 37 ⇒ x = 18.5.

Answer: 18.5 kg
810 tonnes of cow manure is good for 1 acre. How much for a plot of 200 ft × 500 ft? (1 acre = 43,560 sq ft)
Show solution

Plot area = 200 × 500 = 1,00,000 sq ft. Manure : area: 10 : 43560 :: x : 100000.

x = 10 × 10000043560 ≈ 22.96 tonnes.

Answer: about 22.96 tonnes (≈ 22,957 kg)
9A tap fills a 500 mL mug in 15 seconds. How long for a 10-litre bucket?
Show solution

10 L = 10,000 mL = 20 mugs. 500 : 15 :: 10000 : t ⇒ t = 15 × 10000 ÷ 500 = 300 s.

Answer: 300 seconds = 5 minutes
10One acre of land costs ₹15,00,000. What do 2,400 sq ft of the same land cost?
Show solution

1 acre = 43,560 sq ft. 43560 : 1500000 :: 2400 : x ⇒ x = 1500000 × 240043560 ≈ 82,644.6.

Answer: about ₹82,645
11A tractor ploughs 4 times faster than a pair of oxen. Oxen take 6 hours per acre. How long for a 20-acre field with oxen? With a tractor?
Show solution

Oxen: 1 acre → 6 h, so 20 acres → 20 × 6 = 120 hours.

Tractor is 4 times faster, so it takes a quarter of the time: 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 h per acre, 20 × 1.5 = 30 hours.

Answer: oxen 120 hours; tractor 30 hours
12A ₹10 coin (7.74 g) is copper : nickel = 3 : 1. Copper costs ₹906 per kg and nickel ₹1,341 per kg. Cost of the metals in one coin?
Show solution

Copper = 34 × 7.74 = 5.805 g; nickel = 14 × 7.74 = 1.935 g.

₹906 per 1000 g ⇒ copper costs 906 × 5.805 ÷ 1000 ≈ ₹5.26. Nickel: 1341 × 1.935 ÷ 1000 ≈ ₹2.59.

Total ≈ 5.26 + 2.59 = ₹7.85.

Answer: about ₹7.85 (copper ₹5.26 + nickel ₹2.59)

✗ "Image B is just A with 20 mm cut from both sides, so it must look the same."

✓ Shape is kept only when both sides are multiplied by the same factor. Same difference ≠ same ratio.

🔀

✗ 7 : 12 is the same as 12 : 7.

✓ Order matters. "For every 7 there are 12" is different from "for every 12 there are 7".

🎂

✗ Mother : daughter = 30 : 3 now, so in 9 years it will still be 10 : 1.

✓ Adding 9 to both gives 39 : 12 = 13 : 4. Adding the same number changes the ratio.

⏱️

✗ 150 min : 90 km :: 4 h : ?

✓ Use the same units on both sides: 4 h = 240 min. Then 150 : 90 :: 240 : 144.

🏍️

✗ 50 km/h takes 2 h, so 75 km/h takes 3 h (Rule of Three).

✓ Faster means less time. Speed and time for a fixed trip are not in a ratio that grows together; it takes 100 ÷ 75 = 1⅓ h.

🪙

✗ Share ₹4,500 in 2 : 3 → ₹2 and ₹3 … or ₹4,500 ÷ 2 and ₹4,500 ÷ 3.

✓ Count groups first: 2 + 3 = 5 groups of ₹900. Parts ₹1,800 and ₹2,700.

🎨

✗ 15 mL blue + 25 mL yellow, add 20 mL yellow → new ratio (3 : 5) + 20.

✓ Work with actual amounts: blue 15, yellow 45. 15 : 45 = 1 : 3.

🌡️

✗ 20 °C is double 10 °C, so in °F it is also double.

✓ °F = 9/5 × °C + 32. 10 °C = 50 °F, 20 °C = 68 °F. The "+ 32" makes temperature not proportional.

%¾₹×1.1120%GST−5%Part II · Chapter 1

Fractions in Disguise

A percentage is just a fraction wearing an "out of 100" costume. Once you see through the disguise, sales, marks, profits, taxes and growing money all become easy to compare.

💯

💯 Per cent means "by the hundred"

The sign % is read per cent, from the Latin per centum: "by the hundred" or "out of 100". So 25% means 25 out of every 100: 25 people out of 100, ₹25 out of ₹100, 25 marks out of 100.

A percentage is a fraction whose denominator is 100:

z% = z100  ·  20% = 20100 = 15  ·  50% of s = 50100 × s = 12 s

Fraction → percentage. Surya mixes paint for a sunset: red makes up 34 of the mixture. What percentage is red? We want an equal fraction "out of 100":

Method 1: equivalent fraction

34 = 3 × 254 × 25 = 75100 = 75%

Method 2: solve for x

34 = x100 → x = 34 × 100 = 75
🎬 Cut the whole into 100 parts and count

Surya saves 25 of his prize money for a canvas: 25 = 40100 = 40%. Or think of a bar from 0% to 100% cut into 5 equal parts: each part is 20%, so two parts are 40%. Isn't that just 25 of 100?

💡 A fraction is "of one whole"; a percentage is "per 100". To turn a fraction into a percentage, multiply it by 100.

Percentage → fraction. 24% = 24100 = 1250 = 625 = 48200. Any fraction equal to z100 can stand for z%.

🎯
Try thisWhat percentage of Surya's paint is yellow? The rest: 1 − 34 = 14 = 25%. (75% + 25% = 100%, the whole mixture.)

🤔 Why bother with 100?

A biscuit factory tests two recipes. Sugar is 934 of Variety 1 and 1345 of Variety 2. Which is sweeter? Hard to tell at a glance! Now say it as 26.47% and 28.89%: Variety 2 is clearly sweeter. Percentages put every fraction over the same denominator, so comparing is instant.

Why 100 and not 10, 50 or 43? Our number system is base 10, so 100 fits neatly with decimals (31% = 31100 = 0.31). Also 100 is big enough to show detail but small enough to picture easily.

934 written…value
per 10 (per decem)2.647
per 100 (per cent)26.47
per 1000 (per mille)264.7

"Per thousand" and "per lakh" are used in statistics (for example, births per thousand people), but "per hundred" is the everyday favourite.

🤩
Did you know?The idea of "per hundred" is very old. Kautilya's Arthaśāstra (around the 4th century BCE) fixed fair interest rates "per month per cent": about 1¼ paṇas for ordinary loans, 5 for trade, 10 for forest routes and 20 for sea traders! Around the same time the Romans taxed trade at 120 and 1100, and 15th-century Italian merchants wrote "xx p cento" for 20%.

Percentages around us:

≈ 60%of the human body is water (by weight)
30–50%of ice cream is air (by volume)
≈ 99.86%of the Solar System's mass is in the Sun
45%of the world watched part of the 2022 FIFA World Cup

🍪 Percentage of some quantity

Madhu's biscuits have 25% sugar; Madhav's have 35%. Who ate more sugar? We cannot tell from the percentages alone, because they are fractions of different amounts. Madhu ate 120 g and Madhav ate 95 g.

Madhu: 25% sugar means 25 g of sugar in every 100 g, so 25 : 100 :: s : 120. Three ways:

  • 25 g per 100 g → 5 g per 20 g → 30 g per 120 g.
  • Proportion: 25100 = s120 → s = 25100 × 120 = 30 g.
  • Double number line: 25% ↔ 30 g, 50% ↔ 60 g, 100% ↔ 120 g.

Madhav: 100 g has 35 g of sugar, so 1 g has 35100 g, and 95 g has 35100 × 95 = 33.25 g. Madhav ate more sugar 🍬 even though he ate fewer biscuits.

🎬 Walk along a double number line
💡 y% of a value z = y100 × z.   For example, 45% of z = 45100 × z.

🧠 Free-hand computations and the FDP trio

25% is a quarter (25100 = 14), so 25% of 40 = 14 × 40 = 10. Build every other percentage from a few easy blocks:

  • 10%: divide by 10.   1%: divide by 100.
  • 5% = half of 10%.   20% = double 10%.   25% = a quarter.
  • Add blocks: 20% + 5% = 25%, 10% + 5% = 15%, 4 × 10% = 40%.
of →10020050801035287
25%255012.5202.58.7571.75
10%10205813.528.7
20%204010162757.4
5%5102.540.51.7514.35

15%15307.5121.55.2543.05

Notice: 20% is always double 10%, and (20% of y) + (5% of y) = 25% of y, because 20100y + 5100y = 25100y.

🧠
Memory trick75% = 3 quarters, or 100% − 25%.   90% = 100% − 10%.   70% = 7 × 10%.   55% = 50% + 5%.

The FDP trio: Fractions, Decimals, Percentages. 50% = 50100 = 12 = 0.5, so "× 0.5" also gives 50%. To find 10%, multiply by 0.1.

Per cent50%100%25%75%10%1%5%43%

Zubin's A grade: a test is out of 75, and 80% or more gets an A. Fraction: 80100 × 75 = 45 × 75 = 60. Decimal: 0.8 × 75 = 60. Proportion: 80 out of 100 is the same as 60 out of 75. He needs at least 60 marks.

🎯

🥣 Ratios as percentages, and finding the rest

Millet kanji: millet and water are mixed in the ratio 2 : 7. The whole mixture has 2 + 7 = 9 parts, so millet is 29 of it.

Estimate first: half of 9 is 4.5, so 29 is less than 50%; half of 4.5 is 2.25, so it is less than 25%; 20% of 9 is 1.8, so it is more than 20%. Somewhere between 20% and 25%.

Exactly: 29 × 100 = 22.22% millet, and water = 100 − 22.22 = 77.78%. For 500 ml of kanji: 5 × 22.22 ≈ 111.1 ml of millet (exactly 29 × 500 = 111.11 ml).

💡 Ratio → fraction of the whole → percentage. Always estimate first; it catches silly slips.

A cyclist from Delhi to Agra has finished 40% of the trip, which is 92 km. How much is left?

Build up

40% = 92 km, so 20% = 46 km. The rest is 60% = 92 + 46 = 138 km.

Proportion

40 : 92 :: 60 : r → r = 60 × 9240 = 138 km.

Whole first

40100 = 92d → d = 230 km. Left: 230 − 92 = 138 km.
🌍
Real lifeA rough bar diagram, like the one above, often shows you the method straight away.

🚀 Percentages greater than 100

Kishanlal's target is daily sales of ₹5,000. Each day's sales as a percentage of the target is sales5000 × 100.

🎬 Fill the target bar, and keep going past 100%

Day 4: ₹6,000 is ₹1,000 more than the target, and 1000 is 20% of 5000. So it is 100% + 20% = 120%, i.e. 1.2 times the target. Day 7 at 150% means sales of 1.5 × 5000 = ₹7,500; Day 8 at 210% means 2.1 × 5000 = ₹10,500.

Per cent90%110%200%250%15%173%358%28.9%305%
Fraction91011102523201731001795028910006120
Decimal0.91.122.50.151.733.580.2893.05

Wheat harvest: 260 kg last year, 650 kg this year. 650260 × 100 = 250% of last year's harvest: 2.5 times as much.

💡 100% is the whole (the base). 200% is twice the base; 50% is half of it. "He achieved 12 of his target", "50% of his target" and "0.5 of his target" all say the same thing.

⚖️ Comparing proportions — and Know Your Contents

Eesha scored 42/50 in English and 70/80 in Science. She lost fewer marks in English; Reema says she scored more in Science; Vishu says you cannot compare. Convert both to "out of 100":

English: 4250 × 100 = 84%  ·  Science: 7080 × 100 = 87.5%

She did better in Science. Percentages make wholes of different sizes comparable.

KYC (Know Your Contents). Madhu and Madhav read two badam drink-mix labels. DEF (150 g): sugar 99 g, milk solids 30 g, badam powder 12 g, food chemicals 9 g. Zacni (400 g): sugar 272 g, milk solids 64 g, badam powder 40 g, food chemicals 24 g. Divide each by the pack weight and multiply by 100:

SugarMilk solidsBadam powderFood chemicalsTotal
DEF66%20%8%6%100%
Zacni68%16%10%6%100%

Zacni has the larger share of badam (10% vs 8%). Both use the same proportion of food chemicals (6%). And both are about two-thirds sugar — maybe they should be called "sugar drink mix" 😄. Each row adds up to 100%, a good check.

🌍
Real lifeDo KYC! Read the percentages on food labels before you buy processed food.

📈 Percentage increase or decrease

Percentages describe how fast something changes. The change is always compared with the original amount (the base):

Percentage change = amount of increase or decreaseoriginal amount (base) × 100

  • Tomatoes: ₹30 per kg three years ago, ₹42 now. Increase ₹12. 1230 × 100 = 40% increase.
  • Theatre footfall: 160 before COVID, 100 now. Decrease 60. 60160 × 100 = 37.5% decrease.

Same meaning, two ways: "The 1991 population is 165% of the 1961 population" and "The population increased by 65% from 1961 to 1991" say the same thing. If p is the 1961 population and q the 1991 one: q = 1.65p in both cases (q = p + 0.65p).

💡 Increase by r% → multiply by (1 + r). Decrease by r% → multiply by (1 − r). Here r is written as a decimal: 65% → 0.65.

🧥 Profit, loss and discounts

  • Cost price (CP): what the seller paid to buy the item.
  • Marked price (MP): the price the seller quotes (sometimes the MRP).
  • Selling price (SP): what the customer actually pays, after bargaining or discount.

These labels depend on who you are in the chain. Follow one sweater:

🏭 ManufacturerCP ₹230 · MP ₹255 · SP ₹253
→
📦 WholesalerCP ₹253 · MP ₹310 · SP ₹300
→
🏬 Retailer (Kishanlal)CP ₹300 · MP ₹480 · SP ₹430
→
🛍️ Customerpays ₹430

SP > CP → profit; SP < CP → loss. To get a percentage we take the cost price as 100%: Kishanlal's profit is ₹430 − ₹300 = ₹130, and 130300 × 100 ≈ 43.3%. (The manufacturer makes 23230 = 10%; the wholesaler 47253 ≈ 18.58%.)

Margin → selling price

Shambhavi buys notebooks at ₹36 and wants a 20% margin: SP = 120% of 36 = 1.2 × 36 = ₹43.20.

Selling price → cost

She sells crayons at ₹50 with a 25% margin: 125% of CP = 50, so CP = 50 ÷ 1.25 = ₹40.

Loss %

Raghu bought 10 kg rice at ₹35/kg (₹350) and sold it for ₹300. Loss ₹50; 50350 × 100 ≈ 14.29%. Per kg (₹35 vs ₹30) gives the same 535.

Selling at a loss

Shyamala's vase cost ₹2,650; sold at 18% loss. SP = 82% of 2650 = 0.82 × 2650 = ₹2,173 (or 2650 − 477).

Discounts. "30% off" means the shop cuts the marked price by 30%. A cooker with MRP ₹1,800 at 35% off sells for 65% of 1800 = ₹1,170. If it cost the shop ₹900, the profit is ₹270, which is 270900 = 30% of the cost.

🎯
Try thisSnehal sold strawberries at ₹80 per kg at a 12% loss. 88% of CP = 80, so CP = 80 ÷ 0.88 ≈ ₹90.91 per kg.

🧾 Gross profit, net profit, profit on revenue — and taxes

Last month Kishanlal's sales were ₹80,000 and the goods he sold had cost him ₹48,000. Gross profit = ₹32,000. After other expenses (transport, salary, electricity) of ₹8,000, the net profit is ₹24,000. In this chapter "profit" means gross profit unless the question says otherwise.

Percentage of what? Manisha buys a fertiliser bag for ₹500 and sells it for ₹750. Profit ₹250.

🎬 One profit, two bases

Base = cost (investment)

250500 × 100 = 50%. Answers: "How much profit did I make compared with what I spent buying the goods?"

Base = revenue (sales)

250750 × 100 = 33.33%. Answers: "How much of my overall sales money is (net) profit?"

The book uses both, depending on the question. Businesses often quote their profit margin on revenue. Example: in a month Manisha's sales were ₹1,50,000, the goods cost ₹1,00,000 (gross profit ₹50,000) and expenses were ₹5,000. Net profit = ₹45,000, so the net profit percentage on revenue = 45000150000 × 100 = 30%.

🧠
Memory trickRead the question for the base. "Margin with respect to the cost" → divide by CP. "Profit margin" of a company's total sales (revenue) → divide by the revenue. Same profit, bigger base, smaller percentage.

Taxes. GST (Goods and Services Tax) and income tax rates are percentages. GST is added to the bill and goes to the government. On a bill it is often split into CGST (Centre) and SGST (State), each half of the rate.

3 × CFL bulb @ ₹150 ₹450.00
CGST 9% ₹40.50
SGST 9% ₹40.50
Total ₹531.00

Check: 9% of 450 = 40.50, twice that is ₹81 = 18% of 450, and 450 + 81 = 531 ✅ (or 450 × 1.18 = 531).

🏦 Growth, compounding — and decline

Banks pay interest on money kept with them; borrowers pay interest on loans. "10% p.a." means 10% per annum (every year). On a principal of ₹6,000 the interest for one year is 10% of 6000 = ₹600, so the amount becomes 6000 × 1.1 = ₹6,600 (110% of the deposit). In a fixed deposit (FD) the money stays locked for a fixed time.

🎬 Option 1 vs Option 2 for ₹6,000 at 10% for 3 years
No compounding (interest paid out)Compounding (interest added back)
Each year₹600, ₹600, ₹600₹600, ₹660, ₹726
Total received₹7,800 = 6000 × 1.3 (130%)₹7,986 = 6000 × 1.331 (133.1%)
For t yearsp + prt = p(1 + rt)p × (1 + r) × … × (1 + r) = p(1 + r)t

Here p = principal and r = rate written as a decimal (10% → 0.1). Total interest = final amount − p, i.e. prt without compounding and p(1 + r)t − p with it.

💡 Without compounding the money grows by the same step each year (linear growth). With compounding each year's growth is bigger than the last (exponential growth). The same idea fits populations and bacteria.

Decline (depreciation). Many things lose value with age and use. A TV bought for ₹21,000 that depreciates 5% in a year is worth 95% of 21,000 = 0.95 × 21,000 = ₹19,950.

A village of 1,250 people shrinking about 10% each decade: after 3 decades 1250 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 911.25, so about 910 people. (Rounding after each decade gives 1125 → 1013 → 912; either way, about 910.)

🎯
Try thisIn the Explore Lab, slide the rate below zero to see decline, and above zero to see how long money takes to double.

🎭 Tricky percentages

Would you rather? Option A: deposit ₹100, get back ₹300 (a 200% gain). Option B: deposit ₹1000, get back ₹1500 (a 50% gain). A has the bigger percentage, but B gives more rupees (₹500 vs ₹200). Percentages compare proportions, not absolute amounts, so think about what you really want.

20% off or ₹50 off (on bills above ₹150)? 20% of 180 = ₹36 and 20% of 225 = ₹45, so take ₹50 off for those; 20% of 300 = ₹60, so take 20% off for ₹300. They are equal at ₹250.

🎬 Cakely's 30% + 20% vs Cakify's 50%

A mishap. Surbhi priced her cookware at a 50% margin, then offered 50% off to clear stock, thinking she would break even. If the goods cost x:

  • 1.5x × 0.5 = 0.75x = 34 of the cost → a 25% loss.
  • If sales after discount were ₹12,000: 0.75x = 12000 → x = ₹16,000. Loss = ₹4,000 (25%).
  • To break even, the discount d must satisfy 1.5x − d × 1.5x = x → d = 13 ≈ 33.33%.

Change the base, change the percentage. Ariba has 120% of Arun's marbles. Then Arun has 100120 = 56 ≈ 83.33% of Ariba's (not 80%!).

💡 Before any percentage, ask: "per cent of what?" Successive percentages multiply; they do not simply add.

📊 Percentage bar model + How close can you get?

Set a whole and a percentage: see the bar, the value and the FDP trio. Go past 100% to see the bar stretch. Then play the book's estimation game.

🛒 Shop counter

Set the cost price, marked price, discount and GST. Watch the bill, the profit or loss, and how the profit percentage changes when the base is the cost or the revenue.

🌱 Grow or decline

Choose a starting amount, a yearly rate (negative for decline) and the number of years. Blue: without compounding. Orange: with compounding.

📘 Figure it Out · 1.1 Fractions as Percentages pages 3–4

1Express as percentages: (i) 35 (ii) 714 (iii) 920 (iv) 72150 (v) 13 (vi) 511
Show solution

Multiply each fraction by 100 (or make the denominator 100).

  1. 35 = 60100 = 60%
  2. 714 = 12 = 50%
  3. 920 = 45100 = 45%
  4. 72150 = 48100 = 48% (divide top and bottom by 1.5)
  5. 13 × 100 = 1003 = 3313% ≈ 33.33%
  6. 511 × 100 = 50011 = 45511% ≈ 45.45%
Answer: 60%, 50%, 45%, 48%, 33⅓% (≈ 33.33%), 45 5/11% (≈ 45.45%)
2Nandini has 25 marbles; 15 are white. What percentage are white? (10%, 15%, 25%, 60%, 40%, none)
Show solution

1525 = 60100 (multiply top and bottom by 4) = 60%.

Answer: (iv) 60%
315 of the 80 students in a school walk to school. What percentage walk?
Show solution

1580 × 100 = 150080 = 18.75. (Check: 10% of 80 is 8, 20% is 16, so 15 is just under 20% ✓)

Answer: 18.75%
4Four runners A, B, C, D are shown on the track from Start to Finish after 15 minutes. Match each with the approximate percentage of the race completed: 55%, 20%, 38%, 72%, 84%, 93%.
Show solution

Compare each position with the whole track. A is about a third of the way (≈ 32%), B just past halfway (≈ 53%), C about three-quarters (≈ 75%), D almost at the end (≈ 95%). Pick the closest option for each. 20% and 84% are extra options that fit nobody.

Answer: A ≈ 38%, B ≈ 55%, C ≈ 72%, D ≈ 93%
5Write >, < or = without calculating: (i) 50% __ 5% (ii) 510 __ 50% (iii) 311 __ 61% (iv) 30% __ 13
Show solution
  1. 50 hundredths are more than 5 hundredths: >
  2. 510 = 12 = 50%: =
  3. 311 is less than 12 (less than 50%), so it is less than 61%: <
  4. 13 = 33.33% > 30%: <
Answer: (i) > (ii) = (iii) < (iv) <

📘 Figure it Out · 1.2 Percentage of Some Quantity pages 12–14

1Find the missing numbers from the bar models. (i) is done: a bar of 5 equal parts, so each part is 20%; a whole of 75 with 4 parts marked gives 60. (ii) A bar of 10 equal parts with one part marked "?"; a whole of 90 with 6 parts marked "?". (iii) A bar of 4 equal parts with one part marked "?"; a whole of 140 with 3 parts marked "?".
Show solution

(ii) 10 equal parts make 100%, so one part = 10%. Six parts = 60%, and 60% of 90 = 6 × 9 = 54.

(iii) 4 equal parts make 100%, so one part = 25%. Three parts = 75%, and 75% of 140 = 3 × 35 = 105.

Answer: (ii) 10% and 54   (iii) 25% and 105
2Find (and picture as a bar): (i) 25% of 160 (ii) 16% of 250 (iii) 62% of 360 (iv) 140% of 40 (v) 1% of 1 hour (vi) 7% of 10 kg
Show solution
  1. A quarter of 160 = 40 (bar of 4 parts, each 40).
  2. 16100 × 250 = 0.16 × 250 = 40 (1% of 250 is 2.5; 16 × 2.5 = 40).
  3. 0.62 × 360 = 223.2 (50% = 180, 10% = 36, 2% = 7.2; 180 + 36 + 7.2).
  4. 100% = 40 and 40% = 16, so 140% = 56 (the bar goes past the whole).
  5. 1 hour = 60 minutes; 1% = 0.6 min = 36 seconds.
  6. 7% of 10 kg = 0.7 kg = 700 g.
Answer: 40, 40, 223.2, 56, 36 s (0.6 min), 0.7 kg (700 g)
3Surya made 60 ml of deep orange paint. Red made up 34 of it. How much red did he use?
Show solution

34 × 60 = 45 (a quarter of 60 is 15; three quarters is 45). This is 75% of 60.

Answer: 45 ml
4Fill in >, < or =: (i) 50% of 510 ☐ 50% of 515 (ii) 37% of 148 ☐ 73% of 148 (iii) 29% of 43 ☐ 92% of 110 (iv) 30% of 40 ☐ 40% of 50 (v) 45% of 200 ☐ 10% of 490 (vi) 30% of 80 ☐ 24% of 64
Show solution
  1. Same percentage, smaller whole: <
  2. Same whole, smaller percentage: <
  3. Both the percentage and the whole are smaller on the left (12.47 vs 101.2): <
  4. Both smaller on the left (12 vs 20): <
  5. 90 vs 49: >
  6. Both bigger on the left (24 vs 15.36): >
Answer: (i) < (ii) < (iii) < (iv) < (v) > (vi) >
5(i) 30% of k is 70: find 60%, 90%, 120% of k. (ii) 100% of m is 215: find 10%, 1%, 6% of m. (iii) 90% of n is 270: find 9%, 18%, 100% of n. (iv) Make up two such questions.
Show solution

(i) 60% = 2 × 30% = 140; 90% = 3 × 30% = 210; 120% = 4 × 30% = 280.

(ii) 10% = 21.5; 1% = 2.15; 6% = 6 × 2.15 = 12.9.

(iii) 9% is a tenth of 90%: 27; 18% = 2 × 9% = 54; 100% = 270 ÷ 0.9 = 300 (or 10% = 30, so 100% = 300).

(iv) Example: "40% of q is 18; find 20%, 80% and 100% of q" (9, 36, 45).

Answer: (i) 140, 210, 280 (ii) 21.5, 2.15, 12.9 (iii) 27, 54, 300
6(i) 3 is __% of 300. (ii) __ is 40% of 4. (iii) 40 is 80% of __.
Show solution

(i) 3300 × 100 = 1%. (ii) 0.4 × 4 = 1.6. (iii) 80% → 40, so 10% → 5 and 100% → 50.

Answer: 1%, 1.6, 50
7Is 10% of a day longer than 1% of a week?
Show solution

10% of 24 h = 2.4 h = 144 minutes. A week has 7 × 24 = 168 h; 1% of it = 1.68 h = 100.8 minutes. A similar question to try: is 1% of a year longer than 3% of a month?

Answer: Yes — 144 min is longer than 100.8 min
8Mariam's bull: given 2 units of fodder it eats 1; given 3 it eats 2; given 4 it eats 3; … given 100 it eats 99. Write these as percentages. What do you notice?
Show solution

The bull eats nn + 1 of what it gets: 12 = 50%, 23 ≈ 66.67%, 34 = 75%, 45 = 80%, 910 = 90%, 1920 = 95%, … 99100 = 99%.

The percentage keeps rising, but by smaller and smaller steps. It gets closer and closer to 100% but never reaches it, because the bull always leaves 1 unit.

Answer: 50%, 66.67%, 75%, 80%, … 99% — creeping up towards 100%
9Workers take 18 days to pick coffee berries on 20% of a plantation. How many days for the whole plantation, at the same rate? Why is the assumption needed?
Show solution

100% is 5 times 20%, so 5 × 18 = 90 days. This only works if the work is proportional to the area: same number of workers, same speed, and similar berry density everywhere. If the rate changes (rain, fewer workers), the answer changes.

Answer: 90 days
10A 90-minute badminton session is split warm up : play : cool down = 10% : 80% : 10%. How long is each?
Show solution

10% of 90 = 9 min; 80% = 8 × 9 = 72 min. Check: 9 + 72 + 9 = 90 ✓

Answer: warm up 9 min, play 72 min, cool down 9 min
11About 90% of the world's people live in the Northern Hemisphere. Roughly how many is that this year?
Show solution

The world population is a little over 8 billion (about 8.2 billion in 2025, the figure the book uses later, and about 8.3 billion now). 90% of 8.2 billion = 0.9 × 8.2 = 7.38 billion; with 8.3 billion it is about 7.47 billion.

Answer: about 7.4 billion people
12Halwa for 4 people uses rava 40%, sugar 40%, ghee 20%. (i) What are the proportions for 8 people? (ii) If the ingredients weigh 2 kg in total, how much of each?
Show solution

(i) Doubling the recipe doubles every ingredient, so the percentages stay the same: 40%, 40%, 20%.

(ii) 40% of 2 kg = 0.8 kg; 20% of 2 kg = 0.4 kg.

Answer: (i) still 40% : 40% : 20% (ii) rava 800 g, sugar 800 g, ghee 400 g

📘 Figure it Out · 1.3 Using Percentages (profit, discount, change) pages 19–20

The book prints this set as 1–5 and then starts again at 3. We keep the book's numbers and mark the second run with ′ (3′, 4′, …).

1A geometry box is bought for ₹75 and sold for ₹110. What is the profit margin with respect to the cost?
Show solution

Profit = 110 − 75 = ₹35. On the cost: 3575 × 100 = 1403 ≈ 46.67%.

Answer: ≈ 46.67% (46⅔%)
2A chair's materials cost ₹475. The carpenter wants a 50% profit margin. Selling price?
Show solution

SP = 150% of 475 = 1.5 × 475 = 712.5 (or 475 + 237.50).

Answer: ₹712.50
3A company's total sales (revenue) last year were ₹2.5 crore, with a profit margin of 25%. What were its total costs?
Show solution

For a company's overall result, the book measures the profit margin against the revenue ("how much profit did I make on my overall revenue?"). So profit = 25% of ₹2.5 crore = ₹0.625 crore, and costs = 2.5 − 0.625 = ₹1.875 crore. (Costs are 75% of the revenue.)

If someone took the margin on the cost instead, then 125% of cost = 2.5 crore and cost = ₹2 crore. The question says "sales … also called revenue", which points to the revenue base.

Answer: ₹1.875 crore (₹1,87,50,000)
4Shirts are 25% off. A shirt's original price is ₹300. How much does Anwar pay?
Show solution

25% of 300 = 75, so he pays 300 − 75 = 225 (or 75% of 300).

Answer: ₹225
5Petrol was ₹60 in 2015 and ₹100 in 2025. Percentage increase? (50%, 40%, 60%, 66.66%, 140%, 160.66%)
Show solution

Increase = ₹40. Base = the old price ₹60: 4060 × 100 = 6623% ≈ 66.66%. (40% would be wrongly using ₹100 as the base.)

Answer: (iv) 66.66%
3′Samson paid ₹4,40,000 for a car after a 15% discount. What was the original price?
Show solution

He paid 85% of the original price. 0.85 × P = 4,40,000 → P = 4,40,000 ÷ 0.85 = 5,17,647.06…

Answer: about ₹5,17,647 (₹5,17,647.06)
4′1600 people voted and the winner got 500 votes. What percentage did the winner get? What is the least possible number of candidates?
Show solution

5001600 × 100 = 31.25%. The other candidates share 1100 votes, and each must have fewer than 500. With 1 other candidate: 1100 > 500 ✗. With 2: at least one has 550 or more ✗. With 3 others they can each have under 500 (e.g. 400, 400, 300) ✓.

Answer: 31.25%; at least 4 candidates
5′Rice cost ₹38 per kg in 2024 and ₹42 in 2025. What is the rate of inflation (percentage increase in price)?
Show solution

Increase ₹4 on a base of ₹38: 438 × 100 ≈ 10.53%.

Answer: ≈ 10.53%
6′A number increased by 20% becomes 90. What is the number?
Show solution

120% of the number = 90 → number = 90 ÷ 1.2 = 75. Check: 20% of 75 = 15, 75 + 15 = 90 ✓ (Taking 20% off 90 gives 72, which is wrong: the 20% is of the original.)

Answer: 75
7′A milkman sold two buffaloes for ₹80,000 each: 5% profit on one, 10% loss on the other. Overall profit or loss?
Show solution

First buffalo: 105% of CP = 80,000 → CP = 76,190.48. Second: 90% of CP = 80,000 → CP = 88,888.89. Total cost = 1,65,079.37; total sales = 1,60,000. Loss = ₹5,079.37, which is 5079.37165079.37 × 100 ≈ 3.08% of the cost.

Answer: a loss of about ₹5,079 (≈ 3.08%)
8′Elephants in a park increased by 5% in a decade. If the old population was p, the new one is: (i) p × 0.5 (ii) p × 0.05 (iii) p × 1.5 (iv) p × 1.05 (v) p + 1.50
Show solution

New = p + 5% of p = p + 0.05p = 1.05p.

Answer: (iv) p × 1.05
9′"Demand for cameras has fallen by 85% in the last decade." Which statement(s) mean the same? (i) Now is 85% of a decade ago. (ii) A decade ago was 85% of now. (iii) Now is 15% of a decade ago. (iv) A decade ago was 15% of now. (v) A decade ago was 185% of now. (vi) Now is 185% of a decade ago.
Show solution

Falling by 85% leaves 100 − 85 = 15% of the old demand. So "now = 15% of a decade ago" is right. Check (v): if now = 0.15 × old, then old = now ÷ 0.15 ≈ 667% of now, not 185%.

Answer: only (iii)

📘 Figure it Out · Growth and Compounding pages 22–24

1Bank of Yahapur: 10% p.a. Compare ₹20,000 for 2 years with and without yearly compounding.
Show solution

Without: interest ₹2,000 each year → 20,000 + 4,000 = ₹24,000 (= 20000 × 1.2).

With: 20,000 × 1.1 = 22,000; 22,000 × 1.1 = ₹24,200 (= 20000 × 1.21).

Answer: ₹24,000 without, ₹24,200 with (₹200 more)
2Bank of Wahapur: 5% p.a. Compare ₹20,000 for 4 years with and without yearly compounding.
Show solution

Without: ₹1,000 per year × 4 = ₹4,000 → ₹24,000.

With: 20,000 → 21,000 → 22,050 → 23,152.50 → 24,310.125. So 20000 × 1.054 ≈ ₹24,310.13.

Answer: ₹24,000 without, ≈ ₹24,310.13 with (≈ ₹310 more)
3What do you notice in the two answers above?
Show solution

Without compounding both banks give exactly the same ₹24,000, because 10% × 2 years = 5% × 4 years = 20% in total. With compounding Wahapur gives more (₹24,310 vs ₹24,200): more compounding periods mean more "interest on interest", even though the rate is lower.

Answer: same simple total (20% gain); compounding over more periods earns more
4Jasmine invests p for 4 years at 6% p.a. without compounding. Which expression gives the total amount? (i) p × 6 × 4 (ii) p × 0.6 × 4 (iii) p × 0.6100 × 4 (iv) p × 0.06100 × 4 (v) p × 1.6 × 4 (vi) p × 1.06 × 4 (vii) p + (p × 0.06 × 4)
Show solution

Total = principal + interest = p + p × r × t, with r = 6% = 0.06 and t = 4. Options (i)–(iv) only try to give the interest, and with the wrong rate (6, 0.6, 0.006, 0.0006 instead of 0.06). Options (v) and (vi) multiply 1.6 or 1.06 by 4, which is not how simple interest adds up. Only (vii) adds the principal p to the interest p × 0.06 × 4.

Answer: (vii) p + (p × 0.06 × 4) = p(1 + 0.24) = 1.24p
5Post office: 7% p.a. Interest on ₹50,000 for 3 years without compounding? How much more with compounding?
Show solution

Without: 50,000 × 0.07 × 3 = ₹10,500.

With: 50,000 × 1.073 = 50,000 × 1.225043 = ₹61,252.15, so interest = ₹11,252.15. Extra = 11,252.15 − 10,500 = ₹752.15.

Answer: ₹10,500 interest; ₹752.15 more with compounding
6Giridhar borrows ₹12,500 at 12% p.a. for 3 years without compounding; Raghava borrows ₹12,500 at 10% p.a. for 3 years, compounded yearly. Who pays more interest, and by how much?
Show solution

Giridhar: 12,500 × 0.12 × 3 = ₹4,500.

Raghava: 12,500 × 1.13 = 12,500 × 1.331 = 16,637.50 → interest ₹4,137.50.

Answer: Giridhar pays ₹362.50 more
7₹1000 grows at 10% p.a. How long to double, with and without compounding? Is compounding exponential growth and non-compounding linear growth?
Show solution

Without: ₹100 each year, so ₹1000 more takes 10 years. With: 1000 × 1.1t: after 7 years ₹1,948.72, after 8 years ₹2,143.59, so it doubles during the 8th year (about 7.3 years).

Yes. Without compounding the same amount is added each year (a straight line: linear). With compounding the amount is multiplied by 1.1 each year, so the additions keep growing (exponential).

Answer: 10 years without; a little over 7 years (passes double in year 8) with. Yes.
8A city of 1.5 crore people grows about 3% a year. Expected population after 3 years?
Show solution

Growth compounds: 1.5 crore × 1.033 = 1.5 × 1.092727 = 1.639 crore ≈ 1,63,90,905.

Answer: about 1.64 crore
9Bacteria increase 2.5% per hour. Start: 5,06,000. How many after 2 hours?
Show solution

506000 × 1.025 = 518650; × 1.025 again = 531616.25.

Answer: about 5,31,616 bacteria

📘 Figure it Out · End of chapter pages 28–30

1Bengaluru's 2025 population is about 250% of its 2000 population, which was 50 lakh. Population in 2025?
Show solution

2.5 × 50 lakh = 125 lakh.

Answer: about 125 lakh (1.25 crore)
2World population 2025 ≈ 8.2 billion. Match the countries with their approximate share: Germany 83 million, India 1.46 billion, Bangladesh 175 million, USA 347 million. Options: 13%, 8%, 18%, 10%, 1%, 35%, 2%, 2%, 0.1%.
Show solution

Write all in millions: world = 8200 million. Germany 838200 ≈ 1.0%; India 14608200 ≈ 17.8%; Bangladesh 1758200 ≈ 2.1%; USA 3478200 ≈ 4.2%. Estimation: 1% of 8.2 billion is 82 million, so Germany ≈ 1 lot, Bangladesh ≈ 2 lots, USA ≈ 4 lots.

The USA works out to about 4%, which is not among the printed options. The nearest printed values are 2% and 8%; the correct share is about 4%.

Answer: Germany 1%, India 18%, Bangladesh 2%, USA ≈ 4%
3A phone costs ₹8,250 and 18% GST is added. Which give the final price? (i) 8250 + 18 (ii) 8250 + 1800 (iii) 8250 + 18100 (iv) 8250 × 18 (v) 8250 × 1.18 (vi) 8250 + 8250 × 0.18 (vii) 1.8 × 8250
Show solution

Final price = 8250 + 18% of 8250 = 8250 + 8250 × 0.18 = 8250 × 1.18 = ₹9,735.

Answer: (v) and (vi) — both give ₹9,735
4A lab's mice population (start p) changes by +5%, then −2%, then −3% month by month. Which are true? (i) p × 0.05 × 0.02 × 0.03 (ii) p × 1.05 × 0.98 × 0.97 (iii) p + 0.05 − 0.02 − 0.03 (iv) exactly p (v) more than p (vi) less than p
Show solution

Each change multiplies: ×1.05, ×0.98, ×0.97. Product = 1.05 × 0.98 × 0.97 = 0.99813, a little less than 1. The changes "+5 − 2 − 3 = 0" do not cancel, because the decreases act on a bigger number.

Answer: (ii) and (vi)
5A shopkeeper set a 35% profit margin, then gave a 30% discount on that price. Profit or loss?
Show solution

Let cost = x. Price = 1.35x. After 30% off: 1.35x × 0.7 = 0.945x < x. He sells for 94.5% of the cost.

Answer: a loss of 5.5%
6On a dot grid, a square is divided into regions A, B, C, D, E. What percentage of the area is E?
Show solution

Count grid units: the big square is 8 × 8 = 64 square units. A is 4 × 4 = 16, B is 4 × 6 = 24, C is 4 × 2 = 8. The bottom-left 4 × 4 square (16) is cut by its diagonal into two equal triangles, D = 8 and E = 8. Check: 16 + 24 + 8 + 8 + 8 = 64 ✓. E = 864 = 18.

Answer: 12.5%
7Find 5% of 40 and 40% of 5; 25% of 12 and 12% of 25; 15% of 60 and 60% of 15. What do you notice? Compare x% of y with y% of x using algebra.
Show solution

2 and 2; 3 and 3; 9 and 9. They are always equal: x% of y = x100 × y = xy100 = y100 × x = y% of x. Handy trick: 8% of 50 = 50% of 8 = 4.

Answer: x% of y = y% of x, always
8On an excursion, 40% of the students are in Grade 8 (the rest Grade 9); 60% of the Grade 8 students are girls. (i) What percentage of all students are Grade 8 girls? (ii) If 160 students go, how many are Grade 8 girls?
Show solution

(i) 60% of 40% = 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.24 = 24%. (ii) Grade 8 students = 40% of 160 = 64; girls = 60% of 64 = 38.4.

38.4 is not a whole number of people, so the book's numbers cannot all be exact. In real life the answer would be about 38 girls (24% of 160 = 38.4).

Answer: (i) 24% (ii) 38.4 ≈ 38 girls
9The selling price of 3 pencils equals the cost price of 5 pencils. Profit or loss, and what percentage?
Show solution

Let one pencil cost ₹1. Then 3 pencils sell for ₹5, so SP of one = ₹53. Profit per pencil = 53 − 1 = 23, i.e. 23 × 100 ≈ 66.67% of the cost.

Answer: profit of 66⅔% (≈ 66.67%)
10Bus fares rose 3% last year and 4% this year. Overall increase?
Show solution

1.03 × 1.04 = 1.0712. The fare is now 107.12% of the original.

Answer: 7.12% (a little more than 3 + 4 = 7)
11A rectangle's length increases by 10% but its area stays the same. By exactly what percentage does the breadth decrease?
Show solution

New length = 1.1l. Area l × b = 1.1l × b′ → b′ = b1.1 = 1011b. Decrease = 111 of b = 10011% = 9111%.

Answer: 9 1/11 % (≈ 9.09%), not 10%
12A 65 g chips packet: potato 70%, vegetable oil 24%, salt 3%, spices 3%. Find the weight of each.
Show solution

1% of 65 g = 0.65 g. Potato 70 × 0.65 = 45.5 g; oil 24 × 0.65 = 15.6 g; salt and spices 3 × 0.65 = 1.95 g each. Check: 45.5 + 15.6 + 1.95 + 1.95 = 65 ✓

Answer: potato 45.5 g, oil 15.6 g, salt 1.95 g, spices 1.95 g
13Same items, same price (₹100 each). Shop A: buy 1 get 1 free. Shop B: buy 2 get 1 free. Shop C: buy 3 get 1 free. (i) Effective price per item; order cheapest to costliest. (ii) Percentage discount in each. (iii) You need 4 items: which shop?
Show solution

(i) A: ₹100 for 2 → ₹50 each. B: ₹200 for 3 → ₹66.67 each. C: ₹300 for 4 → ₹75 each. Cheapest to costliest: A, B, C.

(ii) Free items ÷ items received: A 12 = 50%, B 13 ≈ 33.33%, C 14 = 25%.

(iii) A: buy 2, get 4 for ₹200. B: buy 3 to get 1 free (4 items) for ₹300. C: buy 3, get 4 for ₹300. Choose Shop A.

Answer: (i) A ₹50, B ₹66.67, C ₹75 (ii) 50%, 33.33%, 25% (iii) Shop A, ₹200
14In a room of 100 people, 99% are left-handed. How many left-handed people must leave to bring it down to 98%?
Show solution

There is 1 right-handed person, and nobody right-handed leaves. For left-handers to be 98%, that one person must be 2% of the room, so the room must have 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50 people: 49 left-handed + 1 right-handed. So 99 − 49 = 50 left-handers must leave. Surprising! A 1% change in the percentage needs half the room to go.

Answer: 50 people
15A bar graph (NSS 2023) shows the percentage of females/males in each age group who can use a computer: children 4%/≈5%, teenage 24%/29%, twenties 26%/37%, thirties 14%/25%, forties 7%/14%, fifties 4%/9%, seniors 2%/4%. Which statements are valid? (i) Twenties are the most computer-literate. (ii) Women lag behind across age groups. (iii) There are more people in their twenties than teenagers. (iv) More than a quarter of people in their thirties can use computers. (v) Less than 1 in 10 aged 60+ can use computers. (vi) Half of people in their twenties can use computers.
Show solution
  1. Valid: 26% and 37% are the highest bars for both females and males.
  2. Valid: in every age group the female bar is shorter.
  3. Not valid: the graph shows percentages within each group, not how many people are in each group.
  4. Not valid: 14% and 25%, so overall it is at most 25%, not more than a quarter.
  5. Valid: 2% and 4% are both far below 10%.
  6. Not valid: 26% and 37% are both well below 50%.
Answer: (i), (ii) and (v)

🎯 Questions inside the chapter pages 1–27

aKishanlal's Days 5 and 6: sales ₹7,800 and ₹9,550 against a ₹5,000 target. Days 7 and 8: 150% and 210% of the target. Find the missing values.
Show solution

78005000 × 100 = 156%; 95505000 × 100 = 191%. 1.5 × 5000 = ₹7,500; 2.1 × 5000 = ₹10,500.

Answer: 156%, 191%, ₹7,500, ₹10,500
bFind the profit percentages of the wholesaler (CP ₹253, SP ₹300) and the manufacturer (CP ₹230, SP ₹253) in the sweater's journey.
Show solution

Wholesaler: 47253 × 100 ≈ 18.58%. Manufacturer: 23230 × 100 = 10%.

Answer: wholesaler ≈ 18.58%, manufacturer 10%
cRaghu's rice: is the loss percentage per kg the same as for the 10 kg?
Show solution

Per kg: bought at ₹35, sold at ₹30, loss ₹5, 535 × 100 ≈ 14.29%. For 10 kg: 50350 — the same fraction, since both numbers are 10 times bigger. (The book writes 14.28%; rounded correctly it is 14.29%.)

Answer: Yes, ≈ 14.29% either way
dA cooker with MRP ₹1,800 is sold at 35% off. Selling price? If it cost ₹900, what is the profit percentage?
Show solution

SP = 65% of 1800 = ₹1,170. Profit = 1170 − 900 = ₹270; 270900 × 100 = 30%.

Answer: ₹1,170; 30% profit
eMath Talk: write formulas for the total interest earned at maturity, without and with compounding.
Show solution

Interest = final amount − principal. Without: p(1 + rt) − p = prt. With: p(1 + r)t − p. For ₹6,000 at 10% for 3 years: 1,800 and 1,986.

Answer: prt and p(1 + r)ᵗ − p
fAriba has 120% of Arun's marbles. What can Arun say?
Show solution

Ariba = 1.2 × Arun, so Arun = Ariba ÷ 1.2 = 56 of Ariba ≈ 83.33%. For example, Arun 10, Ariba 12: 10 is 1012 of 12.

Answer: "I have about 83.33% (5/6) of Ariba's marbles."

🧩 Puzzle · Peaceful Knights page 32

★Place 8 knights on a chessboard so that no knight attacks another. (A knight moves 2 squares one way and 1 square at right angles: an "L".)
Show solution

Every knight move changes the row by 1 or 2, so a knight can never attack a square in its own row. Put all 8 knights in one row and none of them attack each other. (Another way: a knight always jumps to a square of the opposite colour, so knights all on white squares are also safe — you could even fit 32!)

Answer: e.g. all 8 knights along one row

✗ ₹60 → ₹100 is a 40% increase (40 ÷ 100).

✗ Up 20% and then down 20% brings it back to the start.
