⏪

✗ Increased by 20% it is 90, so the number is 90 − 20% of 90 = 72.

✓ 90 is 120% of the number: 90 ÷ 1.2 = 75.

🍳

✗ 50% margin then 50% discount = no profit, no loss.

✓ 1.5 × 0.5 = 0.75 → a 25% loss. To break even the discount must be 33⅓%.

🧾

✗ Profit % is always divided by the same thing.

✓ Ask "percentage of what?" On cost: profit ÷ CP. On revenue (a business's margin on sales): profit ÷ SP. ₹250 on ₹500 is 50%, but on ₹750 it is 33.33%.

🏦

✗ With compounding, 3 years' interest = 3 × the first year's interest.

✓ That is without compounding. With compounding each year earns interest on the interest: 600 + 660 + 726, not 3 × 600.

a²√2b²c²3·4·5◇90°Part II · Chapter 2

The Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem

How do you build a square with double the area? Baudhāyana's answer leads to √2, to a² + b² = c², and to an endless supply of whole-number right triangles.

📐

🟦 2.1 Doubling a square

About 2800 years ago (c. 800 BCE), Baudhāyana wrote a Śulba-Sūtra: a rule book for building fire altars of exact shapes and sizes using ropes and pegs. One of his questions:

💡 How can we construct a square whose area is double the area of a given square?

First guess: double each side. But look: the bigger square holds four copies of the old one. Doubling the side makes the area 2 × 2 = 4 times, not 2 times. ❌

Baudhāyana's beautiful answer (Verse 1.9, in our words): the square drawn on the diagonal of a square has twice its area.

🎬 Build a square on the diagonal and count the triangles

Why does it work? Extend the top side and the right side of the old square (Baudhāyana's "east-west" and "north-south" lines). These two lines are the diagonals of the new tilted square, so they cross at right angles and cut each other in half. That splits the new square into 4 right triangles whose two short sides both equal the side of the old square. The old square is just 2 such triangles. All six triangles are congruent (SAS). So the new square = 4 triangles = 2 × (old square). ✅

🤩
Did you know?"Śulba" means a cord or rope. The Śulba-Sūtras are the oldest geometry texts in India. Their rules for squares, rectangles and right angles were used to lay out altars with great accuracy.

🔁 A chain of doubled squares, and a paper trick

Add more east-west and north-south lines and the doubling repeats: the next square is made of 2, then 4, then 8 congruent triangles. Each square has double the area of the one before.

📄 Doubling with paper. Take two identical paper squares. On Square 1 just draw both diagonals. Cut Square 2 along both its diagonals into 4 triangles (5, 6, 7, 8). Stick one triangle on each side of Square 1 (long side against the square's side). You get a tilted square with double the area: 8 triangles instead of 4.

✂️ 2.2 Halving a square

Now go the other way: make a square with half the area. Just reverse the last idea: join the midpoints of the four sides. The tilted square inside is exactly half.

Why half? The dashed east-west and north-south lines cut the big square into 4 small squares. Each small square is cut in half by one side of the tilted square. So the tilted square holds 4 half-squares, the corners hold the other 4. Inside = outside = half. ✅

📄 With paper: fold each corner of a paper square in to the centre, so the creases join the midpoints of the sides. The folded shape PQRS is a square with half the area: the four flaps exactly cover it!

🎯
Try thisWill a square with half the side have half the area? No! Four such squares fill the original square, so it has only one quarter of the area.
🧠
Why is PQRS a square?Join PR and QS. They are the two midlines of the paper, so they are equal, they bisect each other and they meet at 90°. A quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and are perpendicular bisectors of each other is a square.

📐 2.3 Hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle

In a right triangle the side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse. Take an isosceles right triangle with equal sides 1. How long is its hypotenuse?

The square PEAR (side 1) is made of two such triangles. We do not know the hypotenuse ER yet, but we do know the area of the square REST built on it: it is double, so it is 2.

c × c = c² = 2,  so  c = √2

The general rule. If the equal sides are a and the hypotenuse is c, the square on c is double the square on a:

💡 c² = 2a²   (so c = a√2). Use it to find c from a, or a from c.

Example 1. Equal sides 12: c² = 2 × 144 = 288, so c = √288. Since 16² = 256 and 17² = 289, the hypotenuse is between 16 and 17.

Example 2. Hypotenuse √72: 72 = 2a², so a² = 36 and a = 6.

🔍 How big is √2?

√2 is the side of a square of area 2. Compare it with squares we know:

  • 1² = 1 < 2, so √2 > 1.
  • 2² = 4 > 2, so √2 < 2.

So 1 < √2 < 2. We call 1 a lower bound and 2 an upper bound. Now squeeze closer by squaring decimals:

TrySquareTrySquareTrySquare
1.31.691.401.961.4131.996569
1.41.961.411.98811.4141.999396
1.52.251.422.01641.4152.002225
1.4 < √2 < 1.51.41 < √2 < 1.421.414 < √2 < 1.415
🎬 Zoom in on √2, one digit at a time
🧠
Memory trick√2 ≈ 1.414. So the hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle is about 1.414 × (equal side).

♾️ √2 never ends, and is not a fraction

Can a terminating decimal square to exactly 2? Suppose it could, say 1.414…d, ending in a non-zero digit d. When you square it, the last digit of the answer comes from d × d. Look at the last digits of 1², 2², …, 9²: 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4, 1. Never 0! So the square also ends in a non-zero digit after the decimal point, and can never be 2.000… exactly. So √2's decimal goes on forever.

Can √2 be a fraction mn? If √2 = mn, squaring gives 2 = m²n², i.e. 2n² = m².

  • In any square number, every prime appears an even number of times (primes come in pairs).
  • So in m², the prime 2 appears an even number of times.
  • In n² the 2s are even too, and the extra 2 in front makes the count odd in 2n².

The same number cannot have both an odd and an even number of 2s. Impossible! So √2 is not a fraction.

💡 √2 = 1.41421356… is neither a terminating decimal nor a fraction. It is a non-terminating decimal.
🤩
Did you know?The fraction proof is in Euclid's Elements (c. 300 BCE). Even earlier, the Śulba-Sūtras gave the amazing approximation √2 ≈ 1 + 13 + 13·4 − 13·4·34 = 577408 ≈ 1.414216, correct to 5 decimal places!

➕ 2.4 Combining two different squares

Two copies of the same square combine into one square on the diagonal. What if the two squares have different sizes? Baudhāyana (Verse 1.12) says, in our words:

💡 Make a right triangle whose two shorter sides are the sides of the two squares. The square on its longest side (the "diagonal") has area equal to the sum of the two squares.

When the two squares are equal (a = b), the right triangle is isosceles and its hypotenuse is the diagonal of the square: exactly our doubling method from 2.1! ✅

🧩 Why does Baudhāyana's method work?

In Verse 2.1 Baudhāyana gives the key: mark a rectangle inside the larger square using the side of the smaller square; its diagonal is the side of the combined square. Watch it happen:

🎬 Cut two triangles, swing them up, get one square
  1. Put the squares (sides a and b) side by side. The base is a + b long.
  2. Mark a rectangle a wide and b tall at the right end of the big square. Its diagonal makes triangle X with sides a and b.
  3. Draw the same kind of cut from the top of the small square: triangle W (sides b and a).
  4. Swing W up to position T and X up to position U. The two squares (V + W + X) become the shape T + U + V.

Is T + U + V really a square? Its four sides are hypotenuses of the congruent triangles T, U, W, X, so they are equal. At each corner, the two acute angles of the triangle, x and 90° − x, sit together with a straight line, so each corner is 180° − x − (90° − x) = 90°. Equal sides + right angles = square! Its side is c, the hypotenuse of the a, b right triangle.

c² = T + U + V = W + X + V = a² + b²

⭐ Baudhāyana's Theorem (a² + b² = c²)

📄 Paper check: Join a small square and a big square, make the two cuts, rearrange the three pieces into one big square. Then draw a right triangle with sides a and b, build the square on its hypotenuse, and cover it exactly with your three pieces!

💡 Baudhāyana's Theorem on right-angled triangles: if a right triangle has sides a, b and hypotenuse c, then a² + b² = c².
🎬 Squares on the sides of a 3-4-5 triangle

Using it. Draw a right triangle with shorter sides 3 cm and 4 cm; your ruler reads about 5 cm for the hypotenuse. The theorem says exactly 5: 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5².

Finding a shorter side. Hypotenuse 25, one side 7: b² = 25² − 7² = 625 − 49 = 576, so b = 24. (Subtract when the hypotenuse is known!)

🤩
Did you know?Baudhāyana was the first in history to state this theorem in such a general, modern form. The Greek thinker Pythagoras (c. 500 BCE), who lived a couple of hundred years later, also studied and admired it. That is why we call it the Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem, so that everyone knows which theorem we mean.

🔢 2.5 Baudhāyana triples

Whole numbers (a, b, c) with a² + b² = c² are called Baudhāyana triples (also Pythagorean triples). In Verse 1.13 Baudhāyana lists (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17), (7, 24, 25), (12, 35, 37) and (15, 36, 39).

All triples with numbers up to 20: 3, 4, 5 6, 8, 10 5, 12, 13 9, 12, 15 8, 15, 17 12, 16, 20

Scaling. (6, 8, 10), (9, 12, 15), (12, 16, 20) are just (3, 4, 5) × 2, × 3, × 4. In general, if a² + b² = c², then for any counting number k:

(ka)² + (kb)² = k²a² + k²b² = k²(a² + b²) = k²c² = (kc)²

So (ka, kb, kc) is also a triple, a scaled version. That gives infinitely many triples already!

A triple with no common factor greater than 1 is primitive: (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17) are primitive; (9, 12, 15) is not. Going backwards, if a, b, c share a factor f, divide it out: (9, 12, 15) ÷ 3 = (3, 4, 5), still a triple. So every triple is a primitive one, scaled up. Find all primitive triples and you have found them all.

🌍
Real lifeMasons check a right angle with a 3-4-5 rope or measure 60 cm, 80 cm and 1 m (a scaled 3-4-5) along two walls. If the diagonal is exactly 1 m, the corner is square.

🪜 Making new triples from odd squares

Recall: the sum of the first n odd numbers is n². The n-th odd number is 2n − 1, so

(n − 1)² + (2n − 1) = n²

(You can also check it by expanding: n² − 2n + 1 + 2n − 1 = n².) Now the trick: if the odd number 2n − 1 is itself a square, we get square + square = square!

🎬 The L-shaped 9 becomes a 3 × 3 square
Odd squareIt is the n-th odd number(n − 1)² + odd square = n²Triple
9 = 3²n = 54² + 3² = 5²(3, 4, 5)
25 = 5²n = 1312² + 5² = 13²(5, 12, 13)
49 = 7²n = 2524² + 7² = 25²(7, 24, 25)
81 = 9²n = 4140² + 9² = 41²(9, 40, 41)
🧠
Quick recipePick an odd number k. Then n = (k² + 1) ÷ 2 and the triple is (k, n − 1, n). The hypotenuse is always just 1 more than the middle side.

🏆 2.6 A long-standing open problem

Infinitely many squares are a sum of two squares. In the 17th century the French mathematician Fermat wondered: can a cube be a sum of two cubes? A 4th power a sum of two 4th powers? In other words, does

xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ  (x, y, z counting numbers, n > 2)

ever have a solution? Fermat wrote in the margin of a book that it never does, and that he had a "truly marvellous proof" that the margin was too small to hold. Nobody ever found his proof. This became Fermat's Last Theorem.

🤩
Did you know?For more than 300 years great mathematicians failed to prove it. In 1963 a 10-year-old boy, Andrew Wiles, read about it in a library book and decided he would prove it. In 1994, he did! 🎉 Never give up on a problem you love.
🎯
Try thisCheck that 6³ + 8³ = 216 + 512 = 728, which is just 1 short of 9³ = 729. So close, yet not equal!

🪷 2.7 Further applications: the lotus in the lake

A problem from Bhāskarāchārya's Līlāvatī (Bhāskara II), in our words: a lotus stands 1 unit above the water. A breeze pushes it over, and its tip touches the water 3 units from where it stood. How deep is the lake?

🎬 Sway the lotus and find the depth

Let the depth be x. The whole stem is x + 1. Assume the stem first stood straight up. After it bends, the stem is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with sides x and 3:

3² + x² = (x + 1)² → 9 + x² = x² + 2x + 1 → 9 = 2x + 1 → x = 4

The lake is 4 units deep. It looked like too little information, but the theorem cracked it! 🎉

ShapeRight triangle hidden insideExample
Square, side sdiagonal² = s² + s²s = 5 → diagonal = √50 ≈ 7.07
Rectangle l × bdiagonal² = l² + b²6 × 8 → diagonal 10
Rhombusdiagonals cut each other in half at 90°: side² = (d₁/2)² + (d₂/2)²d = 6, 8 → side 5
Equilateral triangle, side sheight cuts the base in half: h² = s² − (s/2)²s = 2 → h = √3

📐 Squares on a right triangle

Slide the two shorter sides. Watch the three squares, and check that a² + b² = c². When c comes out a whole number, you have found a Baudhāyana triple!

🏭 Triple factory

Make a triple from an odd square, then scale it. The factory tells you whether your triple is primitive.

🔳 Tilted squares on a dot grid

Choose how far each side steps across (p) and up (q). The area is the outer square minus four triangles, which is p² + q². Which areas can you make?

📘 Figure it Out · 2.3 Isosceles right triangles pages 39–40

1Two identical paper squares are each cut along one diagonal into two triangles (1, 2 and 3, 4). Arrange the four pieces into a square with double the area of either square.
Show solution

Each piece is a right isosceles triangle whose two short sides equal the side s of the square. Put the four right-angle corners together at one point, like four slices around a centre. The long sides (the diagonals) form the outside.

The four right angles fill 360° at the centre, and all outer sides are diagonals of the square, so the new shape is a square of side equal to the diagonal. It contains 4 triangles = 2 squares.

Answer: right angles meet at the centre → a tilted square of double area
2The equal sides of an isosceles right triangle are given. Find the hypotenuse, and bounds for it with at least one digit after the decimal point: (i) 3 (ii) 4 (iii) 6 (iv) 8 (v) 9
Show solution

Use c² = 2a², then find the tenths that squeeze c.

ac² = 2a²cCheckBounds
318√184.2² = 17.64, 4.3² = 18.494.2 < c < 4.3
432√325.6² = 31.36, 5.7² = 32.495.6 < c < 5.7
672√728.4² = 70.56, 8.5² = 72.258.4 < c < 8.5
8128√12811.3² = 127.69, 11.4² = 129.9611.3 < c < 11.4
9162√16212.7² = 161.29, 12.8² = 163.8412.7 < c < 12.8

Shortcut check: c = a × √2 ≈ a × 1.414, e.g. 3 × 1.414 = 4.242 ✔

Answer: √18, √32, √72, √128, √162 (≈ 4.24, 5.66, 8.49, 11.31, 12.73)
3The hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle is 10. Find its other two sides.
Show solution

Two such triangles make a square with diagonal 10. The square on the diagonal has area 10² = 100, which is double the small square. So the small square has area 50, and its side is √50.

Check with the formula: c² = 2a² → 100 = 2a² → a² = 50 → a = √50. Since 7.0² = 49 and 7.1² = 50.41, a is between 7.0 and 7.1 (about 7.07).

Answer: both sides are √50 ≈ 7.07

📘 Figure it Out · 2.4 Using Baudhāyana's Theorem page 47

1A right triangle has shorter sides 5 cm and 12 cm. Find the hypotenuse (draw and measure first, then check).
Show solution

c² = 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13². Your measured length should be close to 13 cm.

Answer: 13 cm
2A right triangle has a short side 8 cm and hypotenuse 17 cm. Find the third side.
Show solution

The hypotenuse is known, so subtract: b² = 17² − 8² = 289 − 64 = 225 = 15².

Answer: 15 cm
3How would you construct a square with three times the area of a given square? Five times? (Verse 1.10)
Show solution

Let the square have side s (area s²).

Three times: first make the double square: its side is the diagonal d of the given square (d² = 2s²). Now make a right triangle with shorter sides s and d. The square on its hypotenuse has area s² + 2s² = 3s².

Five times: make a right triangle with shorter sides s and 2s. The square on its hypotenuse has area s² + (2s)² = s² + 4s² = 5s². (Or use sides d and the "triple" side: 2s² + 3s² = 5s².)

Answer: hypotenuse of (s, diagonal) gives 3×; hypotenuse of (s, 2s) gives 5×
4a, b are the shorter sides and c the hypotenuse. Find the missing side: (i) a = 5, b = 7 (ii) a = 8, b = 12 (iii) a = 9, c = 15 (iv) a = 7, b = 12 (v) a = 1.5, b = 3.5
Show solution

(i) c² = 25 + 49 = 74 → c = √74 ≈ 8.60 (between 8 and 9)

(ii) c² = 64 + 144 = 208 → c = √208 ≈ 14.42 (between 14 and 15)

(iii) b² = 15² − 9² = 225 − 81 = 144 → b = 12 (a scaled 3-4-5: × 3)

(iv) c² = 49 + 144 = 193 → c = √193 ≈ 13.89 (between 13 and 14)

(v) c² = 2.25 + 12.25 = 14.5 → c = √14.5 ≈ 3.81 (between 3.8 and 3.9)

Answer: (i) √74 (ii) √208 (iii) 12 (iv) √193 (v) √14.5

📘 Figure it Out · 2.5 Triples from odd squares page 50

1Find 5 more Baudhāyana triples using the odd-square idea.
Show solution

Take an odd square k², find which odd number it is: n = (k² + 1) ÷ 2. Then (n − 1)² + k² = n².

k²nCheckTriple
4925576 + 49 = 625(7, 24, 25)
81411600 + 81 = 1681(9, 40, 41)
121613600 + 121 = 3721(11, 60, 61)
169857056 + 169 = 7225(13, 84, 85)
22511312544 + 225 = 12769(15, 112, 113)
Answer: (7, 24, 25), (9, 40, 41), (11, 60, 61), (13, 84, 85), (15, 112, 113)
2Does this method ever give non-primitive triples?
Show solution

No. The triple is (k, n − 1, n): the hypotenuse n and the side n − 1 are consecutive numbers. Any common factor of all three must divide both n and n − 1, so it divides their difference, 1. So the only common factor is 1.

Answer: No, every triple it makes is primitive
3Are there primitive triples this method cannot produce? Give examples.
Show solution

Yes. This method always gives a hypotenuse just 1 more than a side. But (8, 15, 17) is primitive and 17 − 15 = 2, 17 − 8 = 9. Others: (20, 21, 29) and (12, 35, 37) (37 − 35 = 2), (28, 45, 53).

Answer: Yes, e.g. (8, 15, 17), (20, 21, 29), (12, 35, 37)

📘 Figure it Out · 2.7 Further applications pages 52–54

1Find the diagonal of a square with side 5 cm.
Show solution

d² = 5² + 5² = 50, so d = √50 = 5√2 ≈ 5 × 1.414 ≈ 7.07 cm (7.0 < d < 7.1).

Answer: √50 cm ≈ 7.07 cm
2Find the missing side in each right triangle (the square corner marks the right angle; ? is missing).
Show solution

(a) Shorter sides 7 and 9: c² = 49 + 81 = 130 → c = √130 ≈ 11.40

(b) Shorter sides 4 and 10: c² = 16 + 100 = 116 → c = √116 ≈ 10.77

(c) Side 40, hypotenuse 41: b² = 1681 − 1600 = 81 → b = 9

(d) Side 10, hypotenuse √200: b² = 200 − 100 = 100 → b = 10 (it is an isosceles right triangle!)

(e) Shorter sides 10 and √150: c² = 100 + 150 = 250 → c = √250 ≈ 15.81

(f) Side 27, hypotenuse 45: b² = 2025 − 729 = 1296 → b = 36 (that is 3-4-5 scaled by 9)

Answer: (a) √130 (b) √116 (c) 9 (d) 10 (e) √250 (f) 36
3Find the side of a rhombus whose diagonals are 24 units and 70 units.
Show solution

The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles. So each side is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with sides 24 ÷ 2 = 12 and 70 ÷ 2 = 35.

side² = 12² + 35² = 144 + 1225 = 1369 = 37².

Answer: 37 units
4Is the hypotenuse the longest side of a right triangle? Justify.
Show solution

Yes. c² = a² + b², and b² is more than 0, so c² is bigger than a². For positive lengths, a bigger square means a bigger side, so c > a. In the same way c > b.

(Also: the right angle is the biggest angle of the triangle, the other two add up to 90°, and the longest side is opposite the biggest angle.)

Answer: Yes, because c² = a² + b² is bigger than a² and than b²
5True or False: every Baudhāyana triple is either primitive or a scaled version of a primitive triple.
Show solution

Take any triple (a, b, c). Let f be the HCF of a, b, c. If f = 1 it is primitive. If f > 1, divide: (a/f, b/f, c/f) is still a triple (because (a/f)² + (b/f)² = (a² + b²)/f² = c²/f²) and now has no common factor, so it is primitive. The original is this primitive triple scaled by f. Example: (9, 12, 15) = 3 × (3, 4, 5).

Answer: True
6Give 5 rectangles whose sides and diagonals are all whole numbers.
Show solution

The diagonal of an l × b rectangle satisfies d² = l² + b², so we need Baudhāyana triples.

Answer: 3 × 4 (d 5), 6 × 8 (d 10), 5 × 12 (d 13), 8 × 15 (d 17), 7 × 24 (d 25)
7Construct a square whose area equals the difference of the areas of squares with sides 5 and 7 units.
Show solution

We want area 7² − 5² = 49 − 25 = 24. Use the theorem backwards: in a right triangle with hypotenuse 7 and one side 5, the other side x has x² = 49 − 25 = 24.

  1. Draw AB = 5 units. At B draw a line perpendicular to AB.
  2. With centre A and radius 7 units, draw an arc cutting the perpendicular at C.
  3. BC is the required side (BC = √24 ≈ 4.9). Build a square on BC: its area is 24 sq. units.
Answer: square on side √24 (area 24 sq. units)
8(i) Using grid dots as corners, can you draw a square of area (a) 2 (b) 3 (c) 4 (d) 5 square units? (ii) On an endless grid, which whole-number areas are possible?
Show solution

A grid square whose side steps p across and q up has side² = p² + q², so its area is p² + q².

(a) 2 = 1² + 1² ✔ (b) 3 is not a sum of two squares (0+1, 1+1, 0+4, 1+4 give 1, 2, 4, 5), so no grid square has area 3. (c) 4 = 2² + 0² ✔ (upright 2 × 2) (d) 5 = 1² + 2² ✔

(ii) Exactly the numbers that are a sum of two squares: 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 13, 16, 17, 18, 20, 25, 26, 29, 32, 34, 36, 37, 40, 41, 45, 49, 50, … Numbers like 3, 6, 7, 11, 12, 14, 15, 19, 21 are impossible.

Answer: (i) 2, 4, 5 yes; 3 no. (ii) all areas of the form p² + q²
9Find the area of an equilateral triangle with side 6 units. (Hint: an altitude bisects the opposite side.)
Show solution

Draw the altitude from the top. It splits the triangle into two congruent right triangles (RHS: same hypotenuse 6, common side), so it cuts the base into 3 and 3.

h² = 6² − 3² = 36 − 9 = 27, so h = √27 ≈ 5.20.

Area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 6 × √27 = 3√27 = √243 ≈ 15.59 sq. units (= 9√3).

Answer: 3√27 = 9√3 ≈ 15.59 sq. units

🧩 Puzzle · Find the Colours! page 54

★Three closed boxes hold only red, only blue and only green balls. They are labelled RED, BLUE and GREEN, but every label is wrong. Opening just one box, how can you fix all the labels?
Show solution

Open the box labelled RED (any box works). It is not red, so it is blue or green. Say it is blue.

Now the boxes labelled BLUE and GREEN hold red and green. The box labelled GREEN cannot be green, so it is red, and the box labelled BLUE is green. (If the first box had been green, the same reasoning gives: GREEN-label box = blue, BLUE-label box = red.)

Answer: open one box; the "all labels wrong" rule fixes the other two

✗ (3, 4, 5) + 1 = (4, 5, 6) is a triple

✓ 16 + 25 = 41 ≠ 36. You may multiply a triple by k, not add to it.

a : b : c∷360°xy = k1 : 50×n ÷n🥧Part II · Chapter 3

Proportional Reasoning-2

Ratios grow up: they help us read maps, mix things with many ingredients, share a whole fairly, draw pie charts, and handle quantities that move in opposite directions.

🥧

🍚 3.1 Proportionality: a quick recap

Two related quantities are in a proportional relationship when they both change by the same factor. Idli batter is a good example: one common recipe uses 2 cups of rice for every 1 cup of urad dal, written as the ratio 2 : 1.

Viswanath mixes 6 cups of rice with 3 cups of dal (6 : 3). Puneet mixes 4 cups with 2 cups (4 : 2). Will their idlis taste the same? Check with cross-multiplication:

Both products are 12, so the two ratios are proportional. (Both simplify to 2 : 1.)

💡 a : b and c : d are proportional when a × d = b × c, that is, when ac = bd.
🧠
Memory trick"Outside × outside = inside × inside." In 6 : 3 ∷ 4 : 2, the outer terms are 6 and 2, the inner terms are 3 and 4.

🗺️ 3.2 Ratios in maps

Most maps carry a ratio in a corner, such as RF 1 : 60,00,000. RF means Representative Fraction: the ratio of a distance on the map to the matching distance on the ground.

1 : 60,00,000 means 1 cm on the map = 60,00,000 cm on the ground. Since 1 km = 1,000 m = 1,00,000 cm:

60,00,000 cm ÷ 1,00,000 = 60 km

So every centimetre on this map stands for 60 km. This is the straight-line (geographical) distance, as the crow flies, not the distance by road.

🎬 Measure with a ruler, then use the RF
RF on the map1 cm on the map stands for
1 : 50 (a classroom plan)50 cm = 0.5 m
1 : 1,00,0001,00,000 cm = 1 km
1 : 60,00,00060 km
🎯
Try thisUse two maps with different RFs. The lines between two cities will have different lengths, but after using each map's RF you should get roughly the same real distance. Then sketch your classroom at 1 : 50: a 7 m wall becomes 700 ÷ 50 = 14 cm on paper.

🌶️ 3.3 Ratios with more than 2 terms

Viswanath's spice powder uses 8 spoons coriander, 4 red chillies, 2 spoons toor dal and 1 spoon methi. The ratio is

coriander : chillies : toor dal : methi = 8 : 4 : 2 : 1

A ratio can have many terms, as long as every quantity is scaled by the same factor. Puneet has only 2 chillies, which is half of 4. So he halves everything:

We write 8 : 4 : 2 : 1 ∷ 4 : 2 : 1 : 0.5 (read "is proportional to"). In general,

💡 a : b : c : d ∷ p : q : r : s means ap = bq = cr = ds: one single factor links every pair of terms.
🌍
Real lifeRatio terms do not have to be whole numbers. Half a spoon of methi is perfectly fine: 4 : 2 : 1 : 0.5 is the same taste as 8 : 4 : 2 : 1.

🎨 Know one part? Find all the others

Paint (Example 1). A purple shade needs Red : Blue : White = 2 : 3 : 5. Yasmin has 10 litres of white. White is 5 parts, so

  • 1 part = 10 ÷ 5 = 2 litres
  • Red = 2 parts = 2 × 2 = 4 L; Blue = 3 parts = 3 × 2 = 6 L
  • Total purple paint = 4 + 6 + 10 = 20 L

Concrete (Example 2). Strong concrete for pillars and beams uses cement : sand : gravel = 1 : 1.5 : 3. With 3 bags of cement, the factor is 3, so the ratio becomes 3 : 4.5 : 9, which makes 3 + 4.5 + 9 = 16.5 bags of concrete mixture.

🧠
Memory trickKnown amount ÷ its ratio term = value of 1 part. Then multiply every term by that value.

➗ 3.4 Dividing a whole in a given ratio

To share 12 in the ratio 2 : 1: add the terms (2 + 1 = 3), divide (12 ÷ 3 = 4), and multiply each term: 2 × 4 = 8 and 1 × 4 = 4. The same idea works for any number of terms.

Example 3. We need 110 units of concrete in the ratio 1 : 1.5 : 3. One "batch" of 1 + 1.5 + 3 makes 5.5 units. We need 110 ÷ 5.5 = 20 batches, so we multiply each term by 20:

🎬 Share 110 units of concrete in 1 : 1.5 : 3
💡 To divide a quantity x in the ratio a : b : c : …, the parts are x × aa + b + c + …, x × ba + b + c + …, x × ca + b + c + …, and so on.

Example 4. 50 ml of purple paint in Red : Blue : White = 2 : 3 : 5 (sum 10):
Red = 50 × 210 = 10 ml, Blue = 50 × 310 = 15 ml, White = 50 × 510 = 25 ml.

🎯
Try thisAlways check: the parts must add back to the whole. 10 + 15 + 25 = 50 ✅

🔺 Triangles from ratios

Example 5. Construct a triangle whose angles are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5. The angles of a triangle add up to 180°, so we divide 180° in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5 (sum 9):

∠A = 180° × 19 = 20°,   ∠B = 180° × 39 = 60°,   ∠C = 180° × 59 = 100°

Draw any base AB, make 20° at A and 60° at B; the arms meet at C, and ∠C comes out as 100° automatically.

Sides in a ratio work differently. Sides 3 : 4 : 5 can be 3, 4, 5 cm or 6, 8, 10 cm: all such triangles have the same shape but can have different sizes, so they are not all congruent. Sides 1 : 3 : 5 are impossible: 1 + 3 is less than 5, so the two short sides can never meet.

🧠
Memory trickAngles in a ratio → share 180°. Sides in a ratio → check that the two smaller terms add to more than the largest.

🥧 3.5 A slice of the pie

A pie chart shows how a whole is split into parts. Here are the grades of 40 students:

GradeABCDE
Students1210864

Each slice's angle must be proportional to its number of students. A full turn is 360°, so we divide 360 in the ratio 12 : 10 : 8 : 6 : 4.

Simplify first. Just like a 2-term ratio, divide every term by the HCF. The HCF here is 2, giving 6 : 5 : 4 : 3 : 2 (sum 20). One part = 360° ÷ 20 = 18°.

GradePartsAngle
A66 × 18° = 108°
B55 × 18° = 90°
C44 × 18° = 72°
D33 × 18° = 54°
E22 × 18° = 36°
Total360° ✅
🌍
Real lifePie charts are everywhere: budgets, election results, how you spend your day. One look tells you which part is biggest.

📐 Drawing a pie chart, step by step

You need a compass, a ruler and a protractor. Follow the book's steps:

  1. Draw a circle with centre A and draw one radius AB.
  2. Place the protractor on AB and measure 108° anticlockwise. Draw radius AC: that slice is grade A.
  3. From AC measure 90° and draw AD (grade B).
  4. From AD measure 72° and draw AE (grade C).
  5. Continue with 54° (D); the last slice should come out as 36° (E).
  6. Colour and label each slice.
🎬 Draw the grade pie chart slice by slice
🧠
Memory trickAlways measure each new angle from the last radius you drew, not from AB. The last slice is a free check: it should be exactly the angle left over.

🧱 3.6 Direct proportion and the rule of three

When a : b ∷ c : d, cross-multiplying gives a × d = b × c, so d = b × ca. Knowing three quantities, we find the fourth. This is the rule of three, and such proportions are direct proportions.

Example 1. 5 workers move 4,500 bricks in a day. How many workers move 18,000 bricks in a day?

4,500 : 18,000 ∷ 5 : x  →  x = 18,0004,500 × 5 = 4 × 5 = 20 workers

More bricks → more workers, by the same factor (×4). Both go the same way.

💡 Direct proportion: the quotient stays the same. x1y1 = x2y2 = … = k.

🏍️ Inverse proportion: speed and time

Puneeth's father rides from Lucknow to Kanpur at 30 km/h in 3 hours. By car at 60 km/h, does it take more time? Of course not! Faster means less time. So "30 : 60 ∷ 3 : x" would be wrong here.

WalkBicycleMotorcycleCar
Speed (km/h)5153060
Time (hours)18631.5
Speed × Time90909090

Bicycle is 3 times as fast as walking (15 ÷ 5), and the time drops to one-third (18 ÷ 6 = 3). The two quantities change by the same factor, but in opposite directions. That is an inverse proportion. The product is always 90 km, the fixed distance.

🎬 Faster and faster: the area speed × time stays 90
💡 x and y are inversely proportional if xy = k (a constant). So x1y1 = x2y2, which also means x1x2 = y2y1. Check: walk and car give 560 = 1.518 = 0.0833…
🧠
Memory trickDirect: the quotient is fixed. Inverse: the product is fixed. If one is multiplied by n, the other is multiplied by 1n.

👷 Solving inverse proportion problems

First ask: if one quantity grows, does the other shrink by the same factor? If yes, set the two products equal.

  • Road (Example 3). 20 workers take 4 days. 10 workers? Fewer workers → more days. 20 × 4 = 10 × y, so y = 8 days. Workers halved, days doubled.
  • Pumps (Example 4). 2 pumps fill a tank in 18 h. Add 2 more (4 pumps): 2 × 18 = 4 × x, so x = 9 hours.
  • Food (Example 5). Provisions last 80 students for 15 days. 20 more join (100 students): 80 × 15 = 100 × x, so x = 12 days.
🎬 Workers and days: the area stays the same
🌍
Real lifeThese answers assume every worker (pump, student) works or eats at the same rate, and nothing else changes. Real life is messier, so maths gives the best estimate.

🥕 Working together

Example 6. Ram cuts a pile of vegetables in 1 hour; Shyam takes 1.5 hours. Together? Think of the whole job as 1 unit of work and ask how much each does in 1 hour:

  • Ram: 1 unit per hour.
  • Shyam: 11.5 = 23 unit per hour.
  • Together: 1 + 23 = 53 units per hour.

Work and time are directly proportional: 53 : 1 ∷ 1 : x, so 53 × x = 1 and x = 35 hour = 36 minutes.

🎬 Ram and Shyam cut together
🧠
Memory trickNever add the times (1 + 1.5 = 2.5 h is silly: help cannot make you slower!). Add the work per hour, then flip.
💡 Summary: multi-term ratios scale every term together · divide x in a : b : c by x × aa+b+c, … · pie angles share 360° · direct: fixed quotient · inverse: fixed product.

📘 Figure it Out · 3.4 Dividing a whole in a ratio page 60

1A cricket session of 150 minutes is split as warm-up/cool-down : batting : bowling : fielding = 3 : 4 : 3 : 5. How much time goes to each activity?
Show solution

Sum of the terms = 3 + 4 + 3 + 5 = 15. One part = 150 ÷ 15 = 10 minutes.

Warm-up/cool-down = 3 × 10 = 30 min, batting = 4 × 10 = 40 min, bowling = 3 × 10 = 30 min, fielding = 5 × 10 = 50 min. Check: 30 + 40 + 30 + 50 = 150 ✅

Answer: 30 min, 40 min, 30 min, 50 min
2A library has Odiya : Hindi : English books = 3 : 2 : 1. There are 288 Odiya books. How many Hindi and English books are there?
Show solution

Odiya is 3 parts = 288, so 1 part = 288 ÷ 3 = 96.

Hindi = 2 parts = 2 × 96 = 192. English = 1 part = 96.

Answer: 192 Hindi books and 96 English books
3I have 100 coins: number of ₹10 : ₹5 : ₹2 : ₹1 coins = 4 : 3 : 2 : 1. How much money is this?
Show solution

Sum of terms = 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10, so one part = 100 ÷ 10 = 10 coins.

Coins: 40 of ₹10, 30 of ₹5, 20 of ₹2, 10 of ₹1.

Money = 40 × 10 + 30 × 5 + 20 × 2 + 10 × 1 = 400 + 150 + 40 + 10 = ₹600.

Careful: the ratio is of the number of coins, not of the money.

Answer: ₹600
4Construct a triangle with sidelengths in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5. Will all triangles with this ratio of sides be congruent? Why or why not?
Show solution

Choose a unit, say 2 cm: sides 6 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm. Draw BC = 10 cm, an arc of 6 cm from B and an arc of 8 cm from C; they meet at A. (You will find ∠A = 90°, since 6² + 8² = 10².)

Not all such triangles are congruent. 3, 4, 5 cm and 6, 8, 10 cm both have the ratio 3 : 4 : 5, but their sides are different lengths. They have the same shape (same angles) but different sizes. Congruent triangles must match exactly.

Answer: No; they have the same shape but can have different sizes
5Can you construct a triangle with sidelengths in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5? Why or why not?
Show solution

Take the sides as k, 3k and 5k. In any triangle the two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest side. Here k + 3k = 4k, which is less than 5k. The two short sides cannot reach each other, whatever unit k we choose.

Answer: No, because 1 + 3 < 5

📘 Figure it Out · 3.5 Pie charts pages 62–63

1360 people voted for their favourite season: 90 summer, 120 rainy, the rest winter. Draw a pie chart.
Show solution

Winter = 360 − 90 − 120 = 150 people. There are 360 people and 360°, so each person gets exactly 1°.

Summer 90°, Rainy 120°, Winter 150° (total 360° ✅). Draw a radius, then measure 90°, 120° and 150° in turn.

Answer: Summer 90°, Rainy 120°, Winter 150°
2Draw a pie chart of favourite TV channels: Entertainment 50%, Sports 25%, News 15%, Information 10%.
Show solution

100% is the whole circle, 360°, so 1% = 3.6°.

Entertainment = 50 × 3.6 = 180°, Sports = 25 × 3.6 = 90°, News = 15 × 3.6 = 54°, Information = 10 × 3.6 = 36°. Total 360° ✅

Answer: 180°, 90°, 54°, 36°
3Survey your class: each student picks one favourite subject (Language, Arts Education, Vocational Education, Social Science, Physical Education, Maths, Science). Fill in the table and draw a pie chart.
Show solution

Your numbers will be your own. Here is a sample class of 36 students: Language 6, Arts 4, Vocational 3, Social Science 5, Physical Education 6, Maths 8, Science 4.

Each student = 360° ÷ 36 = 10°. Angles: 60°, 40°, 30°, 50°, 60°, 80°, 40° (total 360° ✅).

Method for any class: angle = (students for that subject ÷ total students) × 360°. Use the Pie chart maker in the Lab to check your own data.

Answer: angle = (number ÷ total) × 360° for each subject

📘 Figure it Out · 3.6 Inverse proportions page 65

1Which of these tables show inverse proportion?
(i) x: 40, 80, 25, 16 · y: 20, 10, 32, 50
(ii) x: 40, 80, 25, 16 · y: 20, 10, 12.5, 8
(iii) x: 30, 90, 150, 10 · y: 15, 5, 3, 45
Show solution

For inverse proportion, x × y must be the same for every column.

(i) 40 × 20 = 800, 80 × 10 = 800, 25 × 32 = 800, 16 × 50 = 800. Always 800 → inverse.

(ii) 800, 800, 25 × 12.5 = 312.5, 16 × 8 = 128. Not constant → not inverse. (Here x ÷ y = 2 every time, so it is a direct proportion.)

(iii) 30 × 15 = 450, 90 × 5 = 450, 150 × 3 = 450, 10 × 45 = 450 → inverse.

Answer: (i) and (iii)
2x and y are in inverse proportion. Fill in the gaps: x: 16, 12, __, 36 · y: 9, __, 48, __
Show solution

k = 16 × 9 = 144, so every x × y = 144.

x = 12 → y = 144 ÷ 12 = 12.   y = 48 → x = 144 ÷ 48 = 3.   x = 36 → y = 144 ÷ 36 = 4.

Answer: x: 16, 12, 3, 36 · y: 9, 12, 48, 4

📘 Figure it Out · end of chapter pages 67–68

1Which pairs are in inverse proportion? (i) taps filling a tank and time taken; (ii) painters hired and days to paint a fixed wall; (iii) distance a car can go and petrol in the tank; (iv) a cyclist's speed and time for a fixed route; (v) length of cloth and price at a fixed rate per metre; (vi) pages in a book and reading time at a fixed speed.
Show solution

Ask: if the first doubles, does the second halve (inverse) or double (direct)?

(i) More taps → less time: inverse. (ii) More painters → fewer days: inverse. (iii) More petrol → farther: direct. (iv) Faster → less time: inverse. (v) More cloth → more money: direct. (vi) More pages → more time: direct.

Answer: (i), (ii) and (iv) are inverse
224 pencils cost ₹120. What do 20 such pencils cost?
Show solution

Direct proportion: 24 : 20 ∷ 120 : x, so x = 20 × 120 ÷ 24 = ₹100. (Or: 1 pencil = ₹5, so 20 pencils = ₹100.)

Answer: ₹100
3A water tank supplies 20 families for 6 days. If 10 more families move in, how long will the water last? What assumptions are needed?
Show solution

More families → fewer days: inverse. Now there are 30 families. 20 × 6 = 30 × x, so x = 120 ÷ 30 = 4 days.

Assumptions: every family uses the same amount of water each day, usage does not change, and the tank is not refilled or leaking.

Answer: 4 days
4Each ring shows a 24-hour day; the blue part is sleep. Match each animal with its hours of sleep from: 15, 2.5, 20, 8, 3.5, 13, 10.5, 18.
Show solution

The whole ring is 24 hours, so a blue fraction f means f × 24 hours. Sort the blue parts from smallest to largest and match them with the sorted list 2.5, 3.5, 8, 10.5, 13, 15, 18, 20.

Giraffe ≈ 110 of the ring → 2.5 h; elephant ≈ 17 → 3.5 h; human = 13 → 8 h; dog a little less than half → 10.5 h; cat a little more than half → 13 h; squirrel ≈ 58 → 15 h; python = 34 → 18 h; bat ≈ 56 → 20 h.

Answer: giraffe 2.5, elephant 3.5, human 8, dog 10.5, cat 13, squirrel 15, python 18, bat 20 hours
5A pie chart shows how children get to school: Walk 90°, Bus 120°, Cycle 60°, Two-wheeler 60°, and a Car slice (angle not marked). (i) Most common mode? (ii) What fraction go by car? (iii) If 18 children go by car, how many took part? How many use taxis? (iv) Which two modes have equal numbers?
Show solution

Car angle = 360° − (90° + 120° + 60° + 60°) = 30°.

(i) The biggest slice is Bus (120°). (ii) Car = 30 ÷ 360 = 112. (iii) 112 of the children = 18, so total = 18 × 12 = 216 children. There is no taxi slice, so 0 children use taxis. (iv) Cycle and Two-wheeler (60° each, 36 children each).

Answer: (i) Bus (ii) 1/12 (iii) 216 children; none by taxi (iv) Cycle and Two-wheeler
6Three workers paint a fence in 4 days. If one more worker joins, how many days will it take? What are the assumptions?
Show solution

Inverse: 3 × 4 = 4 × x, so x = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 days.

Assumptions: all workers paint at the same speed, work the same hours each day, and do not get in each other's way.

Answer: 3 days
7A pump fills 2 equal tanks in 6 hours. How long for 5 such tanks with the same pump?
Show solution

This is direct: more tanks → more time. 1 tank takes 6 ÷ 2 = 3 hours, so 5 tanks take 5 × 3 = 15 hours.

Answer: 15 hours
8Chairs are set in 25 rows of 12. If they are rearranged with 20 chairs in each row, how many rows are there?
Show solution

Total chairs stay fixed: 25 × 12 = 300. Rows × chairs per row = 300, so rows = 300 ÷ 20 = 15.

Answer: 15 rows
9A school has 8 periods of 45 minutes a day. With 9 periods in the same school day, how long is each period?
Show solution

School time = 8 × 45 = 360 minutes, which stays fixed. 9 × x = 360, so x = 40 minutes.

Answer: 40 minutes
10A small pump fills a tank in 3 hours, a large one in 2 hours. How long do both together take?
Show solution

In 1 hour: small pump fills 13 tank, large pump fills 12 tank. Together 13 + 12 = 56 tank per hour.

Time for 1 tank: 56 × x = 1, so x = 65 hours = 1.2 hours = 1 hour 12 minutes.

Answer: 6/5 hours = 1 hour 12 minutes
1142 machines make a batch of toys in 63 days. How many machines are needed to make it in 54 days?
Show solution

Fewer days → more machines: inverse. 42 × 63 = 54 × x, so x = 2,646 ÷ 54 = 49.

Answer: 49 machines
12A car takes 2 hours at 60 km/h. How long at 80 km/h?
Show solution

Distance fixed = 60 × 2 = 120 km. 80 × x = 120, so x = 1.5 hours = 1 hour 30 minutes.

Answer: 1.5 hours

8ⁿ❄△⬡🐜3ⁿ▦Part II · Chapter 4

Exploring Some Geometric Themes

Shapes that hide smaller copies of themselves, and clever ways to see, unfold, project and draw solid objects on flat paper.

🧊

🌿 Fractals: shapes with copies of themselves inside

Look closely at a fern leaf. Each small leaflet looks like a tiny copy of the whole leaf, and each leaflet has even tinier copies on it! A shape that repeats the same pattern at smaller and smaller sizes is called a fractal. We say it is self-similar.

  • 🌳 A tree: trunk → big limbs → branches → twigs. Each part branches like the whole tree.
  • ☁️ Clouds, ⛰️ mountains, ⚡ lightning and 🏖️ coastlines also look "the same" when you zoom in.

Mathematicians make perfect fractals by a rule that is repeated again and again. Each repeat is called a step: Step 0, Step 1, Step 2, … The fractal is what the steps get closer and closer to.

💡 A fractal = one simple rule, repeated forever, at smaller and smaller sizes.

🟪 The Sierpinski Carpet

The Polish mathematician Wacław Sierpinski made this fractal. The rule: cut a square into a 3 × 3 grid of 9 equal squares and remove the middle one. Then do the same to each of the 8 squares that are left, and so on.

🎬 Build the carpet step by step and count

Let Rn = number of squares remaining at Step n, and Hn = number of holes.

  • Every remaining square turns into 8 smaller ones: Rn+1 = 8 × Rn, so Rn = 8n.
  • Every remaining square also makes one new hole, and old holes stay: Hn+1 = Hn + Rn.
  • So Hn = 1 + 8 + 82 + … + 8n−1.
Step n01234
Squares Rn = 8n18645124,096
Holes Hn01973585
Area left189648151272940966561
🧠
ShortcutThe holes form a pattern: 0, 1, 9, 73, 585 … Each is 8 times the one before, plus 1. A neat formula: Hn = (8n − 1) ÷ 7. Check: (64 − 1) ÷ 7 = 9 ✓

🔺 The Sierpinski Gasket (Triangle)

Same idea with a triangle. Join the midpoints of the sides of an equilateral triangle. This cuts it into 4 identical equilateral triangles. Remove the middle one, then repeat on the 3 triangles that remain.

Why are all 4 pieces equilateral? Look at corner triangle ARP. AR and AP are each half of a side, so they are equal: the triangle is isosceles with a 60° angle at A. Its other two angles are equal and add to 120°, so each is 60°. All angles 60° → equilateral, with side = half the big side. The same is true at B and C, and then the middle triangle PQR has all three sides equal to half the big side too.

Step n0123n
Triangles left139273n
Holes014131 + 3 + … + 3n−1
Area left1349162764(34)n
🎯
Try thisEach step keeps 34 of the area. After 10 steps only about 5.6% is left, but the shape still stretches right across the original triangle! 😮

❄️ The Koch Snowflake

Named after the Swedish mathematician Helge von Koch (1904). Start with an equilateral triangle. On every side:

  1. divide the side into 3 equal parts,
  2. raise an equilateral triangle on the middle part, and remove that middle part.

Each straight side becomes a "bump" of 4 pieces, each 13 as long. Then repeat on every new side.

🎬 Grow the snowflake and watch the sides multiply
Step n0123n
Number of sides312481923 × 4n
Length of one side1131912713n
Perimeter341636493 × (43)n
💡 Each step multiplies the perimeter by 43, so it grows without end, yet the snowflake always fits inside a small circle!
🤩
Fractals in artSome of the oldest human-made fractals are in Indian temples. The Kandariya Mahadev Temple at Khajuraho (about 1025 CE) is a tall tower made of smaller copies of itself, which carry even smaller copies! Temples in Madurai, Hampi, Rameswaram and Varanasi show this too. Fulani wedding blankets from Nigeria have diamonds inside diamonds, and the Dutch artist M. C. Escher drew lizards that get "smaller and smaller" towards the edge.

🧠 Build it in your imagination: profiles of solids

Great engineers like Nikola Tesla built machines in their minds first. Practise "seeing" shapes without drawing them:

  • Cut the 4 corners off a square, joining midpoints of neighbouring sides → a smaller square (tilted), with half the area. The 4 corner triangles fit together into another square of the same size!
  • Cut the corners of an equilateral triangle up to the "thirds" marks → a regular hexagon.
  • Do the same with a square → an octagon (but not a regular one).

When we look at a solid from one direction, we see its profile (outline). The same solid can have very different profiles! Imagine the solid crashing through a wall like a cartoon character: the hole it leaves is the profile.

🎯
Try thisA cylinder: rectangle from the side, circle from the top. A cone: triangle and circle. A bucket: trapezium and circle. Can you find a solid that looks like a pentagon from one side and a rectangle from another? (Hint: think of a pencil 😉)

🧊 Solids: faces, edges, vertices, prisms and pyramids

Faces are the flat surfaces on the boundary of a solid. Edges are the line segments where faces meet. Vertices are the corner points where edges meet. A cube or cuboid has 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices.

Prism: two congruent polygons as opposite faces, with edges joining matching corners. All the other faces are parallelograms (rectangles in an upright prism). It is named after its end polygon.

Pyramid: a polygon base and one point outside it (the apex), joined to every corner of the base. A triangular pyramid is also called a tetrahedron.

End/base has n sidesFacesEdgesVertices
Prismn + 23n2n
Pyramidn + 12nn + 1
Prism, n = 10123020
Pyramid, n = 10112011
🧠
How to rememberPrism edges: n on top + n on the bottom + n going up = 3n. Pyramid edges: n round the base + n up to the apex = 2n.

📦 Nets of a cube and a tetrahedron

Many solids can be made by folding a flat sheet. The flat shape that folds into a solid is called its net. Think of it as the solid "unfolded" onto the table. (Extra flaps for glue are useful in real life, but they are not part of the net.)

This cross shape (Fig. 4.1) folds into a cube: the column of 4 wraps around, and the two side squares become the left and right faces.

🎬 Fold a net into a cube

A cube has exactly 11 different nets (we count two nets as the same if one is a turned or flipped copy of the other):

A regular tetrahedron (4 equilateral triangle faces) has only 2 nets: a big triangle split into 4, and a strip of 4 triangles.

Quick checks for cube netsExactly 6 squares · no 2 × 2 block · never 5 in a row · two squares that would both land on the same face → not a net.

🥫 Nets of a cylinder, cone, octahedron … and a sphere?

Cylinder: unfold the two circles and slit the curved surface along its height. The curved part opens into a rectangle: one side is the height h, the other is the distance round the circle, 2πr.

🎬 Peel the label off a tin

Cone: slit it along a line from the tip O to the base. Every point of the base circle is the same distance from O (the slant height), so the curved part unrolls into a part of a circle with centre O (a sector). Add the circular base.

Octahedron: two square pyramids glued base to base → 8 equilateral triangles. Like the cube, it has 11 nets. Here is one:

🤩
Did you know?A dodecahedron has 12 regular pentagon faces, and mathematicians have counted exactly 43,380 different nets for it! But a sphere has no net: any flat paper wrapped round a ball must wrinkle, overlap or leave gaps. That is why world maps always stretch some countries 🌍

🐜 Shortest paths on a cuboid: the ant and the laddu

On flat paper the shortest path between two points is a straight line. But a hungry ant on a box must walk on the surface. Which path to the laddu is shortest?

Big idea: unfold the box into a net. Any path on the box becomes a path of the same length on the net, and the other way round. So the shortest path on the box is a straight line on a suitable net.

🎬 Unfold the box and draw a straight line

Box 8 cm × 4 cm × 4 cm. The ant is at the centre of an end face; the laddu sits on the bottom front edge, 2 cm from that end.

✗ line leaves the net
✓ unfold differently

In the second net the end face is attached to the front face. The ant is 2 cm from the edge and 2 cm above the bottom; the laddu is 4 cm along. Shortest path = √(42 + 22) = √20 ≈ 4.47 cm.

💡 The way you unfold matters! A line that goes outside the net is not a real path. Try every sensible unfolding and pick the shortest straight line.
🎯
The trickier case (30 × 12 × 12 box)Ant 1 cm below the top on one end, laddu 1 cm above the bottom on the other end. Going straight up, across and down is 1 + 30 + 11 = 42 cm. But a clever net that crosses 5 faces gives a right triangle with legs 24 and 32: d2 = 242 + 322 = 1600, so d = 40 cm, shorter! (This is the famous "spider and fly" puzzle.)
42 cm
40 cm 🏆

🔦 Projections

Drawings help engineers and builders share exact information about objects. One way to draw a solid on paper is by projection.

Take a point P and a plane M. Drop a line from P that is perpendicular to the plane (it makes 90° with every line in the plane through its foot O). The foot O is the projection of P on M. Projecting every point of an object gives the projection of the whole object, like the hole it would make if pushed straight through the plane.

🎬 Tilt a stick and watch its projection shrink

Stick AB has length l; its projection DC has length p. Draw AE parallel to DC. AECD is a rectangle, so AE = p. Triangle AEB has a right angle at E, so the hypotenuse AB is the longest side: p ≤ l.

p = l only when the stick is parallel to the plane. If the stick is perpendicular to the plane, its projection is just a point.

  • A square can project to a square, a rectangle, a parallelogram, or a line segment (edge-on).
  • Parallel lines project to parallel lines (or both to points). So a parallelogram always projects to a parallelogram, never to some other quadrilateral (or to a segment when edge-on).
  • Different objects can give the same projection: a cube, a short cuboid and a long cuboid all project to the same square if they stand end-on.

👀 Front view, top view, side view … and shadows

One projection is not enough to know an object. So we use three planes at right angles:

  • Front view = projection on the vertical plane in front.
  • Top view = projection on the horizontal plane below.
  • Side view = projection on the side plane.
🎬 Top, front and side views of a cube stack

Example: a stack of cubes and its three views (in the side view, the front of the stack is on the left):

Front
Top
Side
☀️
ShadowsShine a torch straight at a wall with an object in between: the shadow looks like the projection, but bigger, and it shrinks as you move the torch further back. The Sun is so far away that its rays are almost parallel, so when sunlight falls perpendicular to a surface, the shadow is just the projection! Turn a cardboard parallelogram in sunlight: its shadow is always a parallelogram.

⬡ Isometric projection and isometric drawing

Balance a cube perfectly on one corner and project it straight down. Now all 12 edges project to the same length, because every edge makes the same angle with the floor. This is the isometric projection (Greek: "equal measure"). The outline is a regular hexagon.

Tile the page with these hexagons and you get an isometric grid. Its lines go in three directions: | for height, and the two slanting families for length and depth.

🎬 Draw a cube edge by edge on isometric paper

Why it works: parallel edges stay parallel when projected, so the three families of edges of a solid become the three families of grid lines, and one unit along any axis is the same length on paper. Count units along each direction as you draw.

The five Tetris shapes (four squares joined edge to edge) become these solids when you use cubes:

I (row of 4)
O (square)
T
L
S / Z

📘 Figure it Out · Sierpinski Triangle page 72

1Draw the first few steps (at least up to Step 2) of the shape sequence that leads to the Sierpinski Triangle.
Show solution

Step 0: an equilateral triangle. Step 1: join the midpoints of its sides and remove the middle triangle. Step 2: do the same in each of the 3 small triangles that are left.

Answer: see the drawing (1, 3, then 9 shaded triangles)
2Find the number of holes and the number of triangles remaining at each step.
Show solution

Each remaining triangle becomes 3 smaller ones, so the number of triangles is multiplied by 3 every step: Tn+1 = 3 × Tn, giving Tn = 3n.

Each remaining triangle also creates one new hole, and old holes stay: Hn+1 = Hn + Tn. So H0 = 0, H1 = 1, H2 = 1 + 3 = 4, H3 = 1 + 3 + 9 = 13, …

In general Hn = 1 + 3 + 32 + … + 3n−1 = (3n − 1) ÷ 2. Check: (27 − 1) ÷ 2 = 13 ✓

Answer: triangles 3ⁿ; holes 1 + 3 + … + 3ⁿ⁻¹ = (3ⁿ − 1)/2
3Find the area remaining at Step n for both Sierpinski fractals, taking the starting square / triangle to have area 1 square unit.
Show solution

Carpet: at each step every remaining square loses its middle ninth, so 89 of the area stays. Area at Step n = (89)n. (Also: 8n squares, each of area 19n.)

Gasket: every remaining triangle loses its middle quarter, so 34 stays. Area at Step n = (34)n. (Also: 3n triangles, each of area 14n.)

Both areas get closer and closer to 0 as n grows.

Answer: carpet (8/9)ⁿ, gasket (3/4)ⁿ square units

📘 Figure it Out · Koch Snowflake page 73

1Draw the first few steps (at least up to Step 2) of the sequence that leads to the Koch Snowflake.
Show solution

Step 0: equilateral triangle. Step 1: on each side, raise a triangle on the middle third (a 6-pointed star with 12 sides). Step 2: do it again on all 12 sides.

Answer: see the drawing
2Find the number of sides at Step n.
Show solution

Each side is replaced by a bump made of 4 sides. So the number of sides is multiplied by 4 at each step: 3, 12, 48, 192, …

Answer: 3 × 4ⁿ sides
3Find the perimeter at Step n, if the starting triangle has side 1 unit.
Show solution

At Step n each side has length 13n (each step cuts the length into thirds), and there are 3 × 4n sides.

Perimeter = 3 × 4n × 13n = 3 × (43)n. For example Step 1: 4 units, Step 2: 163 units, Step 3: 649 units.

Answer: 3 × (4/3)ⁿ units (it keeps growing)

📘 Build it in Your Imagination pages 75–77

1Picture your name and read its letters backwards by sight.
Show solution

There is no single answer: close your eyes, "see" the name written large, and move your mind's eye from the last letter to the first. Example: BHAVANA → A, N, A, V, A, H, B. Practise with longer names to build visualisation power.

Answer: a visualisation exercise
2Cut off the four corners of a square, each cut joining midpoints of adjacent sides. What is left? How can the four corners make another square?
Show solution

The cuts join the 4 midpoints, leaving a square turned through 45° whose area is half of the original. Each corner piece is a right isosceles triangle. Put the 4 right angles together at one point, with the long sides outside: they form a second square, the same size as the one left over.

Answer: a smaller (tilted) square; the 4 corners make an equal square
3Mark each side of an equilateral triangle in thirds and cut off each corner up to the marks. What shape remains?
Show solution

Each cut-off corner is an equilateral triangle of side 13. What is left has 6 sides, all equal to 13 of the original side, and all angles 120°.

Answer: a regular hexagon
4Do the same with a square (cut corners up to the "thirds" marks). What shape is left?
Show solution

8 sides remain: 4 are the middle thirds of the old sides (length 13 of a side) and 4 are the cuts (each is the slanting side of a right isosceles triangle with legs 13, so it is longer). All angles are 135°, but the sides are not all equal.

Answer: an octagon (not a regular one)
5–7Describe a solid and a viewpoint that give a (5) square, (6) circular, (7) triangular outline.
Show solution
  • (5) A cube seen face-on (or a square pyramid from above, a cylinder whose height equals its diameter from the side).
  • (6) A sphere from any direction, or a cylinder or cone from above.
  • (7) A cone from the side, or a triangular prism looking along its length.
Answer: e.g. cube, sphere/cylinder, cone
8–12Find solids with these pairs of profiles: (8) rectangle and circle, (9) circle and triangle, (10) rectangle and triangle, (11) trapezium and circle, (12) pentagon and rectangle. Are the answers unique?
Show solution
  • (8) A cylinder: side → rectangle, top → circle.
  • (9) A cone: top → circle, side → triangle.
  • (10) A triangular prism (like a tent): end → triangle, side → rectangle.
  • (11) A bucket (a cone with its tip cut off): side → trapezium, top → circle.
  • (12) A pentagonal prism (like a pencil with 5 flat faces): end → pentagon, side → rectangle.

They are not unique. For (10), a wedge (a cuboid cut in half along a diagonal of one face) also works; for (6), a sphere, a cylinder and a cone all give circles; for (12), a house-shaped prism (a cuboid with a triangular roof on top) gives a pentagon from the end and a rectangle from the front. Many solids work.

Answer: cylinder, cone, triangular prism, bucket, pentagonal prism (others possible)

📘 Try these from the text · Solids and nets pages 79–83

aA prism has 10-sided end faces. How many faces, edges and vertices? What if they have n sides?
Show solution

Faces: 2 ends + 10 side faces = 12. Edges: 10 + 10 + 10 = 30. Vertices: 10 + 10 = 20. For n sides: n + 2 faces, 3n edges, 2n vertices.

Answer: 12 faces, 30 edges, 20 vertices; (n + 2, 3n, 2n)
bA pyramid has a 10-sided base. How many faces, edges and vertices? What if the base has n sides?
Show solution

Faces: 1 base + 10 triangles = 11. Edges: 10 round the base + 10 to the apex = 20. Vertices: 10 + apex = 11. For n sides: n + 1 faces, 2n edges, n + 1 vertices.

Answer: 11 faces, 20 edges, 11 vertices; (n + 1, 2n, n + 1)
cWhich of these are nets of a regular tetrahedron?
A
B
C
D
Show solution

A tetrahedron has 4 faces and 3 faces meet at each corner. A (big triangle) and C (strip of 4) fold up perfectly. B has 4 triangles meeting at one point, but only 3 faces meet at a corner of a tetrahedron, so two faces would overlap. D has 5 triangles, one too many.

Answer: A and C (these are the only 2 nets)
dDraw nets, with measurements, for a regular tetrahedron, a square pyramid and a triangular prism.
Show solution

Tetrahedron: draw an equilateral triangle of side 10 cm, mark the midpoints and join them (net A above): every face is a 5 cm equilateral triangle. Square pyramid: a 5 cm square with an equilateral triangle of side 5 cm on each side. Triangular prism: three 10 cm × 4 cm rectangles side by side, with a 4 cm equilateral triangle on each end of the middle one.

square pyramid
triangular prism
Answer: see the nets
eWhat are the side lengths of the rectangle in the net of a cylinder? What does a cone's net look like?
Show solution

The rectangle is h (height) by 2πr (the circumference of the base circle), because it wraps exactly once round the circle. A cone opens into a sector of a circle (centre at the tip O, radius = slant height) plus the base circle. If you roll the same sector up so that O is not the centre of the curved edge, the edge is not at a fixed distance from the tip, so you get a slanting, lopsided cone whose base edge does not lie in one flat circle.

Answer: h × 2πr; a sector + a circle

📘 Figure it Out · Nets of a cube pages 80–81

1Which of these are nets of a cube?
(i)
(ii)
(iii)
(iv)
(v)
(vi)
Show solution
  • (i) ✗ The row of 4 wraps round to make 4 side faces. The square above its first square is the top. The extra square stuck to the left of the top folds down onto the left side, which is already covered by the 4th square of the row: overlap.
  • (ii) ✓ Two rows of 3 joined in a staircase: they fold into a cube.
  • (iii) ✓ The 2-2-2 staircase: each pair folds onto a new pair of faces.
  • (iv) ✓ A row of 4 with one square above and one below: the classic cross.
  • (v) ✗ The row of 4 gives the side faces; the square below the 2nd square is the bottom; the square under that would fold up onto the side face opposite the 2nd square, which is already used.
  • (vi) ✓ Row of 4 with one square above and one below (on different columns): a net.

You can test them in the Cube net tester lab too.

Answer: (ii), (iii), (iv), (vi) are nets; (i) and (v) are not
2A cube has 11 different nets (turned or flipped copies count as the same). Find all 11.
Show solution

Sort them by their longest row. Row of 4 (with one square on each side of it): 6 nets. Row of 3 as the longest: 4 nets. Rows of 2 only (the 2-2-2 staircase): 1 net. Total 6 + 4 + 1 = 11. (Checked by a computer search through all 35 shapes made of 6 squares.)

3Draw a net of a cuboid with sides (i) 5 cm, 3 cm, 1 cm (ii) 6 cm, 3 cm, 2 cm.
Show solution

A cuboid has 3 pairs of equal rectangles: l × b, l × h and b × h. Put the four faces that go round the box in a column (l × h, l × b, l × h, l × b) and the two b × h ends on either side of one l × b face.

(i) 5 × 3 × 1
(ii) 6 × 3 × 2

Check the area: (i) 2(15 + 5 + 3) = 46 cm²; (ii) 2(18 + 12 + 6) = 72 cm².

Answer: see the nets (areas 46 cm² and 72 cm²)

📘 Try these from the text · Shortest paths pages 84–87

aThe ant is at the centre of a side face of a cuboid and the laddu at the centre of the top face. What is the shortest path? Is a path that goes along the top edge and then turns the shortest?
Show solution

Unfold the side face so it lies flat next to the top face. The shortest path is the straight line between them on this net, which crosses the common edge at a right angle. A path that bends (like going to a corner first) becomes a bent line on the net, so it is longer.

Answer: the path that is straight on the net
bBox 8 cm × 4 cm × 4 cm, ant at the centre of an end face, laddu on the bottom front edge 2 cm from that end. Find the shortest path.
Show solution

If the end face is attached to the top face, the straight line goes outside the net, so it is not a real path. Attach the end face to the front face instead. Now the ant is 2 cm beyond the end and 2 cm above the bottom edge, and the laddu is on the bottom edge 2 cm before the end. Horizontal gap 2 + 2 = 4 cm, vertical gap 2 cm.

d = √(4² + 2²) = √20 ≈ 4.47 cm. (Attaching the end face to the bottom face gives the same length.)

Answer: √20 ≈ 4.47 cm
cBox 30 cm × 12 cm × 12 cm. Ant on one end, 1 cm below the top, centred; laddu on the far end, 1 cm above the bottom, centred. Length of the shortest path?
Show solution

Straight up, along the top and down: 1 + 30 + 11 = 42 cm. Another unfolding (end, floor, side wall, top, end) makes a right triangle with legs 24 cm and 32 cm: d² = 24² + 32² = 576 + 1024 = 1600, d = 40 cm. We checked every possible route with a computer (cutting the surface into a fine mesh): nothing is shorter than 40 cm.

42
40
Answer: 40 cm

📘 Try these from the text · Projections pages 88–91

aCompare the length l of a line and the length p of its projection. When are they equal?
Show solution

In right triangle AEB, AB = l is the hypotenuse and AE = p is a leg, so p ≤ l. They are equal only when B is at the same height as A, i.e. the line is parallel to the plane.

Answer: p ≤ l; equal when the line is parallel to the plane
bWhat projections can a square, a parallelogram and a regular n-sided polygon have?
Show solution

Square: a square (parallel to the plane), a rectangle (tilted about one edge), a parallelogram (tilted any other way) or a line segment (edge-on). Parallelogram: always a parallelogram (or a segment), never any other quadrilateral, because each pair of parallel sides projects to a parallel pair. Regular n-gon: a "squashed" n-gon whose opposite parallel sides stay parallel; it is regular only when the polygon is parallel to the plane, and it becomes a segment when edge-on.

Answer: parallel lines stay parallel; shapes get squashed, not "bent"
cFind another object with the same projection as a cone.
Show solution

A cone standing on its base projects to a triangle on a wall behind it: a flat cardboard triangle or a triangular prism seen end-on gives the same triangle. Its projection on the floor is a circle: a cylinder, a coin or a sphere of the same width gives the same circle.

Answer: e.g. a flat triangle (front) or a cylinder/disc (top)

📘 Figure it Out · Views pages 92–93

1Look at the front, top and side views of the different lines in Fig. 4.6 (lines in a horizontal plane, all with the same front view). Is there a relation between their lengths?
Show solution

All the front views are the same length. The more a line points "into" the page, the longer its side view and its top view. Because these lines are horizontal, the top view shows the true length. The line is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the front view and the side view, so by the Baudhayana theorem:

(top view)² = (front view)² + (side view)²

For any line at all, with sides a, b, c of its "box": front² + top² + side² = (a² + c²) + (a² + b²) + (b² + c²) = 2 × (true length)².

Answer: top² = front² + side² (for these horizontal lines)
