5Find the number of cubes in the stack (a pyramid-like corner stack showing 4, 3, 2, 1 cubes in its rows).
Show solution

Every cube must rest on cubes below, so the hidden layers count too. The stack is built in layers against a back corner: the top layer has 1 cube, the next 1 + 2 = 3, then 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, then 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 on the floor.

Total = 1 + 3 + 6 + 10 = 20 (10 can be seen, 10 are hidden).

Answer: 20 cubes
6What shapes can the projection of a cube make in different positions?
Show solution

Face-on: a square. Turned about one edge: a rectangle (two faces show). Turned any other way: a hexagon (three faces show), which is a regular hexagon when the cube is balanced on a corner.

Answer: square, rectangle or hexagon

📘 Figure it Out · Isometric drawing pages 100–102

1Besides the 5 Tetris shapes, are there other ways to glue four cubes together along faces?
Show solution

Yes! Three shapes do not lie flat: the tripod (three cubes on a corner cube, pointing in three directions) and two screws that twist left and right (mirror images of each other). So there are 5 + 3 = 8 shapes (7 if you count the two mirror screws as one).

tripod (corner)
left screw
right screw
Answer: yes, 3 more (tripod and two screws)
2Draw the three given figures (an L-shaped wall, a T-shaped step and a staircase) on the isometric grid.
Show solution

Count units along height (|), length and depth as you go, and decide for each edge whether it goes up or down, forwards or backwards. Here they are drawn with cubes so you can count the units:

Answer: see the drawings
3Is there anything strange about the path of the ball on the staircase? Recreate it on the grid.
Show solution

The ball goes down step after step round the loop, yet it comes back to where it started! That is impossible. Any small part of the drawing is a real staircase, but the parts cannot all fit together in 3D. The trick works because in isometric drawing, moving one unit along each of the three axes adds up to zero on paper: a climb along the hidden (viewing) direction looks like no climb at all. This is the Penrose staircase.

Answer: the ball always goes down but returns to its start (impossible staircase)
4Observe the "impossible triangle". (i) Can it be built from real cubes? What are its front, top and side profiles? (ii) Draw it on the grid. (iii) Why does the illusion work?
Show solution

(i) Not as a closed triangle. But you can build three straight bars of cubes, each along a different axis (up, then sideways, then towards you), joined end to end. From exactly one viewpoint the free end seems to touch the start. From the front, the top and the side, each profile is just an L-shape (two bars at right angles, with the third bar seen end-on as one square).

(ii) Draw one bar along each of the three grid directions, each the same length, so the third bar ends where the first began.

(iii) On isometric paper, equal steps along length, depth and height add up to zero, so the drawing "closes". Our eyes then assume the ends really touch. This is the Penrose triangle.

Answer: no; profiles are L-shapes; it is an optical illusion
🟪

✗ The carpet has 8 holes at Step 2 (one in each square)

✓ Old holes stay! H₂ = 1 + 8 = 9. Always add the new holes to the old ones.

❄️

✗ The Koch perimeter stays the same because the bump just "replaces" the middle third

✓ The bump has 2 pieces where there was 1, so each side grows by 43. The perimeter keeps growing.

🔺

✗ A pyramid with an n-sided base has 3n edges, like a prism

✓ A pyramid has 2n edges (n round the base + n to the apex). A prism has 3n.

📦

✗ Any 6 squares joined together make a cube net

✓ Only 11 of the 35 such shapes work. A 2 × 2 block, 5 in a row, or two flaps landing on the same face → not a net.

🐜

✗ Any straight line on any net is the shortest path

✓ If the line goes outside the net it is not a path on the box. Try different unfoldings and compare.

🔦

✗ A projection can be longer than the object

✓ A projection is never longer (p ≤ l). It is equal only when the line is parallel to the plane. (A shadow from a nearby torch can be bigger, but that is not a projection.)

👀

✗ One view is enough to know a solid

✓ Many solids share the same view (a cube and a long cuboid seen end-on). That is why we use front, top and side views together.

⬡

✗ On isometric paper, vertical lines on the paper can mean length

✓ Vertical | always means height. The two slanting directions are length and depth.

x̄⚖️• • •📈Σ ÷ n=SUM()⋮Part II · Chapter 5

Tales by Dots and Lines

The mean is a balancing point: see how it (and the median) moves when data changes. Then let spreadsheets do the adding, and let line graphs tell the story of data over time.

📊

⚖️ The balancing act: the mean is the centre

Quick recap: the mean (average) is the sum of the values ÷ the number of values. The median is the middle value once the data is sorted. Now let us look at the mean in a new way, using dot plots (one dot for each value on a number line).

Two numbers: the mean of 3 and 7 is (3 + 7) ÷ 2 = 5. The mean of 8 and 9 is 8.5. Each time, the mean sits exactly halfway between them.

Three or more numbers: is the mean still halfway between the smallest and largest? Not always! For 2, 4, 9 the mean is 15 ÷ 3 = 5, but halfway between 2 and 9 is 5.5. What is always true is this:

💡 Add up the distances of the values below the mean from the mean, and the distances of the values above it. The two totals are always equal. The mean is where the data balances, like a see-saw.

6, 7, 8 → left 1 = right 1

2, 4, 9 → left 3 + 1 = 4, right 4

10, 10, 11, 17 → left 2 + 2 + 1 = 5, right 5

2, 6, 10, 12 → left 5.5 + 1.5 = 7, right 2.5 + 4.5 = 7

🎬 Slide the pivot until the see-saw balances

Is there only one such centre? Yes. Take 10, 10, 11, 17 (mean 12). Move the pivot right to 13: every left distance grows and the right distance shrinks (left 8, right 4). Move it left to 11: left shrinks, right grows (left 2, right 6). Only at 12 do they match.

try 13: left 3 + 3 + 2 = 8, right 4 ✗

try 11: left 1 + 1 = 2, right 6 ✗

🧠
Memory trickMean = balance point. Median = middle seat. The mean cares how far each value is; the median only cares about order.

➕ Including or removing a value

Will a new value pull the mean up or down? Think of the see-saw.

  • New value greater than the mean → extra weight on the right → the mean increases to rebalance.
  • New value less than the mean → the mean decreases.
  • New value equal to the mean → it adds no distance on either side → the mean stays the same.

Example: 5, 5, 10, 24 has mean 44 ÷ 4 = 11. Include 17 (above 11): new mean = 61 ÷ 5 = 12.2 — it went up.

🎬 Drop a new dot in and watch the mean line move

Removing works the other way round: removing a value above the mean makes the mean fall; removing one below makes it rise; removing a value equal to the mean changes nothing.

🌍
Fair-share viewFive friends share sweets equally, 11 each. A new friend arrives with 17 sweets (more than the fair share) — after re-sharing, everyone gets a bit more. A friend who brings exactly 11 changes nothing.

🔁 Unchanging mean

Can we include two values and keep the mean the same? Yes: put them at equal distances on opposite sides of the mean. With mean 9, adding 7 and 11 keeps it 9 (2 below, 2 above).

What about three values, two below and one above? The distances must still balance. With mean 9, include 7, 7 (2 + 2 = 4 below) and 13 (4 above):

Green dots are the new values. Check: the old data 3, 5, 7, 8, 8, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 12, 15 adds to 108 (mean 108 ÷ 12 = 9). With 7, 7, 13 the total is 135 and 135 ÷ 15 = 9 ✓

💡 Any group of new values whose own mean equals the old mean leaves the mean unchanged. (7 + 7 + 13 = 27 = 3 × 9.) The same works for removing such a group.
🎯
Try thisKeep the mean 9 by including 2 values above it and 1 below. (One answer: 10, 12 and 5, because 1 + 3 = 4.)

↔️ Relatively unchanged: adding to or multiplying every value

Data: 8, 3, 10, 13, 4, 6, 7, 7, 8, 8, 5. Sum 79, 11 values, mean = 79 ÷ 11 ≈ 7.18. Now add 10 to every value: 18, 13, 20, … The quick way? The whole dot plot just slides 10 to the right, and the balance point slides with it: new mean ≈ 17.18. Subtract 1 from every value and the mean becomes ≈ 6.18.

🎬 Slide every dot, then stretch them all

Why, using algebra. Let the n values be x₁, x₂, …, xₙ with mean a, so (x₁ + x₂ + … + xₙ) ÷ n = a. Add 3 to every value:

[(x₁ + 3) + (x₂ + 3) + … + (xₙ + 3)] ÷ n = (x₁ + … + xₙ + 3n) ÷ n = (x₁ + … + xₙ) ÷ n + 3n ÷ n = a + 3

Multiply every value by 5: by the distributive property, 5x₁ + 5x₂ + … + 5xₙ = 5 × (x₁ + … + xₙ), so the new mean = 5a. Doubling the data above gives mean ≈ 2 × 7.18 = 14.36.

Do this to every valueThe mean…
add kincreases by k
subtract kdecreases by k
multiply by kis multiplied by k
🌍
Real lifeEveryone in a class was measured wearing 1 cm shoes. No need to measure again: just subtract 1 cm from the average height!

🧩 Tinkering with the median

The median has as many values below it as above it. Data 4, 7, 8, 12, 14 has median 8.

Include 11 (bigger than 8). Now there are more values above 8 than below it, so 8 cannot be the middle any more. With 6 values the median is the mean of the two middle ones: (8 + 11) ÷ 2 = 9.5. The median went up.

  • Include a value above the median → the median increases (or stays the same if there are repeated values at the middle).
  • Include a value below the median → the median decreases (or stays the same).
  • How far away the new value is does not matter for the median — 11 or 1100 give the same new median. The mean, however, would jump a lot!

🔍 Finding the unknown

Since mean = total ÷ count, we also know total = mean × count. That one fact rescues smudged or wrong data.

A smudged weight. Coach Balwan's 10 wrestlers have mean weight 39.2 kg; nine weights are 42, 40, 39, 33, 48, 38, 42, 35, 32 kg. Call the smudged one w.

(349 + w) ÷ 10 = 39.2 → 349 + w = 392 → w = 43 kg

A wrong count. Venkayya's 15 coconut trees average 25.6 coconuts each, but one tree's count was written 3 more than it really was. We do not know the individual counts — and we do not need them!

recorded total = 25.6 × 15 = 384 → true total = 384 − 3 = 381 → true mean = 381 ÷ 15 = 25.4

🧠
ShortcutAn error of 3 in one value changes the total by 3, so it changes the mean by 3 ÷ 15 = 0.2. 25.6 − 0.2 = 25.4 ✓

📋 Mean and median with frequencies

Family sizes of the 36 students in a class:

Family size345678910
Frequency311973111

⚠️ A tempting mistake: (3 + 4 + … + 10) ÷ 8 = 6.5. That treats each size as if only one student had it! Size 4 appears 11 times, so it must be added 11 times.

Mean = (3×3 + 4×11 + 5×9 + 6×7 + 7×3 + 8×1 + 9×1 + 10×1) ÷ (3 + 11 + 9 + 7 + 3 + 1 + 1 + 1) = 188 ÷ 36 ≈ 5.22

Median without writing 36 numbers: the middle values are the 18th and 19th. Keep a running total of the frequencies: 3 (sizes 3 fill positions 1–3), 3 + 11 = 14 (size 4 fills up to position 14), 14 + 9 = 23 (size 5 fills positions 15–23). Both the 18th and 19th are 5, so the median is 5.

🎬 Line the students up and find the middle

💻 Spreadsheets: let the computer add

A teacher, Sudhakar, has the marks of 22 students in 6 subjects — 132 numbers! A spreadsheet (like a digital notebook of little boxes called cells) can total and average them in a blink.

ABCDEFG
1NameOdiaTeluguEnglishMathsSocial Sc.Science
2Ratna253929363437
3Nagesh414348394039
4Ashwin293133343028
5Farooq474638424944
6…………………
  • A cell is named by its column letter then its row number. Farooq's Maths mark is in cell E5.
  • A block of cells is written Start:End. Nagesh's six marks are B3:G3; the English marks of the first five students are D2:D6.
  • A formula starts with “=”. =SUM(B3:G3) gives Nagesh's total (250). =AVERAGE(B7:D7) gives Gowri's average in Odia, Telugu and English (30).
  • The class average in Science (column G, rows 2 to 23) is =AVERAGE(G2:G23) ≈ 33.14.
🤩
Did you know?Change one mark and every formula that uses it updates by itself. That is why offices, shops and scientists love spreadsheets. Try it in the Lab!

📈 Line graphs: data across time

A clustered column graph of the monthly maximum temperature in Kerala and Punjab (2023) needs 24 bars. Put a dot at the top of each bar, join the dots month by month, and remove the bars: that is a line graph. Line graphs are best for showing how something changes over time.

🎬 Turn the columns into a line graph

Values read approximately from the book's graph. Different marker shapes (● and ■) help when printed in black-and-white or for readers who find colours hard to tell apart.

Read any graph in two steps:

  1. Identify what is given — what each axis shows, the scale (here 0 to 40 °C in steps of 10), which line is which.
  2. Infer and interpret — Punjab warms from about 19 °C in January to a peak near 38 °C in June, stays around 35 °C till September, then cools to about 23 °C in December. Kerala stays almost flat (about 29–33 °C) all year. So Punjab's temperature varies much more.
🌍
Ask how the data was madeA “monthly maximum for a state” is probably the highest reading among all its weather stations that month. Knowing how data is collected tells us what it can — and cannot — tell us.

🚀 Reading trends: space launches and rainfall

Space Jam. The number of objects launched into space each year (satellites, probes, crewed craft…):

Approximate values, redrawn from the book's graph (source: UN Office for Outer Space Affairs).

  • The world total peaked in 2023 (about 2900) and dipped slightly in 2024 (about 2850).
  • USA + China + Russia do not add up to the world line, so other countries' launches are not drawn.
  • Steeper segment = bigger change. The USA's climb from 2022 to 2023 is steeper than from 2023 to 2024.
  • From 2016 to 2017 and from 2019 to 2020 the world count more than doubled.

Why a line graph? As columns, 13 years × 4 groups = 52 bars — far too crowded. Lines show the trends at a glance.

Catch the pattern in rain. Monthly average rainfall (averaged over many years) for six coastal cities:

Kovalam, Udupi and Mumbai (west coast) get heavy rain in June–August (the south-west monsoon), and much more of it. Rameswaram and Chennai (east coast) get most rain in October–December (the north-east monsoon). Puri, though on the east coast, peaks in July–September. January–March is dry everywhere.

🗺️ Infographics and activity strips

An infographic packs data into a picture. The book shows a map of India coloured by preference for rice versus wheat: the difference between per-person rice and wheat use is squeezed onto a scale from −100 (mostly wheat) to +100 (mostly rice). Here are the same values as a bar chart:

Values from the book's infographic (NSS 2011–12 data). +100 does not mean “no wheat at all”, only the strongest preference for rice.

Notice the geographical split: the north-west prefers wheat; the east, south and north-east prefer rice.

What can a strip say? Manoj colours a strip of 48 boxes (one per half hour, midnight to midnight) to record what he does. Here are his strips for Friday, Saturday and Sunday (in some order):

SleepingEatingFriends, hobbies, media, familyClasses, study, homeworkBath, dressing, yogaTravelling

Reading the strips is real data detective work: long yellow stretches look like school; a grey box (travel) before and after a long orange stretch looks like an outing. See the Book Exercises tab for a full reading.

🎯
Try thisMake a strip for your own weekday and one for a vacation day. How different are they? Make one for an adult at home too.

😴 Data story: Sleepy-Deepy

Humans usually sleep 7–9 hours a day, but it changes with age. This graph (from the National Time Use Survey 2024) shows typical daily sleep of Indians aged 6 to 80:

Redrawn approximately. Notice the vertical axis starts at 7, not 0 — this “zooms in” so the small changes are visible.

  • 6-year-olds sleep about 9.5 hours.
  • Sleep falls through the teenage years to about 8 hours between ages 30 and 50.
  • After 50 it rises again, to about 8.5 hours and more.

With about 80 data points packed close together, the line looks like a smooth curve. A column graph would need 70+ columns and look heavy; a line graph is light and shows the pattern clearly.

🤩
WonderWhy do babies sleep so long? Do people in other countries sleep differently? Good data answers one question and raises three more!

📘 Figure it Out · 5.1 The Balancing Act pages 113–116

1Find the mean and share your observations: (i) the first 50 natural numbers, (ii) the first 50 odd numbers, (iii) the first 50 multiples of 4.
Show solution

(i) 1 to 50: pair the first and last, 1 + 50 = 2 + 49 = … = 51, giving 25 pairs. Sum = 25 × 51 = 1275, mean = 1275 ÷ 50 = 25.5.

(ii) 1, 3, 5, …, 99: pairs 1 + 99 = 3 + 97 = … = 100, 25 pairs → sum 2500, mean = 50.

(iii) 4, 8, …, 200: each is 4 times a natural number 1 to 50, so the mean is 4 × 25.5 = 102 (multiplying every value by 4 multiplies the mean by 4).

Observation: for equally spaced numbers the mean is exactly halfway between the first and last: (1 + 50) ÷ 2, (1 + 99) ÷ 2, (4 + 200) ÷ 2. The dots are spread evenly, so the balance point is the middle — the mean equals the median.

Answer: (i) 25.5 (ii) 50 (iii) 102
2The dot plot shows some data, but one dot is missing. Mark the missing value so that the mean is 9.
Show solution

The dots: 4, 7, 8, 8, 9, 9, 9, 9, 9, 11 (10 values, sum 83). With the missing dot there are 11 values, and for mean 9 the total must be 9 × 11 = 99.

Missing value = 99 − 83 = 16. Balance check: distances below 9 are 5 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 9; above 9: 2 + 7 = 9 ✓

Answer: 16
3Shreyas found the average height of the 24 students to be 150.2 cm, but everyone wore uniform shoes adding 1 cm. (i) Must all heights be measured again, or is there a simpler way? (ii) What is the correct average? Options: (a) 174.2 (b) 126.2 (c) 150.2 (d) 149.2 (e) 151.2 (f) none (g) insufficient information.
Show solution

(i) No re-measuring needed. Every height is 1 cm too much, i.e. 1 is added to every value, so the mean is also exactly 1 cm too much.

(ii) Correct average = 150.2 − 1 = 149.2 cm. (The number of students, 24, does not even matter.)

Answer: (i) simply subtract 1 cm (ii) (d) 149.2 cm
4Three dot plots A, B and C show song lengths (in minutes) of three albums. Which one has mean 5.57 minutes? Explain.
Show solution

A mean always lies between the smallest and largest values. In B the largest song is 5 minutes, in C it is 4.5 minutes — both below 5.57, so their means cannot be 5.57. Only A has values on both sides of 5.57.

Check A: 5 + 5 + 5.25 + 5.5 + 5.75 + 6 + 6.5 = 39, and 39 ÷ 7 ≈ 5.57 ✓ (B's mean is about 2.41 and C's about 3.91.)

Answer: A
5Find the median of 8, 10, 19, 23, 26, 34, 40, 41, 41, 48, 51, 55, 70, 84, 91, 92. (i) Which single value could we include without changing the median? (ii) Which two values? (iii) Which single value could we remove without changing it?
Show solution

16 values (already sorted): the middle two are the 8th and 9th, both 41. Median = (41 + 41) ÷ 2 = 41.

(i) Any value at all! With 17 values the median is the 9th. If the new value is below 41, the old 8th value (41) moves to 9th place; if it is above 41, the old 9th value (41) stays 9th. Either way the median is 41. (This happens only because the two middle values are equal.)

(ii) One value ≤ 41 and one value ≥ 41, e.g. 10 and 90, or 41 and 41. With 18 values the median is the mean of the 9th and 10th, which are then the old 8th and 9th: 41 and 41. (Two values below would give (40 + 41) ÷ 2 = 40.5; two above would give (41 + 48) ÷ 2 = 44.5.)

(iii) Any value. With 15 values the median is the 8th. Removing a value below 41 makes the old 9th value (41) the 8th; removing one above leaves the old 8th (41) in place.

Answer: median 41; (i) any value (ii) one ≤ 41 and one ≥ 41 (iii) any value
6Always, sometimes or never true? (i) Removing a value less than the median decreases the median. (ii) Including a value less than the mean decreases the mean. (iii) Including any 4 values does not affect the median. (iv) Including 4 values less than the median increases the median.
Show solution

(i) Never. Taking away a value from below the middle shifts the middle position upward, so the median increases or (when values repeat) stays the same. E.g. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 → remove 1 → median 3.5 (up); 1, 3, 3, 3, 5 → remove 1 → median 3 (same).

(ii) Always. A value below the mean adds weight on the left of the balance, so the balance point must move left.

(iii) Sometimes. True if, say, 2 go below and 2 above the median (2, 4, 6 with 1, 1, 9, 9 → still 4); false if all 4 go above (2, 4, 6 with 10, 11, 12, 13 → median 10).

(iv) Never. Four values below the median push the middle position down, so the median decreases or stays the same — it can never increase.

Answer: (i) never (ii) always (iii) sometimes (iv) never
7The mean of 8, 13, 10, 4, 5, 20, y, 10 is 10.375. Find y.
Show solution

8 values, so the total = 10.375 × 8 = 83. The known values add to 8 + 13 + 10 + 4 + 5 + 20 + 10 = 70.

y = 83 − 70 = 13.

Answer: y = 13
8The mean of 15 values is 134. Find their sum.
Show solution

Sum = mean × number of values = 134 × 15 = 2010.

Answer: 2010
9Data: 12, 47, 8, 73, 18, 35, 39, 8, 29, 25, p. Which of these could p be if the median is 29? (i) 10 (ii) 25 (iii) 40 (iv) 100 (v) 29 (vi) 47 (vii) 30
Show solution

Sorted without p: 8, 8, 12, 18, 25, 29, 35, 39, 47, 73. With p there are 11 values, so the median is the 6th.

If p ≥ 29, the first six values are 8, 8, 12, 18, 25, 29 → median 29 ✓. If p ≤ 25, then p joins the lower part and the 6th value becomes 25 ✗. If p were between 25 and 29, the 6th value would be p itself, not 29.

So p must be 29 or more: 40, 100, 29, 47 and 30 work; 10 and 25 do not (median would be 25).

Answer: (iii), (iv), (v), (vi), (vii)
10The dot plot shows how many times students rode their cycles in a week (four students rode twice). (i) Find the mean. (ii) Find the median. (iii) Which statements are valid? (a) Everyone used their cycle at least once. (b) Almost everyone used their cycle a few times. (c) Some students cycled more than once on some days. (d) Exactly 5 students used their cycles more than once on some days. (e) If next week everyone cycles 1 more time, what are the new mean and median?
Show solution
Rides012345678910
Students31477546302

(i) Students = 42. Total rides = 0 + 1 + 8 + 21 + 28 + 25 + 24 + 42 + 24 + 0 + 20 = 193. Mean = 193 ÷ 42 ≈ 4.6 rides.

(ii) The median is the mean of the 21st and 22nd values. Running totals: 3, 4, 8, 15, 22 → positions 16–22 are all 4. Median = 4.

(iii) (a) Not valid — 3 students never rode. (b) Valid — 38 of 42 rode two or more times. (c) Valid — a week has 7 days, so students with 8 or 10 rides must have ridden more than once on some day. (d) Not valid — we know at least 5 (the 3 + 2 with 8 or 10 rides) did, but someone with, say, 4 rides could also have ridden twice in one day. We cannot say “exactly”.

(e) Adding 1 to every value: mean ≈ 4.6 + 1 = 5.6, median = 4 + 1 = 5.

Answer: (i) ≈ 4.6 (193/42) (ii) 4 (iii) b, c valid; a, d not (e) mean ≈ 5.6, median 5
11Darts: number of throws needed to hit the bull's eye — trials 1 to 10 with 1, 0, 0, 1, 4, 9, 12, 15, 10, 10 students. Describe the data using minimum, maximum, mean and median.
Show solution

Students = 62. Minimum = 1 throw, maximum = 10 throws.

Total throws = 1×1 + 4×1 + 5×4 + 6×9 + 7×12 + 8×15 + 9×10 + 10×10 = 473. Mean = 473 ÷ 62 ≈ 7.63.

Median = mean of the 31st and 32nd values. Running totals: 1, 1, 1, 2, 6, 15, 27, 42 → positions 28–42 are 8. Median = 8.

So a typical player needed about 8 throws; only one lucky player hit it first time, and most needed 6 or more.

Answer: min 1, max 10, mean ≈ 7.63, median 8

📘 Figure it Out · Line graphs pages 122–123

1Average customers visiting and purchasing at a shop: Mon–Sun visiting 16, 19, 10, 14, 20, 22, 35; purchasing 10, 8, 7, 11, 12, 16, 26. Show this on a line graph.
Show solution

Days go on the horizontal axis, customers on the vertical axis (0 to 40 in steps of 5). Plot one line for each row and use different markers.

What it shows: both lines are lowest on Wednesday and shoot up on Sunday (35 visitors, 26 buyers). The purchasing line is always below the visiting line; on Tuesday the gap is widest (19 visit, only 8 buy).

Answer: line graph as shown
2Average number of rainy days per month (Jan–Dec): Mangaluru 0.1, 0, 0.1, 1.8, 6.2, 24.1, 27.7, 24.5, 14, 8.8, 3.9, 0.9; Port Blair 2.4, 1.3, 0.9, 3.3, 15.5, 18.7, 17.3, 18.8, 16.8, 14.1, 11.3, 5.4; Rameswaram 2.6, 1.3, 1.9, 3.4, 2.5, 0.4, 1, 1, 1.9, 8.1, 10.4, 7.8; New Delhi is given only as a line on the graph. (i) How might this data be compiled? (ii) Plot Mangaluru, Port Blair and Rameswaram (rounded). (iii) Fill New Delhi's row from its line. (iv) Which city has the most rainy days in a year, and which the least? (v) When is the rainy season in New Delhi and in Rameswaram?
Show solution

(i) A weather station in each city records every day whether it rained (above some small amount). Count the rainy days in each month, do this for many years, and average them — that is why we see decimals like 24.1.

(ii) Rounded: Mangaluru 0, 0, 0, 2, 6, 24, 28, 25, 14, 9, 4, 1; Port Blair 2, 1, 1, 3, 16, 19, 17, 19, 17, 14, 11, 5; Rameswaram 3, 1, 2, 3, 3, 0, 1, 1, 2, 8, 10, 8.

(iii) New Delhi (read from the line, approximately): 1.3, 1.5, 1.5, 1.1, 1.5, 3.8, 9.7, 9.7, 4, 1, 0.3, 1.

(iv) Yearly totals: Port Blair ≈ 125.8, Mangaluru ≈ 112.1, Rameswaram ≈ 42.3, New Delhi ≈ 36.4. Most: Port Blair. Least: New Delhi.

(v) New Delhi: July–August (roughly late June to September, the south-west monsoon). Rameswaram: October–December (the north-east monsoon).

Answer: (iv) most Port Blair, least New Delhi (v) Delhi Jul–Aug; Rameswaram Oct–Dec
3The line graph shows the number of births in each month in India. (i) What do you observe? (ii) About how many births were there in July 2017? (iii) What time period does it cover? (iv) Compare January 2018, 2019 and 2020. (v) Estimate the births in 2019. (The book prints this question as a second “2”.)

Redrawn approximately from the book's graph (source: Nambiar et al., “Seasonal variations in births in India”).

Show solution

(i) The pattern repeats every year: births peak around August–October (close to 2 million a month) and are lowest around March–April (about 1.45–1.5 million). Births are seasonal!

(ii) July 2017 ≈ 1.8 million (about 1.77 million).

(iii) From April 2017 to March 2020 — 36 months, i.e. three years.

(iv) January 2018 ≈ 1.68 million, January 2019 ≈ 1.76 million, January 2020 ≈ 1.78 million. January 2018 was the lowest; 2019 and 2020 were almost the same.

(v) Adding the 12 monthly values of 2019 gives about 21.4 million. A quick estimate: about 1.8 million × 12 ≈ 21.6 million. So roughly 21–22 million births.

Answer: (ii) ≈ 1.8 million (iii) Apr 2017 – Mar 2020 (v) ≈ 21.5 million

📘 Think and answer · questions inside the text pages 120–125

ASpace Jam: which inferences are valid? (1) The world count rose every year from 2012 to 2024. (2) The USA launched about ¾ of the world count in 2022–24. (3) Nepal launched nothing in 2012–24. (4) China + Russia launched about 400 in 2024. Also: find consecutive years when the world count increased 2 times or more.
Show solution

(1) Not valid — it dipped in 2016, 2018 and 2024. (2) Valid — e.g. 2023: 2245 of 2910 ≈ 0.77 ≈ ¾. (3) Not valid — Nepal is not shown; the graph cannot tell us. (4) Valid — about 290 + 115 ≈ 400.

Doubling: 2016 → 2017 (≈ 235 → 480) and 2019 → 2020 (≈ 605 → 1275).

Answer: (2) and (4) valid; 2016→2017 and 2019→2020
BRice vs wheat infographic: (i) guess Karnataka's hidden value; (ii) top 5 rice states; (iii) top 5 wheat states; (iv) states where the preference is roughly balanced.
Show solution

(i) Karnataka is shaded a medium purple, like its rice-loving neighbours Goa (+57), Kerala (+79), Tamil Nadu (+85) and Andhra (+92), but a little lighter — a sensible guess is about +60 to +75.

(ii) Rice: Manipur (+100), Nagaland (+99), Mizoram (+97), Tripura (+96), Meghalaya (+95).

(iii) Wheat: Rajasthan (−93), Haryana (−81), Punjab (−78), Madhya Pradesh (−60), Delhi (−45).

(iv) Balanced (close to 0): Bihar (+3), Maharashtra (−15), Uttarakhand (−18), Himachal Pradesh (−19).

Answer: see the lists above
CManoj's strips: (i) Which colour is which activity? (ii) Which strip is Friday, Saturday, Sunday? (iii) When did he go out for a long movie? (iv) When is his school lunch break? (v) What else do the strips tell us?
Show solution

This is open-ended; here is one careful reading, using the strips as redrawn above.

(i) Light blue = sleeping (night). Purple = bath, dressing, yoga (always early morning). Green = eating (short boxes near 8–9 am, 12:30–1:30 pm and 7 pm). Grey = travelling (short boxes just before and after time away from home). Yellow = classes, study, homework (the long 9 am–4:30 pm block on strip 2). Orange = friends, hobbies, media, family.

(ii) Strip 2 = Friday: travel at 8:30, classes 9:00–4:30 with a lunch break, travel home — a full school day. Strip 3 = Saturday: classes only till 12:30 (a half day), travel home, lunch and a nap; he also sleeps later (about 9:30 pm) because the next day is a holiday. Strip 1 = Sunday: no school, studies a little in the morning and evening.

(iii) On Sunday afternoon (strip 1): grey at 1:00 pm, a 3-hour orange block 1:30–4:30 pm, grey again at 4:30 pm — out with friends at a long movie. (Saturday's 3:00–6:30 pm block followed by travel is another possible answer.)

(iv) On Friday he eats at 12:30 pm and is free (orange) till 1:30 pm, so the lunch break is about 12:30–1:30 pm.

(v) For example: he sleeps about 9 to 10½ hours each night; he wakes at 6:30–7:00; he has a short nap on Saturday and Sunday afternoons.

Answer: one reading — Friday = strip 2, Saturday = strip 3, Sunday = strip 1; lunch ≈ 12:30 pm

📘 Figure it Out · end of chapter pages 127–132

1Mean grids: (i) Fill a 3 × 3 grid with 9 different numbers so that the average along every row, column and diagonal is 10. (ii) Can we change a few numbers and still get average 10 everywhere?
Show solution

Average 10 along 3 cells means each line must add to 30. Put the mean, 10, in the centre and place pairs that balance around 10 opposite each other through the centre (like 6 and 14, 9 and 11).

(i) One answer (every row, column and diagonal adds to 30):

(ii) Yes, in many ways. For example, double each number's distance from 10 (8 = 10 − 2·1, 18 = 10 + 2·4, …):

Answer: e.g. 9 14 7 / 8 10 12 / 13 6 11; yes, many grids work
2Give two examples of: (i) 3 numbers with mean 8; (ii) 4 numbers with median 15.5; (iii) 5 numbers with mean 13.6; (iv) 6 numbers with mean = median; (v) 6 numbers with mean > median.
Show solution

(i) Sum must be 24: 7, 8, 9 or 2, 10, 12.

(ii) The two middle numbers must average 15.5: 10, 15, 16, 20 or 1, 14, 17, 30.

(iii) Sum must be 13.6 × 5 = 68: 10, 12, 14, 15, 17 or 1, 2, 3, 4, 58.

(iv) Evenly spaced or symmetric data: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 (both 3.5) or 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 (both 7).

(v) One big value pulls the mean up but not the median: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 100 (mean ≈ 19.17, median 3.5) or 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 8 (mean 3, median 2).

Answer: examples above (many others are possible)
3Fill the blanks so the median of 5, 21, 14, __, __, __ is 13. How many possibilities are there if only counting numbers are allowed?
Show solution

6 values → median = mean of the 3rd and 4th sorted values, which must add to 26. Since 13 is below 14, the given 14 is in 4th place or later.

Case 1: 4th value = 14 → 3rd value = 12. Blanks: 12, one number from 1 to 12 (it sits with 5 in places 1–2), and one number 14 or more (it sits with 21 in places 5–6). E.g. 5, 21, 14, 12, 3, 50 → sorted 3, 5, 12, 14, 21, 50 → median 13 ✓

Case 2: 3rd and 4th both 13. Blanks: 13, 13 and one number from 1 to 13 (13 ways).

The number “14 or more” in case 1 can be as large as we like, so there are infinitely many possibilities. (If the largest blank were limited, the count would be finite — e.g. with all values up to 30 there are 217 sets of blanks.)

Answer: e.g. 12, 3, 50; infinitely many possibilities
4Fill the blanks so the mean of 3, 11, __, __, 15, 6 is 6.5. How many possibilities with counting numbers?
Show solution

Total needed = 6.5 × 6 = 39. Known: 3 + 11 + 15 + 6 = 35, so the blanks add to 4.

Counting-number pairs: (1, 3), (2, 2), (3, 1).

Answer: 3 possibilities (2 if (1, 3) and (3, 1) count as the same)
5True or false? Justify. (i) The average of two even numbers is even. (ii) The average of any two multiples of 5 is a multiple of 5. (iii) The average of any 5 multiples of 5 is a multiple of 5.
Show solution

(i) False (only sometimes true). 2 and 4 average 3, which is odd. Algebra: (2m + 2n) ÷ 2 = m + n, which is even only when m + n is even.

(ii) False. 5 and 10 average 7.5. Algebra: (5m + 5n) ÷ 2 = 5(m + n) ÷ 2 is a multiple of 5 only when m + n is even.

(iii) False. 5, 10, 15, 20, 30 add to 80 and average 16. Algebra: (5a + 5b + 5c + 5d + 5e) ÷ 5 = a + b + c + d + e, which can be any whole number.

Answer: all three are false (true only sometimes)
6Two students join Sudhakar's class (24 students, average height 150.2 cm). (i) Which are correct? (a) The average will increase because there are 2 new values. (b) It will stay the same. (c) The new students' heights must be measured to find the new average. (d) Everyone must be measured again. (ii) Their heights are 149 cm and 152 cm. Will the average stay the same, increase, decrease, or is there not enough information? (iii) Will the median stay the same, increase, decrease, or is there not enough information?
Show solution

(i) Only (c). The new values could be above or below 150.2, so (a) and (b) cannot be claimed. We do not need (d): the old total, 24 × 150.2 = 3604.8 cm, is already known; we only need the two new heights.

(ii) (b) increase. Together the newcomers average (149 + 152) ÷ 2 = 150.5 cm, which is above 150.2. Check: (3604.8 + 149 + 152) ÷ 26 = 3905.8 ÷ 26 ≈ 150.22 cm.

(iii) (d) not enough information. We do not know the median of the 24 heights. If the median lies between 149 and 152, one value goes on each side and the median stays the same; but if, say, the median were 153, both new values would be below it and the median could fall.

Answer: (i) c (ii) b — new mean ≈ 150.22 cm (iii) d
7Is 17 the average of the data in this dot plot? Explain your method.
Show solution

Balance method: distances below 17: 14 (×2) → 6, 15 (×2) → 4, 16 (×3) → 3, total 13. Distances above 17: 18 (×4) → 4, 19 (×4) → 8, 20 (×3) → 9, 21 → 4, 23 → 6, total 31. The right side is much heavier, so the balance point is to the right of 17. No.

Direct check: 25 values, sum 443, mean = 443 ÷ 25 = 17.72.

Answer: No — the mean is 17.72
8Last month a group's mean weight was 65.3 kg and median 67 kg. This month one person lost 2 kg and two people gained 1 kg each. What can we say about the mean and the median?
Show solution

Mean: the total changes by −2 + 1 + 1 = 0 and the number of people is the same, so the mean stays 65.3 kg.

Median: we cannot be sure. It depends on who changed. If the changes happen far from the middle, it stays 67 kg. But take 60, 64, 67, 70, 71 (median 67): if the 67 kg person loses 2 kg and the 70 and 71 kg people gain 1 kg, the data becomes 60, 64, 65, 71, 72 and the median drops to 65.

Answer: mean unchanged; median may or may not change
9January retail price (₹) of iodised salt, 2016–2025 — Andaman & Nicobar: 16, 12, 12, 12, 13.88, 18.22, 18.73, 20.63, 19.73, 20.99; Assam: 6, 12, 12, 12, 12, 15, 14, 12.02, 13.72, 12.35; Gujarat: 16.5, 14.75, 14.75, 14.75, 13, 14.45, 14.28, 14.54, 14.8, 19.2; Mizoram: 20, 20, 22, 22, 20, 22, 25, 27.65, 29.03, 29.8; Uttar Pradesh: 16.15, 16.97, 16.18, 18.24, 18.96, 20.63, 21.3, 25.39, 26.9, 24.81; West Bengal: 9.47, 11.65, 11.63, 11.43, 11.11, 12.79, 16.14, 18.43, 21.66, 23.99. (i) Draw a line graph for 3 states. (ii) What is interesting? (iii) Compare Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh. (iv) Where did the price increase most from 2016 to 2025? (v) What would you explore further?
Show solution

(i) For example Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal (rounded to whole rupees), with ₹0–30 on the vertical axis in steps of 5:

(ii) Most states got costlier, especially after 2021. Assam's price doubled in one year (₹6 → ₹12 in 2017) and then hardly changed. Mizoram is the most expensive in almost every year.

(iii) Gujarat is nearly flat — about ₹13–15 from 2017 to 2024 — and then jumps to ₹19.2 in 2025. Uttar Pradesh rises fairly steadily from about ₹16 to ₹26.9 in 2024, then falls a little to ₹24.81. UP's price varied much more.

(iv) Increases 2016 → 2025: A&N ₹4.99, Assam ₹6.35, Gujarat ₹2.70, Mizoram ₹9.80, UP ₹8.66, West Bengal ₹14.52 (9.47 → 23.99, about 2.5 times — also the biggest percentage rise).

(v) For example: why did Gujarat (a big salt-producing state) stay cheap? What happened in 2021–2023 to push prices up?

Answer: (iv) West Bengal (+₹14.52)
10Main source of household lighting over time (rural and urban). Which are valid? (i) In 1983 most rural homes used kerosene while most urban homes used electricity. (ii) Kerosene use fell over time in both rural and urban areas. (iii) In 2000, 10% of urban homes used electricity. (iv) In 2023 there were no power cuts.

Redrawn approximately from the book's graph (source: NSSO, Data For India).

Show solution

(i) Valid — rural kerosene ≈ 84% (a majority), urban electricity ≈ 64% (a majority).

(ii) Valid — both kerosene lines go down all the way to nearly 0%.

(iii) Not valid — around 2000 almost 90% of urban homes used electricity; it is kerosene that was about 10%.

(iv) Not valid — the graph shows the main source of lighting, not whether the supply was ever cut. It says nothing about power cuts.

Answer: (i) and (ii) are valid
11Average daily time on hobbies and games (urban and rural children). (i) How long do 10-year-olds in urban areas spend? (ii) At what age do rural children average 1.5 hours: 8, 10, 12, 14 or 18? (iii) Correct or not? (a) 15-year-olds spend twice as long as 10-year-olds. (b) All rural 15-year-olds spend at least 1 hour every day.

Redrawn approximately from the book's graph.

Show solution

(i) About 2 hours a day (the urban line is just above 2 h at age 10).

(ii) The rural line crosses 1.5 h at about age 14 → option (d).

(iii)(a) Incorrect — it is the other way round: at 15 the time (about 1.1–1.3 h) is roughly half of the time at 10 (about 2.1–2.4 h). (b) Incorrect — the graph shows an average. Some rural 15-year-olds may spend much less than 1 hour; an average does not describe every child.

Answer: (i) ≈ 2 hours (ii) (d) 14 years (iii) both incorrect
12Individual project: make activity strips for different days of your week. (i) Do you eat and sleep at regular times? How long are you outdoors? (ii) Find the average time per activity and draw an “average day” strip. (iii) Compare with an adult at home.
Show solution

Use 48 boxes per day (half-hour each), one colour per activity, for 5–7 days. For each activity, count its boxes each day, add over the days and divide by the number of days; then convert boxes to hours (2 boxes = 1 hour). Example: sleep boxes 18, 18, 19, 18, 17, 20, 22 → total 132 → average 132 ÷ 7 ≈ 18.9 boxes ≈ 9.4 hours. Colour an average strip with each activity's average number of boxes (rounded) so that they add to 48.

Answer: your own data — use the mean of each activity
13Group project (3–4 members): (i) track the daily sleep (night sleep + naps) of all family members for a week, show it on strips, and find the average and median sleep of children, adults and elders; or (ii) collect Grade 8 school timings from different schools (Manoj's school runs 9:30 am – 4:30 pm, i.e. 7 hours) and analyse them.
Show solution

(i) Put everyone's daily totals into a table (one row per person, one column per day) — a spreadsheet makes =AVERAGE and =MEDIAN easy. Group the rows into children, adults, elders and compare. Compare with the Sleepy-Deepy graph: do children really sleep longest?

(ii) For each school, record start, end, total hours and break time. Make a dot plot of the total school hours; find the mean and median; look for patterns (government vs private, state to state). A line graph is not the right choice here, since the data is not changing over time.

Answer: your own data — present it with strips, dot plots and mean/median
14Sunrise and sunset times through the year at Kibithu, Ghuar Moti, Srinagar and Kanyakumari. Which lines are sunrise and which sunset? (i) Where does the sun rise earliest in January, and what is the day length there? (ii) Which place has the longest day over the year? (iii) What do you notice and wonder?

Redrawn approximately from the book's graphs.

Show solution

The lower lines (between 04:00 and 08:00) are the sunrise times; the upper lines (16:00–20:00) are sunset. Day length = sunset − sunrise = the gap between a place's two lines.

(i) Kibithu (far east, Arunachal Pradesh): sunrise about 5:55 am, sunset about 4:30 pm in January → day length ≈ 10.5 hours.

(ii) Srinagar: in June the sun rises at about 5:20 am and sets at about 7:45 pm — roughly 14.5 hours, the widest gap of all.

(iii) Kanyakumari (far south, near the equator) has almost the same day length all year (about 12 hours); northern Srinagar swings the most — long summer days, short winter days. Kibithu (far east) sees the sun about 2 hours before Ghuar Moti (far west, Gujarat), yet the whole country uses one clock time (IST). One might wonder: should India have two time zones?

Answer: (i) Kibithu, about 10.5 hours (ii) Srinagar
15The graph shows moonrise and moonset times over one month. (i) On what dates were amavasya (new moon) and purnima (full moon)? (ii) What do you notice and wonder?

Redrawn from the book's graph.

Show solution

(i) On purnima the full moon rises around sunset (about 6 pm) and sets around sunrise (about 6 am): that happens around the 13th–14th (moonrise 5:30–6:30 pm, moonset 6:40–7:30 am). On amavasya the moon rises and sets with the sun, so we cannot see it at night: around the 28th (moonrise ≈ 6:15 am, moonset ≈ 5 pm).

(ii) The moon rises about 50 minutes later each day (the lines climb steadily). Because of this, there is one day with no moonrise at all (around the 21st — it rises just after midnight the next day) and one day with no moonset (around the 6th). From new moon to full moon takes about 15 days, half the cycle.

Answer: purnima ≈ 13th–14th; amavasya ≈ 28th

✗ Mean of a frequency table = (3 + 4 + 5 + … + 10) ÷ 8 = 6.5

✓ Each value must be counted as often as its frequency: Σ(value × frequency) ÷ total frequency = 188 ÷ 36 ≈ 5.22.

🔀

✗ Median of 9, 2, 7, 4, 5 is 7 (the middle of the list as written)

✓ Sort first: 2, 4, 5, 7, 9 → median 5.

✌️

✗ Median of 3, 6, 8, 10 is “6 or 8”

✓ With an even count, take the mean of the two middle values: (6 + 8) ÷ 2 = 7.

⚖️

✗ The mean is halfway between the smallest and largest values

✓ Only for two values (or symmetric data). The mean is where the total distances on the two sides balance: for 2, 4, 9 it is 5, not 5.5.

➕

✗ Including a new value always increases the mean

✓ Only if the new value is above the mean. Below the mean → it decreases; equal → no change.

↔️

✗ Adding 3 to each of 10 values raises the mean by 3 ÷ 10

✓ It raises the total by 3 × 10 = 30, so the mean rises by 30 ÷ 10 = 3. Adding k to every value adds k to the mean.

💻

✗ The range B3:G3 has 5 cells (G − B = 5)

✓ Both ends are included: B, C, D, E, F, G = 6 cells.

📈

✗ “The average 10-year-old plays 2 hours a day, so every child plays at least 2 hours”

✓ An average describes the group, not each person. Also on a line graph, a steeper segment means a bigger change.

x + 24a+16a+2b+c9(b−a)100M+D11(a+b)■ = 9Part II · Chapter 6

Algebra Play

Magic tricks, number pyramids, calendar puzzles and story riddles. Letter-numbers show us why each one works, and help us invent our own.

🎩

🎩 'Think of a Number' tricks

Algebra is not only for solving equations. It is also a detective tool: it can explain why a magic trick works for every number, not just the few we tried.

Here is a classic trick. Think of a number, double it, add 4, divide by 2, and subtract the number you started with. You get 2. Every time!

StepStart with 7Start with 30Start with x
Think of a number730x
Double it14602x
Add 418642x + 4
Divide by 2932x + 2
Subtract the start22x + 2 − x = 2

Trying 7 and 30 only shows the trick works for 7 and 30. The last column, with the letter-number x, shows it works for all numbers: the x cancels out and only 2 is left.

🎬 Watch the bag of x disappear
💡 A trick that "always gives the same answer" is one where the starting number cancels out of the expression.

🛠️ Invent your own trick

Now that we can see inside the trick, we can change it. In the trick above, "add 4" became "+2" after halving. So:

  • To end with 3: double, add 6, halve, subtract the start → x + 3 − x = 3.
  • To end with 5: double, add 10, halve, subtract the start → 5.

A longer trick that still ends in 5:

Say thisAlgebra
Think of a numberx
Add 3x + 3
Multiply by 44x + 12
Subtract 24x + 10
Divide by 22x + 5
Take away twice your number5

Another kind of trick lets you find the secret number. "Multiply by 2, add 10, tell me the answer." If your friend says 36, you think: 2x + 10 = 36, so x = 13. You just undo the steps!

🎯
Try thisMake a trick where the answer is always 10. Hint: multiply by 3, add 30, divide by 3, then subtract the start.

📅 The birthday (date) trick

Shubham asks Mukta to think of a date, do some steps, and tell him only the final answer. From that, he names her date! Let the month be M and the day be D.

StepMukta (26 January)Algebra
Multiply the month by 51 × 5 = 55M
Add 6115M + 6
Multiply by 44420M + 24
Add 95320M + 33
Multiply by 5265100M + 165
Add the day291100M + 165 + D

To decode, Shubham subtracts 165: 291 − 165 = 126 = 100M + D. The day D is at most 31, so it uses the last two digits: D = 26. What is in front is the month: M = 1. Republic Day, 26/01! 🇮🇳

🎬 Decode a secret date

Another one: answer 1390 → 1390 − 165 = 1225 → month 12, day 25: Christmas, 25 December.

🧠
Why it worksThe steps multiply the month by 5 × 4 × 5 = 100. That pushes the month two places to the left, leaving two empty places for the day. The extra 165 is just a disguise.

🔺 Number pyramids

In a number pyramid, each box holds the sum of the two boxes just below it.

1 + 9 = 10, 9 + 4 = 13, 10 + 13 = 23

Going up is easy: just add. But what if some boxes in the middle or bottom are missing? Then we subtract. If a box and its lower-left neighbour are known, the lower-right one is their difference.

  • Top 10, left 4: the box beside 4 is 10 − 4 = 6.
  • 4 sits on 1 and ?: so ? = 4 − 1 = 3.
  • 6 sits on 3 and ?: so ? = 6 − 3 = 3.
🎯
Try thisFill the pyramid with bottom row 5, 4, 5, 0. (You should get 9, 9, 5, then 18, 14, then 32 at the top.)

🔤 When subtraction is not enough: use letters

Look at this pyramid. No box has both a known neighbour and a known box above it. Where do we start? 🤔

Give the empty boxes letter-numbers a, b, c. The pyramid rule gives three equations:

a + b = 60  ·  a = 12 + c  ·  b = c + 8

Put a and b into the first equation: (12 + c) + (c + 8) = 60, so 2c + 20 = 60, 2c = 40, c = 20. Then a = 32 and b = 28.

🎬 Crack a pyramid with a letter-number
💡 Name the unknown box, write each rule as an equation, then solve. The bottom-middle number is counted twice on its way to the top.

🧮 The top number, straight from the bottom row

Is there a shortcut from the bottom row to the top? Put letter-numbers in the bottom row and add upwards.

RowsTop numberHow often each bottom number counts
2a + b1, 1
3a + 2b + c1, 2, 1
4a + 3b + 3c + d1, 3, 3, 1

Example: bottom row 4, 13, 8 → top = 4 + 2 × 13 + 8 = 38, without building the pyramid.

🤩
Did you know?The counts 1, 2, 1 and 1, 3, 3, 1 are rows of the Meru-prastāra, a number triangle described by Halāyudha (about 10th century CE) while explaining the work of Piṅgala on poetic metres. The next pyramid size gives 1, 4, 6, 4, 1.
🎯
Virahāṅka-Fibonacci pyramidsRecall 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, … (each number is the sum of the two before it). Put 1, 2, 3 in the bottom row: you get 3, 5 and then 8. Every box is again a Virahāṅka-Fibonacci number! Can you see why?

📆 Calendar magic

Your friend picks a 2 × 2 square on a calendar page and tells you only the sum of its 4 dates. Can you find the 4 dates?

6 + 7 + 13 + 14 = 40

Let the top-left date be a. The next day is a + 1. The date just below is one week later: a + 7, and beside it a + 8.

a + (a + 1) + (a + 7) + (a + 8) = 4a + 16

If the sum is 36: 4a + 16 = 36 → 4a = 20 → a = 5. So the square is 5, 6, 12, 13. 🎉

🎬 Read a friend's mind from a calendar
🎯
Make your own calendar trickTry other shapes: a 3 × 3 square (sum = 9 × the centre), a plus shape (5 × the centre), three dates in a column (3 × the middle). Try it in the Explore Lab!

🟦 Algebra grids

In these grids each shape stands for a number. The last column is the sum of the row. We use one row to unlock the next.

■■■27
●●■19
  • Row 1 has three equal squares: 3 × ■ = 27, so ■ = 9.
  • Row 2: ● + ● + 9 = 19, so 2 × ● = 10 and ● = 5.

When no row has just one kind of shape, combine rows. For 2■ + ● = 27 and ● + ● + ■ = 21: adding gives 3■ + 3● = 48, so ■ + ● = 16. Taking this from row 1 leaves ■ = 11, so ● = 5.

🧠
Memory trickLook for the row with the fewest kinds of shape first. If every row is mixed, add or subtract whole rows.

✖️ The largest product

Put the digits 2, 3 and 5 in ☐☐ × ☐, each once. Which gives the largest product? There are only 3 × 2 = 6 ways, so let us be systematic and pair them by the multiplier.

MultiplierThe pairBigger one
235 × 2, 53 × 253 × 2 = 106
325 × 3, 52 × 352 × 3 = 156
523 × 5, 32 × 532 × 5 = 160 ✅

Why does 32 × 5 beat 52 × 3? Split by place value: 32 × 5 = 3 × 10 × 5 + 2 × 5 and 52 × 3 = 5 × 10 × 3 + 2 × 3. The first parts are equal (150), and 2 × 5 > 2 × 3.

Always? Take digits p < q < r. The best candidates are rp × q and qp × r:

qp × r = 10qr + pr    rp × q = 10rq + pq

The 10qr parts match, and pr > pq because r > q. So the winner is qp × r.

💡 Use the largest digit as the multiplier, and write the other two digits in decreasing order.

➗ Decoding divisibility tricks

Mukta's trick: choose a 2-digit number with different digits, reverse it, subtract the smaller from the larger, and divide by 9. There is never a remainder! (47 → 74 − 47 = 27 = 9 × 3.)

Write the number ab in general form: ab = 10a + b, its reverse ba = 10b + a. If b > a:

(10b + a) − (10a + b) = 9b − 9a = 9(b − a)

So the difference is always 9 times the difference of the digits. If a > b, we get 9(a − b) in the same way.

🎬 Why ab + ba and ab − ba behave so nicely
TrickAlgebraSo it is divisible by
ab − ba9(a − b)9
ab + ba11(a + b)11
abc + bca + cab111(a + b + c)37 and 3 (111 = 3 × 37)
abcabc1001 × abc7, 11 and 13 (1001 = 7 × 11 × 13)

🧞 Story puzzles: Karim and the Genie

A genie offers Karim a deal: walk round a magic tree and your coins double, but pay me 8 coins after each round. After three rounds Karim has exactly 8 coins, which he must pay. He ends with nothing! How many did he start with?

🎬 Follow Karim's coins round the tree

Let the start be x:

x → 2x − 8 → 4x − 24 → 8x − 56

Ending with nothing: 8x − 56 = 0, so x = 7. Check: 7 → 14 − 8 = 6 → 12 − 8 = 4 → 8 − 8 = 0 ✅.

Many puzzles in this chapter follow the same plan: name the unknown, turn each sentence into an expression, then solve. Some can also be solved without letters, for example by working backwards (0 ← 8 ← 4 ← …) or by a clever guess.

🌍
Heads and legs, without letters55 animals (horses and hens) have 150 legs. If all were hens: 110 legs. The extra 40 legs come from horses, 2 extra each, so 20 horses and 35 hens.
💡 Algebra lets us model a situation and justify a claim for every case at once. That is why it appears all over mathematics and science.
