📘 In-text · 6.2 The date trick page 137

Each final answer is 100M + 165 + D. Subtract 165; the last two digits are the day, the rest is the month.

(i)The final answer is 1269. What was the date?
Show solution

1269 − 165 = 1104 = 100M + D. Last two digits: D = 4. Front: M = 11.

Answer: 4 November
(ii)The final answer is 394. What was the date?
Show solution

394 − 165 = 229 = 100M + D. Last two digits: D = 29. Front: M = 2.

Answer: 29 February (a leap-year date)
(iii)The final answer is 296. What was the date?
Show solution

296 − 165 = 131 = 100M + D. Last two digits: D = 31. Front: M = 1.

Answer: 31 January
★Can you change the steps of the trick and still find the date? Devise your own trick.
Show solution

Yes. Any steps work as long as the month ends up multiplied by 100 (so the day has two places to itself). For example: multiply the month by 4, add 3, multiply by 25, add the day. That gives 100M + 75 + D, so you subtract 75 instead of 165. Example: 15 August → 4 × 8 = 32, 35, 875, 890 → 890 − 75 = 815 → month 8, day 15.

Answer: any steps that give 100M + (a fixed number) + D

📘 In-text · 6.3 Filling number pyramids pages 138–139

1Fill the pyramids with bottom rows (a) 6, 2 (b) 3, 4, 3 (c) 5, 4, 5, 0.
Show solution

Add each pair of neighbours to get the row above.

  • (a) 6 + 2 = 8.
  • (b) 7, 7, then 14.
  • (c) 9, 9, 5, then 18, 14, then 32.
Answer: (a) 8 (b) 7, 7 / 14 (c) 9, 9, 5 / 18, 14 / 32
2A 4-row pyramid: top 50, second row from top has 22 on the right, bottom row is 4, ☐, 6, ☐. Fill it.
Show solution

Let the bottom row be 4, x, 6, y. The right box of row 3 is the top of the small pyramid on x, 6, y: x + 12 + y = 22, so x + y = 10. The top is 4 + 3x + 18 + y = 50, so 3x + y = 28. Subtracting: 2x = 18, x = 9, y = 1.

Rows: 4, 9, 6, 1 → 13, 15, 7 → 28, 22 → 50 ✅

Answer: bottom 4, 9, 6, 1; then 13, 15, 7; then 28, 22; top 50
3A 4-row pyramid: second row from top starts with 40, the row below ends with 9, bottom row is 5, ☐, 7, ☐. Fill it.
Show solution

Bottom 5, x, 7, y. The box above 7 and y is 9, so y = 2. The left box of row 3 is 5 + 2x + 7 = 40, so x = 14. Now build up: 19, 21, 9 → 40, 30 → 70.

Answer: bottom 5, 14, 7, 2; then 19, 21, 9; then 40, 30; top 70
4A 4-row pyramid: top 35, the row above the bottom ends with 7, bottom row is 3, 5, ☐, ☐. Fill it.
Show solution

Bottom 3, 5, x, y. Then x + y = 7. The top is 3 + 3 × 5 + 3x + y = 35, so 3x + y = 17. Subtract: 2x = 10, x = 5, y = 2. Build up: 8, 10, 7 → 18, 17 → 35 ✅

Answer: bottom 3, 5, 5, 2; then 8, 10, 7; then 18, 17; top 35

📘 Figure it Out · 6.3 Number Pyramids page 140

1Find the top of a 3-row pyramid without building it, for bottom rows (i) 4, 13, 8 (ii) 7, 11, 3 (iii) 10, 14, 25.
Show solution

Top = a + 2b + c.

  • (i) 4 + 26 + 8 = 38
  • (ii) 7 + 22 + 3 = 32
  • (iii) 10 + 28 + 25 = 63
Answer: (i) 38 (ii) 32 (iii) 63
2Write an expression for the top of a 4-row pyramid in terms of the bottom row.
Show solution

Bottom a, b, c, d → a + b, b + c, c + d → a + 2b + c, b + 2c + d → add these two.

Answer: a + 3b + 3c + d
3Find the top of a 4-row pyramid for bottom rows (i) 8, 19, 21, 13 (ii) 7, 18, 19, 6 (iii) 9, 7, 5, 11.
Show solution

Top = a + 3b + 3c + d.

  • (i) 8 + 57 + 63 + 13 = 141
  • (ii) 7 + 54 + 57 + 6 = 124
  • (iii) 9 + 21 + 15 + 11 = 56
Answer: (i) 141 (ii) 124 (iii) 56
4Put the first three Virahāṅka-Fibonacci numbers 1, 2, 3 in the bottom of a 3-row pyramid. What numbers appear? Are they all Virahāṅka-Fibonacci numbers?
Show solution

1 + 2 = 3, 2 + 3 = 5, then 3 + 5 = 8. The numbers are 1, 2, 3, 5, 8: all Virahāṅka-Fibonacci numbers. The top is 8.

Answer: rows 1, 2, 3 / 3, 5 / 8: all are Virahāṅka-Fibonacci numbers; top 8
5(i) The first four such numbers in a 4-row pyramid. (ii) The first 29 in a 29-row pyramid. What can you say?
Show solution

(i) 1, 2, 3, 5 → 3, 5, 8 → 8, 13 → 21. All are Virahāṅka-Fibonacci numbers again.

Why: two neighbours in the sequence add to the next-but-one term, which is again in the sequence. So each new row is just the sequence shifted along by two places: row 2 starts at 3, row 3 at 8, row 4 at 21, … Every box is a Virahāṅka-Fibonacci number.

(ii) The same happens in a 29-row pyramid. With 1 = 1st term, 2 = 2nd, 3 = 3rd, the top of an n-row pyramid is the (2n − 1)th term (3-row: 5th term 8; 4-row: 7th term 21). For 29 rows the top is the 57th term, which is 591,286,729,879 (checked by computer).

Answer: (i) top 21, all Virahāṅka-Fibonacci numbers (ii) all boxes are Virahāṅka-Fibonacci numbers; the top is the 57th term, 591286729879
6If the bottom row of an n-row pyramid holds the first n Virahāṅka-Fibonacci numbers, what can we say?
Show solution

Every number in the pyramid is a Virahāṅka-Fibonacci number, since each row is the row below shifted two places along the sequence. Each row has one number fewer, and the rows go up as: 1st–nth terms, 3rd–(n + 1)th, 5th–(n + 2)th, … The top (row n) is the (2n − 1)th Virahāṅka-Fibonacci number.

Answer: all are Virahāṅka-Fibonacci numbers; the top is the (2n − 1)th term

📘 In-text · 6.4 Algebra grids page 142

1Rows: ■ ■ ● = 27; ● ● ■ = 21; ● ■ ● = ?. Find the shapes and fill the empty square.
■■●27
●●■21
●■●?
Show solution

Row 1: 2■ + ● = 27. Row 2: ■ + 2● = 21. Add: 3■ + 3● = 48, so ■ + ● = 16. Then ■ = 27 − 16 = 11 and ● = 5. Row 3 is ● + ■ + ● = 5 + 11 + 5 = 21.

Answer: ■ = 11, ● = 5, empty square = 21
2Rows: ● ◆ ◆ = 18; ◆ ● ● = 15; ◆ ● ● = ?. The bottom row holds the column sums. Find the shapes and fill all empty squares.
●◆◆18
◆●●15
◆●●?
????
Show solution

Row 1: ● + 2◆ = 18. Row 2: ◆ + 2● = 15. Add: 3● + 3◆ = 33, so ● + ◆ = 11. Then ◆ = 18 − 11 = 7 and ● = 4.

Row 3 = 7 + 4 + 4 = 15. Column sums: ● + ◆ + ◆ = 18, ◆ + ● + ● = 15, ◆ + ● + ● = 15, and the corner total is 18 + 15 + 15 = 48.

Answer: ● = 4, ◆ = 7; row 3 sum 15; column sums 18, 15, 15; corner 48

📘 Figure it Out · 6.5 The Largest Product page 144

1Fill 1, 3, 7 in ☐☐ × ☐ to make the largest product.
Show solution

Largest digit 7 is the multiplier; 3 and 1 in decreasing order make 31. 31 × 7 = 217. Check the close rival 71 × 3 = 213 (smaller). The others: 13 × 7 = 91, 17 × 3 = 51, 37 × 1 = 37, 73 × 1 = 73.

Answer: 31 × 7 = 217
2Fill 3, 5, 9 in ☐☐ × ☐ to make the largest product.
Show solution

Multiplier 9; the other digits make 53. 53 × 9 = 477. Rival: 93 × 5 = 465. Others: 35 × 9 = 315, 39 × 5 = 195, 59 × 3 = 177, 95 × 3 = 285.

Answer: 53 × 9 = 477

📘 Figure it Out · 6.6 Decoding Divisibility Tricks pages 145–147

1In the reverse-and-subtract trick, what is the quotient when you divide by 9? How is it related to the number?
Show solution

The difference is 9(b − a), so the quotient is b − a: the difference between the two digits. Example: 74 − 47 = 27, 27 ÷ 9 = 3 = 7 − 4.

Answer: the difference of the two digits
2Instead of subtracting, add the number and its reverse (31 + 13 = 44, 28 + 82 = 110, 12 + 21 = 33). Is the sum always divisible by 11? Justify.
Show solution

(10a + b) + (10b + a) = 11a + 11b = 11(a + b). So yes, it is always a multiple of 11, and the quotient is the digit sum a + b.

Answer: yes: ab + ba = 11(a + b)
3For a 3-digit number abc, add abc + bca + cab. Show the sum is divisible by 37. Is it divisible by 3?
Show solution

abc + bca + cab = (100a + 10b + c) + (100b + 10c + a) + (100c + 10a + b) = 111a + 111b + 111c = 111(a + b + c).

Since 111 = 3 × 37, the sum is always divisible by 37 and also by 3. Example: 123 + 231 + 312 = 666 = 37 × 18.

Answer: sum = 111(a + b + c) = 3 × 37 × (a + b + c): divisible by 37 and by 3
4Write abc twice to make abcabc. Divide by 7, then 11, then 13. What do you get, and why?
Show solution

You get back abc. Example: 385385 ÷ 7 = 55055, ÷ 11 = 5005, ÷ 13 = 385.

Why: abcabc = abc × 1000 + abc = abc × 1001, and 7 × 11 × 13 = 1001.

Answer: the original 3-digit number abc
5Magic ponds double the flowers. A man dips all his flowers in pond 1, places some at shrine 1, dips the rest in pond 2, places some at shrine 2, dips the rest in pond 3 and places all at shrine 3. Each shrine gets the same number. How many flowers did he start with, and how many at each shrine?
Show solution

Let the start be x and the number at each shrine be s.

  • After pond 1 and shrine 1: 2x − s
  • After pond 2 and shrine 2: 4x − 3s
  • Pond 3 doubles this, and all of it is s: 8x − 6s = s, so 8x = 7s.

The smallest whole-number answer is x = 7, s = 8. Check: 7 → 14, place 8 → 6 → 12, place 8 → 4 → 8, place 8 ✅. (Any multiple works too: 14 and 16, 21 and 24, …)

Answer: he started with 7 flowers and placed 8 at each shrine (or any multiple: 7k and 8k)
6A farm has horses and hens: 55 heads and 150 legs. How many of each? Can you do it without letter-numbers?
Show solution

With algebra: h horses, 55 − h hens: 4h + 2(55 − h) = 150 → 2h + 110 = 150 → h = 20.

Without letters: if all 55 were hens there would be 110 legs. The extra 40 legs come from horses, each having 2 more legs than a hen: 40 ÷ 2 = 20 horses. Hens = 55 − 20 = 35. Check: 80 + 70 = 150 ✅

Answer: 20 horses and 35 hens
7A mother is 5 times her daughter's age. In 6 years she will be 3 times her daughter's age. How old is the daughter now?
Show solution

Daughter d, mother 5d. In 6 years: 5d + 6 = 3(d + 6) = 3d + 18 → 2d = 12 → d = 6. Mother 30. Check: in 6 years 36 = 3 × 12 ✅

Answer: 6 years (mother 30)
8Naina has twice as many cows as Gauri. If Naina gave Gauri 3 cows, they would have equal numbers. How many cows does each have?
Show solution

Gauri g, Naina 2g. After giving: 2g − 3 = g + 3 → g = 6. Naina has 12. Check: 9 and 9 ✅

Answer: Gauri 6, Naina 12
9A dosa cart: rent ₹5000 a day; each dosa costs ₹10 to make. (i) Selling 100 dosas a day, what price gives a profit of ₹2000? (ii) If customers pay only ₹50, how many dosas must be sold for ₹2000 profit?
Show solution

(i) Costs = 5000 + 100 × 10 = ₹6000. Needed income = 6000 + 2000 = ₹8000. Price = 8000 ÷ 100 = ₹80.

(ii) Each dosa earns 50 − 10 = ₹40 over its cost. 40n = 5000 + 2000 = 7000 → n = 175.

Answer: (i) ₹80 per dosa (ii) 175 dosas
10Evaluate 13, 1 + 35 + 7, 1 + 3 + 57 + 9 + 11, … What do you notice? Why?
Show solution

4/12 = 1/3 and 9/27 = 1/3: every fraction equals 1/3.

Why: the top is the sum of the first n odd numbers = n². The bottom is the next n odd numbers. The first 2n odd numbers add to (2n)² = 4n², so the bottom is 4n² − n² = 3n². So each fraction is n² / 3n² = 1/3.

Answer: always 1/3
11Karim and the Genie: each round round the tree doubles Karim's coins, then he pays 8 coins. After the 3rd doubling he has exactly 8, which he pays, leaving nothing. (i) How many coins did he start with? (ii) For what cost per round should he agree, to increase his coins? (iii) How should the genie set the cost to take all of Karim's coins?
Show solution

(i) Start x: 2x − 8 → 4x − 24 → 8x − 56 = 0, so x = 7. Check 7 → 6 → 4 → 0 ✅

(ii) After a round he has 2x − c. This is more than x only when c < x. So Karim should agree only if the cost per round is less than the coins he has (with 7 coins: at most 6 coins a round). Then his coins keep growing.

(iii) For 3 rounds, 8x − 7c = 0, so the genie should set c = 8x ÷ 7 (for 7 coins: 8). In general, for n rounds, c = 2ⁿx ÷ (2ⁿ − 1). The genie must make the cost a little more than Karim's coins.

Answer: (i) 7 coins (ii) a cost less than his coins (iii) cost = 8/7 of his coins for 3 rounds
🔍

✗ The trick worked for 3, 10 and 25, so it always works.

✓ Examples are not a proof. Use a letter-number x: if x cancels out, the trick works for every number.

🔺

✗ Top of a 3-row pyramid = a + b + c.

✓ The middle number is used by both boxes above it: top = a + 2b + c. For 4 rows: a + 3b + 3c + d.

📅

✗ 394 − 165 = 229, so the date is 22/9.

✓ The day takes the last two digits: 229 → day 29, month 2 → 29 February.

📆

✗ In a calendar, the date below a is a + 1.

✓ One row down is one week later: a + 7. The date to the right is a + 1.

✖️

✗ Put the biggest digit in the tens place: 93 × 5 = 465 is the largest with 3, 5, 9.

✓ The largest digit should be the multiplier: 53 × 9 = 477 is larger.

➖

✗ 47 − 74 = −27, so the trick fails for 47.

✓ The trick subtracts the smaller from the larger: 74 − 47 = 27 = 9 × 3.

👩‍👧

✗ Mother 5d, in 6 years: 5d + 6 = 3d.

✓ Both people get older: 5d + 6 = 3(d + 6), so d = 6.

🧞

✗ Karim: x → x × 2 × 2 × 2 − 8 = 0.

✓ He pays after every round: 2x − 8, then 2(2x − 8) − 8, … giving 8x − 56 = 0.

cm²½bhb×h½d₁d₂½h(a+b)in²✂️Part II · Chapter 7

Area

Why do the area formulas work? Cut a shape, move the pieces, and it turns into a rectangle with exactly the same area.

📏

🧩 Same area, different shapes

How many ways can you cut a square into 4 parts of equal area? Two cuts through the middle give 4 small squares. But we can be much more creative!

Take each small square and push in one of its edges a little, while pushing out another edge by exactly the same amount. The piece changes shape, but it loses as much area as it gains. Do the same to all four pieces and you get a "pinwheel" in which every piece still has one quarter of the area.

💡 Area is "how much surface" a region covers. Changing the shape does not have to change the area. This whole chapter uses that idea: cut, move, compare.
🎯
Try thisInvent your own way to split a square into 4 equal-area parts. Hint: make all four pieces copies of one piece, turned through 90° each time.

🟦 Rectangles, squares and unit squares

Two rangoli rectangles: one is 7 cm × 4 cm, the other 8 cm × 3 cm. Which needs more rangoli powder? Count how many unit squares (1 cm × 1 cm) fit inside each one, without overlapping.

🎬 Fill the rectangles with unit squares
Area of a rectangle = length × width  ·  Area of a square = side × side

We write the answers as 28 sq. cm or 28 cm2. The small 2 reminds us that area is length × length. A unit square can also be cut into fractions, so areas need not be whole numbers.

The diagonal of a rectangle cuts it into two congruent triangles, so each triangle has half the area: ½ × 7 × 4 = 14 cm2.

🌍
Real lifeAn A4 sheet is 21 cm × 29.7 cm, so its area is 21 × 29.7 = 623.7 cm2. How many A4 sheets would cover your table? 📄

📏 Why can't perimeter measure area?

The perimeter is the length of the boundary. It is tempting to think "longer boundary means bigger area", but that is false. Two shapes can have the same perimeter but different areas, and a shape with a larger perimeter can even have a smaller area.

Region 1 has the larger perimeter (20 > 16) but the smaller area (9 < 16). The same thing happens with other shapes: a "comb" with long thin teeth has a huge boundary but little inside it.

💡 That is why area is measured by counting unit squares, not by measuring the boundary.

🔺 Area of a triangle

In a rectangle ABCD, join D and C to any point X on AB. Wherever X is, ∆XDC is half the rectangle. Drop the altitude XY: it splits the rectangle into two smaller rectangles, and the triangle takes exactly half of each one.

🎬 Draw a rectangle round a triangle

For any triangle ABC, draw a line l through A parallel to BC and perpendiculars to BC at B and C. You get a rectangle BCDE whose sides are the base BC and the height (the altitude from A).

Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height

What if the altitude falls outside? In the triangle below, the foot D of the altitude from A lies outside BC. Then ∆ABC = ∆ADC − ∆ADB:

½ × h × DC − ½ × h × DB = ½ × h × (DC − DB) = ½ × h × BC

💡 The formula works for every triangle: acute, right-angled or obtuse. Any side can be the base, as long as you use the height to that side.

🎯 Using the area formula cleverly

1. Finding an altitude. In ∆ABC, BC = 5, the altitude AX = 3 and AC = 4. How long is the altitude BY to AC?

Write the area in two ways: ½ × BC × AX = ½ × 5 × 3 = 15/2, and also ½ × AC × BY = ½ × 4 × BY = 2 BY. So 2 BY = 15/2, giving BY = 15/4 = 3.75 units.

2. The diagonals of a rectangle make 4 triangles that are not congruent, yet all have equal area! Compare triangles 1 and 2: take bases OD and OB. They are equal (diagonals bisect each other) and both triangles have the same altitude from A.

💡 In a triangle, the line from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side cuts it into two triangles of equal area (equal bases, same height).

🪞 Triangles between parallel lines

Line l is parallel to BC. Every triangle with base BC and its third vertex A on l has the same height, so they all have the same area, however slanted they look. But their perimeters are different! Which one has the smallest perimeter?

🎬 Slide A along the line, then use a mirror

Treat l as a mirror and reflect C to C′. Then AC = AC′ (the two triangles AYC and AYC′ are congruent), so the path B → A → C is exactly as long as B → A → C′. The shortest path from B to C′ is a straight line, so the best A is where the straight line BC′ crosses l. That point is exactly halfway along, so A lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC and the best triangle is isosceles.

🌍
Real lifeLight uses the same trick: a ray bouncing off a mirror always takes the shortest path. Gopal can use it too, to fetch water from a river with the least walking (Book Exercise 8) 🚶

🔷 Area of any polygon

A quadrilateral ABCD can be split by the diagonal AC into two triangles. Both have base AC, so we need only AC and the two perpendiculars BM and DN:

Area of quadrilateral = ½ × AC × (BM + DN)
💡 Every polygon can be divided into triangles. So if you can find the area of a triangle, you can find the area of ANY polygon.
🌍
Real lifeSurveyors measure an odd-shaped field by walking one long line across it and measuring the perpendicular distances to its corners. Then they add up triangles 🌾

▱ Parallelogram: cut and slide

Draw the height AX ⊥ CD. Cut off ∆AXD and slide it to the other end. Does it fit exactly? Extend XC and drop BY ⊥ XC. Then BY = AX, ∠BYC = ∠AXD = 90° and BC = AD, so ∆BYC ≅ ∆AXD by the RHS rule. The triangle fills the gap perfectly and we get the rectangle ABYX.

🎬 Turn a parallelogram into a rectangle

Since DX = CY, adding XC to both gives XY = DC, the base. So:

Area of a parallelogram = base × height

You can use any side as the base, with its own height. Below, the base is AD and the height is CZ: cutting along CZ also gives a rectangle.

This cut-and-move process is called dissection. It never changes the area.

🏛️ Dissection in the Śulba-Sūtras

The Śulba-Sūtras are ancient Indian texts about building fire altars. An altar had to have an exact shape and an exact area, so the authors solved problems like "change this shape into that shape without changing its area". Euclid's Elements has similar problems.

An isosceles triangle into a rectangle: cut along the altitude AD. The two right triangles are mirror images. Turn one over and join their long sides: they make a rectangle with sides BD (half the base) and AD (the height).

🎬 Turn an isosceles triangle into a rectangle

Any triangle into a rectangle: cut across at half the height (through the midpoints P, Q of AB and AC). Split the small top triangle along its altitude and turn the two pieces down into the bottom corners. You get a rectangle with base BC and height h/2: area ½ × BC × h again!

🤩
Did you know?The Śulba-Sūtras (Baudhāyana, Āpastamba, Kātyāyana and others) are among the oldest geometry texts in the world. They also turn rectangles into squares and squares into circles of (nearly) the same area!

🔶 Rhombus: half the product of the diagonals

A rhombus is a parallelogram, so base × height works. But its diagonals are perpendicular bisectors of each other, which gives a lovely Śulba-Sūtra dissection: cut along both diagonals into 4 right triangles, flip two of them, and the rhombus becomes a rectangle.

🎬 Cut a rhombus into 4 and rebuild a rectangle

The rectangle WXYZ has one side = the whole diagonal AC and the other = half of BD. So

Area of a rhombus = AC × BD/2 = ½ × product of diagonals

Another way: BD splits the rhombus into ∆ADB and ∆CDB, with heights AO and CO onto BD. Area = ½ × AO × BD + ½ × CO × BD = ½ × BD × (AO + CO) = ½ × BD × AC. Same formula! ✅

🎯
Try thisA rhombus with diagonals 20 cm and 15 cm has area ½ × 20 × 15 = 150 cm2.

🪜 Trapezium: three ways to the formula

Way 1: rectangle + two triangles. In trapezium WXYZ (WX ∥ ZY), drop WM and XN perpendicular to ZY. WXNM is a rectangle (co-interior angles make ∠MWX = ∠NXW = 90°). Call WX = a, ZY = b, the height h, and the two leftover bits of the base x and y.

🎬 Break a trapezium into easy pieces

Area = ½hx + ha + ½hy = ½h(x + y + 2a) = ½h(b − a + 2a) = ½h(a + b)

(we used b = x + y + a, so x + y = b − a).

Area of a trapezium = ½ × height × (sum of parallel sides)

Way 2: when the trapezium leans over (the foot of the height falls outside), draw BG ∥ AD. Now ABGD is a parallelogram (area a × h) and ∆BGC has base b − a and height h: a·h + ½(b − a)·h = ½h(a + b). This works for any trapezium, using the longer parallel side as b.

Way 3: two copies. Take a second copy, turn it upside down and join it along BC. Because AB ∥ CD, the angles at B add to 180°, so the edges line up straight: the two copies make a parallelogram with base a + b and height h. One trapezium is half of it.

🎬 Two trapeziums make a parallelogram

🌍 Areas in real life: units

Furniture is often measured in inches (in) and feet (ft): 1 in = 2.54 cm 1 ft = 12 in

Lengths: 5 in = 5 × 2.54 = 12.7 cm; 7.4 in = 18.796 cm. Backwards: 5.08 cm = 5.08 ÷ 2.54 = 2 in; 11.43 cm = 4.5 in.

Careful with area! A 1 in × 1 in square is 2.54 cm × 2.54 cm, so

1 in2 = 2.542 cm2 = 6.4516 cm2  ·  1 ft2 = 122 = 144 in2

So 10 in2 = 64.516 cm2, and 161.29 cm2 = 161.29 ÷ 6.4516 = 25 in2.

WhatUsual unitFact
paper, book, tabletopcm2, in21 in2 = 6.4516 cm2
classroom, houseft2, m21 ft2 = 144 in2; 1 m2 = 10,000 cm2
farm landacre1 acre = 43,560 ft2
village, city, statekm21 km2 = 1000 × 1000 = 10,00,000 m2
🤩
Did you know?Different parts of India use their own land units: bigha, gaj, katha, dhur, cent, ankanam… Ask an elder which one is used where you live! 🏡
💡 Converting areas: square the length conversion. 1 m = 100 cm, but 1 m2 = 100 × 100 = 10,000 cm2.

🪞 Slide the top vertex

Move A along the line l (parallel to BC). Watch the area stay fixed while the perimeter changes. Turn on the mirror to find the shortest perimeter.

✂️ Shape → rectangle of equal area

Pick a shape and change its measurements. The orange pieces stick out of the dashed rectangle; the green gaps are exactly the same size. Press “Move the pieces” to rebuild the rectangle.

📏 Perimeter vs area

Build two rectangles. Can you make rectangle A have the larger perimeter but the smaller area?

📘 Figure it Out · 7.1 Rectangles and squares pages 150–152

1Identify the missing sidelengths.
Show solution

(i) Work from the shape whose numbers you know.

  • 21 in² rectangle: width 7 in, so its height = 21 ÷ 7 = 3 in.
  • 28 in² rectangle: its height is 4 + 3 = 7 in, so its width = 28 ÷ 7 = 4 in.
  • 35 in² rectangle: its width is 3 + 4 = 7 in, so its height = 35 ÷ 7 = 5 in.
  • 14 in² strip: its height is 5 + 2 = 7 in, so its width = 14 ÷ 7 = 2 in.
Answer (i): ? = 2 in

(ii) Top-left width = 29 ÷ 4 = 7.25 m; top-right width = 11 ÷ 4 = 2.75 m. The bold rectangle (50 m²) has the same width 7.25 m, so its full height = 50 ÷ 7.25 ≈ 6.90 m, and the missing height of the lower part = 50 ÷ 7.25 − 4 = 84/29 ≈ 2.90 m.

Note: if you read “50 m²” as the area of the lower part alone, its height would be 50 ÷ 7.25 ≈ 6.90 m. The bold outline suggests the whole left column.

Answer (ii): 7.25 m, 2.75 m, about 2.90 m
2A path (shaded) is laid around a rectangular park EFGH inside a bigger rectangle ABCD. (i) What must be measured to find the path's area? Choose values and give a formula. (ii) If only the width of the path on each side is known, is that enough? (iii) Does the path's area change if the outer rectangle is moved, keeping EFGH inside it?
Show solution

(i) Area of path = area ABCD − area EFGH. Measure the length and width of both rectangles. Example: ABCD 20 m × 15 m, EFGH 16 m × 11 m: path = 300 − 176 = 124 m².

Area of path = L × B − l × b

(ii) The widths alone are not enough: a wide park and a tiny park can have paths of the same width but very different areas. We also need the park's length l and width b. With widths p (left), q (right), t (top), u (bottom), break the path into 4 rectangles: top strip (l + p + q) × t, bottom strip (l + p + q) × u, and side strips b × p and b × q.

Area = (l + p + q)(t + u) + b(p + q)

Example: park 16 m × 11 m, path 2 m wide on every side: 20 × 4 + 11 × 4 = 80 + 44 = 124 m² (matches part (i)).

(iii) No. The path is always ABCD minus EFGH, and neither area changes when ABCD slides around EFGH. Only the widths on the different sides change.

Answer: path = outer area − park area; e.g. 124 m²; moving the outer rectangle does not change it
3A plot 14 m × 12 m has a crosspath (one path parallel to each side). What else must be measured? Choose values, find the area and give a formula.
Show solution

We need the widths of the two paths: w₁ (path running along the 12 m side) and w₂ (path running along the 14 m side). The square where they cross is inside both strips, so subtract it once.

Area = 12 × w₁ + 14 × w₂ − w₁ × w₂

With w₁ = w₂ = 1 m: 12 + 14 − 1 = 25 m². With w₁ = w₂ = 2 m: 24 + 28 − 4 = 48 m². (The position of the paths does not matter!)

Answer: e.g. 25 m² for 1 m wide paths
4A spiral tube of width 1 unit has arms (outer lengths) 20, 20, 20, 15, 15, 10, 10, 5, 5. Find its area. What length of straight tube (also 1 unit wide) has the same area?
Show solution

The hint: an L-shaped tube with arms 5 and 5 (outer lengths) is a 5 × 1 strip plus a 4 × 1 strip, area 5 + 4 = 9. It equals a straight tube of length 9: at each bend the corner square would be counted twice.

So: add all the arm lengths, then subtract 1 for each of the 8 bends.

20 + 20 + 20 + 15 + 15 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 5 = 120; 120 − 8 = 112

(Checked by counting unit squares on a grid.) A straight tube of width 1 and length 112 has the same area.

Answer: 112 sq. units; straight tube of length 112 (L-shape in the hint: 9)
5A square is divided into regions 1, 2 and 3 by a diagonal and a line from a corner to the centre (see figure). If the sidelength is doubled, by how much does each region's area increase?
Show solution

With side s: region 3 is half the square (s²/2). Regions 1 and 2 split the other half by a median, so each is s²/4.

Doubling the side makes every length twice as long, so every area becomes 2 × 2 = 4 times as large: the increase is 3 times the old area.

  • Region 1: s²/4 → s², increase 3s²/4
  • Region 2: s²/4 → s², increase 3s²/4
  • Region 3: s²/2 → 2s², increase 3s²/2
Answer: each region becomes 4 times as big (increase = 3 × old area)
6Cut a square into 4 parts by two perpendicular lines through its inside (as in the figure). Rearrange the pieces to make a larger square with a hole in it.
Show solution

If both lines pass through the centre of the square and are perpendicular, the 4 pieces are congruent (each is the next one turned through 90°). Each piece has two right-angled corners: one at the centre and one at a corner of the square.

Turn each piece so its square corner (from the original square's corner) points inwards and place the four around a small square: the outer edges (the cut lines, all equal) now form a bigger square, and a small square hole is left in the middle. The hole's side is the difference of the two parts into which a cut line meets each side of the square.

This is the famous puzzle behind a proof of the Baudhāyana-Pythagoras theorem.

Answer: the 4 congruent pieces surround a square hole to make a bigger square

📘 Figure it Out · Triangles pages 157–159

1Find the areas of the triangles: (i) base BC = 4 cm, height AE = 3 cm; (ii) EF = 5 cm with altitude DN = 3.2 cm to it; (iii) right angle at A, AN = 4 cm, AT = 3 cm.
Show solution

(i) ½ × 4 × 3 = 6 cm². (The 4 cm is the whole base BC; the height AE meets it at 90°.)

(ii) Use EF as the base and DN as its height: ½ × 5 × 3.2 = 8 cm².

(iii) The two sides at the right angle are base and height: ½ × 3 × 4 = 6 cm².

Answer: (i) 6 cm² (ii) 8 cm² (iii) 6 cm²
2In ∆ABC, BC = 6 units, AC = 8 units and the altitude AX (falling outside, on CB extended) = 4 units. Find the altitude BY to AC.
Show solution

Area with base BC: ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 sq. units (the height is AX even though X is outside BC).

Area with base AC: ½ × 8 × BY = 4 BY. So 4 BY = 12.

Answer: BY = 3 units
3∆SUB is isosceles (SU = SB), SE ⊥ UB and the area of ∆SEB is 24 sq. units. Find the area of ∆SUB.
Show solution

In an isosceles triangle the altitude SE from the apex meets UB at its midpoint (∆SEU ≅ ∆SEB by RHS). So SE is a median, and the two halves have equal area.

Answer: 2 × 24 = 48 sq. units
4[Śulba-Sūtras] Give a method to transform a rectangle into a triangle of equal area.
Show solution

Method 1 (construction): rectangle ABCD with base DC and height AD. Extend DC to E so that CE = DC. Join A to E. ∆ADE has base 2 × DC and height AD, so its area is ½ × 2DC × AD = DC × AD, the rectangle's area.

Method 2 (dissection): cut the rectangle along a diagonal into two congruent right triangles. Turn one over and place the two back to back along the side AD: the two bottom edges line up into one straight base 2 × DC, and you get an isosceles triangle with height AD (see Exercise 8 of the next set).

Answer: a triangle with base 2 × length and height = width has the same area
5[Śulba-Sūtras] Give a method to transform a triangle into a rectangle of equal area.
Show solution

Triangle ABC with base BC and height h. Mark the midpoints P of AB and Q of AC; PQ is at height h/2. Drop the altitude AX from A to PQ. Cut off the top triangle APQ along PQ, then cut it along AX into ∆APX and ∆AQX.

Turn ∆APX through 180° about P: A goes to B, and it fills the gap between B, side AB and the line PQ. Do the same with ∆AQX about Q. The result is a rectangle with base BC and height h/2: area BC × h/2 = ½ × BC × h. ✅ (See the Lab “Shape → rectangle”.)

Answer: rectangle with base BC and height half the triangle's height
6ABCD, BCEF and BFGH are identical squares (H above B, line DH drawn). (i) If the red region (∆DCH) is 49 sq. units, what is the blue region (the part of square ABCD left of DH)? (ii) If red + blue = 180 sq. units, what is the area of each square?
Show solution

Let each square have side s. ∆DCH is right-angled at C with DC = s and CH = 2s, so red = ½ × s × 2s = s², one whole square!

DH rises 2s while moving s across, so at the height of AB (height s) it has moved only s/2: it cuts AB at its midpoint. Blue = ½ × s × s/2 = s²/4 = ¼ of red.

(i) s² = 49, so blue = 49/4 = 12.25 sq. units. (ii) red + blue = s² + s²/4 = 5s²/4 = 180, so s² = 144.

Answer: (i) 12.25 sq. units (ii) 144 sq. units
7M and N are the midpoints of XY and XZ. What fraction of the area of ∆XYZ is ∆XMN? (Hint: join NY.)
Show solution

YN joins Y to the midpoint N of XZ, so ∆XYN is half of ∆XYZ.

In ∆XYN, NM joins N to the midpoint M of XY, so ∆XMN is half of ∆XYN.

Answer: ½ × ½ = 1/4
8Gopal walks from his house to the river (a straight bank) and then to the water tank, both on the same side. What is the shortest path?
Show solution

Reflect the tank in the river bank to get Tank′. For any point P on the bank, P→Tank is as long as P→Tank′. So the walk House → P → Tank is as long as House → P → Tank′, which is shortest when it is a straight line.

So: join House to Tank′ with a straight line. Where it meets the bank is P. Walk House → P → Tank (the orange path).

Answer: go to the point P where the line from the house to the tank's mirror image meets the river

📘 Figure it Out · Area of any polygon page 160

1Quadrilateral ABCD: AC = 22 cm, BM = 3 cm and DN = 3 cm, both perpendicular to AC. Find its area.
Show solution

Split along AC: ∆ABC = ½ × 22 × 3 = 33 cm² and ∆ADC = ½ × 22 × 3 = 33 cm².

Answer: 66 cm²
2ABCD is a rectangle, AB = 18 cm (AE = 10 cm, EB = 8 cm), AD = BC = 10 cm (AF = 6 cm, FD = 4 cm). Find the area of the shaded region FECD.
Show solution

Rectangle = 18 × 10 = 180 cm². Remove the two white right triangles:

  • ∆AEF: ½ × 10 × 6 = 30 cm²
  • ∆EBC: ½ × 8 × 10 = 40 cm²

Shaded = 180 − 30 − 40.

Answer: 110 cm²
3What measurements would you need to find the area of a regular hexagon?
Show solution

Lines from the centre to the 6 corners cut a regular hexagon into 6 identical equilateral triangles, each with side s (the side of the hexagon). So we need the side s and the height of one of those triangles (the distance from the centre to a side). Then Area = 6 × ½ × s × height = 3 × s × height.

(Later you can work out that height from s alone, using the Baudhāyana-Pythagoras theorem, so really one length, the side, is enough.)

Answer: the side and the centre-to-side distance (in fact, the side alone fixes it)
4Inside a rectangle, a point P is joined to all four corners; the top and bottom triangles are blue. What fraction of the rectangle is blue?
Show solution

Both blue triangles have base = the length L of the rectangle. Their heights are the distances from P to the top and to the bottom, which add up to the width W.

Blue = ½ L × h₁ + ½ L × h₂ = ½ L (h₁ + h₂) = ½ L W.

Answer: 1/2 (wherever P is)
5Give a method to get a quadrilateral whose area is half that of a given quadrilateral.
Show solution

Join the midpoints of the four sides, in order. The inner quadrilateral has half the area.

Why: the diagonal AC splits ABCD into ∆ABC and ∆ACD. The corner triangle cut off at B (between the midpoints of AB and BC) is ¼ of ∆ABC (it is the "midpoint triangle" of Exercise 7 in the last set); the one at D is ¼ of ∆ACD. So these two corners together remove ¼ of ABCD. In the same way, the corners at A and C remove another ¼. Half is left.

Answer: join the midpoints of the sides

📘 Figure it Out · Parallelogram pages 162–164

1Seven parallelograms (a)–(g) are drawn on a grid, each with the top and bottom sides 5 squares long and 3 squares apart, leaning by different amounts. (i) What about their areas? (ii) Their perimeters? Which seems largest and smallest?
Show solution

(i) Each has base 5 and height 3, so every area = 5 × 3 = 15 square units. All equal!

(ii) The top and bottom always add 5 + 5 = 10. The slanting sides get longer the more the parallelogram leans (the height is fixed at 3, the sideways shift grows). So the perimeters are different. The one leaning the most, (g) (about 3 squares sideways), has the largest perimeter; the most upright one, (a), has the smallest.

Answer: same area (15 sq. units); perimeters differ: largest (g), smallest (a)
2Find the areas: (i) base 7 cm, height 4 cm; (ii) base 5 cm, height 3 cm; (iii) side 5 cm with height 4.8 cm to it; (iv) side 2 cm with height 4.4 cm to it.
Show solution

Area = base × height, using any side with its own perpendicular height.

(i) 7 × 4 = 28 cm² · (ii) 5 × 3 = 15 cm² (the diagonal in the picture is not needed) · (iii) 5 × 4.8 = 24 cm² · (iv) 2 × 4.4 = 8.8 cm²

Answer: 28 cm², 15 cm², 24 cm², 8.8 cm²
3Parallelogram PQRS has SR = 12 cm, PS = 7.6 cm, height QM = 6 cm (onto SR). Find QN, the height onto PS.
Show solution

Area = SR × QM = 12 × 6 = 72 cm². Also Area = PS × QN = 7.6 × QN.

QN = 72 ÷ 7.6 = 180/19 ≈ 9.47 cm.

Answer: QN ≈ 9.47 cm
4A rectangle and a parallelogram both have sides 5 cm and 4 cm. Which has the greater area?
Show solution

Build both on the same 5 cm base. The rectangle's height is the full 4 cm. In the parallelogram the 4 cm side leans, so its height (the perpendicular distance) is less than 4 cm.

Answer: the rectangle (20 cm²); the parallelogram has less than 20 cm²
5Give a method to get a rectangle whose area is twice that of a given triangle. Find different methods.
Show solution

Method 1: draw the line through A parallel to BC, and perpendiculars to BC at B and C. The rectangle BCDE (base BC, height h) has area BC × h = 2 × triangle.

Method 2: make a copy of the triangle, turn it through 180° and join it along a side to make a parallelogram (area 2 × triangle). Then cut-and-slide the parallelogram into a rectangle.

Method 3: a rectangle with base 2 × BC and height h/2, or base BC/2 and height 2h… any rectangle with area BC × h.

Answer: e.g. the rectangle on base BC with the triangle's height
6[Śulba-Sūtras] Give a method to get a rectangle with the same area as a given triangle.
Show solution

Take the rectangle of Exercise 5 (area 2 × triangle) and halve it: keep the base BC and use half the height. Construct the midpoints P, Q of AB and AC and draw perpendiculars from B and C up to the line PQ. This rectangle BC × h/2 can even be obtained by dissection: cut off triangle APQ, split it along its altitude and turn the halves down into the two corners (see the Lab).

Answer: rectangle with base BC and height h/2
7[Śulba-Sūtras] Convert an isosceles triangle ABC (AB = AC, altitude AD) into a rectangle by a simpler dissection.
Show solution

Cut along AD. ∆ADB and ∆ADC are congruent right triangles (RHS: AB = AC, AD common). Each one is half of a rectangle BD × AD. Turn ∆ADC over and place its hypotenuse AC against AB, with C on A and A on B: the two triangles form a rectangle with sides BD = BC/2 and AD = h. Area = ½ × BC × h ✅ (watch the animation in Learn).

Answer: cut along the altitude, flip one half, join along the equal sides
8[Śulba-Sūtras] Convert a rectangle into an isosceles triangle by dissection.
Show solution

Reverse Exercise 7. Cut the rectangle (length L, width W) along a diagonal into two congruent right triangles. Turn one over and place them back to back along a side of length W, with the right angles together at the bottom. Now the two legs of length L lie in one straight line (two right angles make 180°), forming a base 2L, and the apex is at height W. The two hypotenuses are equal, so the triangle is isosceles. Area = ½ × 2L × W = L × W ✅

Answer: cut along a diagonal, put the halves back to back
9Which is larger: an equilateral triangle or a square of the same side? Two identical equilateral triangles together, or the square?
Show solution

Let the side be s and the triangle's height h. The height is perpendicular to the base, so it is shorter than the slanting side: h < s.

One triangle: ½ × s × h < ½ × s × s, less than half the square. Two triangles: 2 × ½ × s × h = s × h < s × s. (In fact h ≈ 0.87 s.)

Answer: the square is larger in both cases

📘 Figure it Out · Rhombus and trapezium pages 169–170

1Find the area of a rhombus with diagonals 20 cm and 15 cm.
Show solution

½ × 20 × 15 = 150.

Answer: 150 cm²
2Give a method to convert a rectangle into a rhombus of equal area using dissection.
Show solution

Reverse the rhombus dissection. Rectangle WXYZ with sides p (long, vertical) and q. Cut it into two rectangles p/2 × q (top and bottom halves). Cut each along a diagonal into 2 right triangles with legs p/2 and q, so 4 congruent right triangles in all. Arrange the 4 triangles with their right angles meeting at one point O, the legs of length p/2 pointing up and down and the legs of length q pointing left and right (turn pieces over where needed). The hypotenuses form a rhombus with diagonals p and 2q. Area = ½ × p × 2q = p × q ✅

Answer: 4 right triangles from the rectangle, arranged around a point → rhombus with diagonals p and 2q
3Find the areas: (i) trapezium with parallel sides 10 ft and 7 ft, 16 ft apart; (ii) parallel sides 24 m and 36 m, height 14 m; (iii) parallel (vertical) sides 14 in and 6 in, 10 in apart; (iv) parallel sides 12 ft and 18 ft, height 8 ft.
Show solution

Area = ½ × height × (sum of parallel sides).

  • (i) ½ × 16 × (10 + 7) = 8 × 17 = 136 ft²
  • (ii) ½ × 14 × (24 + 36) = 7 × 60 = 420 m²
  • (iii) ½ × 10 × (14 + 6) = 5 × 20 = 100 in²
  • (iv) ½ × 8 × (12 + 18) = 4 × 30 = 120 ft²
Answer: 136 ft², 420 m², 100 in², 120 ft²
4[Śulba-Sūtras] Convert an isosceles trapezium into a rectangle by dissection.
Show solution

Drop perpendiculars from the two top corners. This cuts the trapezium into a middle rectangle (a × h) and two congruent right triangles at the ends (legs x = (b − a)/2 and h), congruent because the trapezium is isosceles.

Cut off one end triangle, turn it over and join it to the other along their hypotenuses: together they make a rectangle x × h. Put it beside the middle rectangle: one rectangle of length a + x = (a + b)/2 and height h. ✅

(Or: cut each end triangle at half height, as in Exercise 5.)

Answer: rectangle (a + b)/2 by h
5Trapezium ABCD is turned into rectangle EFGH of equal area, with ∆AHI ≅ ∆DGI and ∆BEJ ≅ ∆CFJ. How do we find E, F, G, H?
Show solution

Mark I and J, the midpoints of the slanting sides AD and BC. Through I and J draw lines perpendicular to DC. They meet DC at G and F and line AB (extended) at H and E.

Why it works: at I, AI = ID (midpoint), the angles at I are vertically opposite, and ∠H = ∠G = 90°, so ∆AHI ≅ ∆DGI (AAS). Likewise ∆BEJ ≅ ∆CFJ. Each orange triangle cut off at the bottom fills the green gap at the top, so EFGH has the same area as ABCD.

Bonus: HE = GF = (a + b)/2, so area = ½ (a + b) × h, the trapezium formula again!

Answer: I, J = midpoints of the legs; perpendiculars to DC through them give H, G and E, F
6Construct a trapezium of area 144 cm².
Show solution

Start from a rectangle of area 144 cm², say 16 cm × 9 cm. Reverse Exercise 5: keep the height 9 cm and choose parallel sides whose average is 16 cm, e.g. 12 cm and 20 cm. Check: ½ × 9 × (12 + 20) = ½ × 9 × 32 = 144 ✅

To construct: draw DC = 20 cm, a parallel line 9 cm above it, and mark AB = 12 cm on it (anywhere). Join AD and BC. (Many other answers work: height 8 cm with sides 15 cm and 21 cm, etc.)

Answer: e.g. parallel sides 12 cm and 20 cm, 9 cm apart
7A regular hexagon is divided into a trapezium, an equilateral triangle and a rhombus (as shown). Find the ratio of their areas.
Show solution

Joining the centre to all 6 corners cuts the hexagon into 6 identical equilateral triangles. The long diagonal leaves 3 of them in the trapezium (top half). The lower half has 3 more: 1 forms the equilateral triangle and 2 form the rhombus.

Answer: trapezium : triangle : rhombus = 3 : 1 : 2
8ZYXW is a trapezium with ZY ∥ WX. A is the midpoint of XY, and ZA extended meets WX extended at B. Show that area ZYXW = area ∆ZWB.
Show solution

Compare ∆AYZ and ∆AXB: AY = AX (A is the midpoint), ∠YAZ = ∠XAB (vertically opposite), and ∠AYZ = ∠AXB (alternate angles, since ZY ∥ WB). So ∆AYZ ≅ ∆AXB (ASA) and they have equal areas.

Trapezium = quadrilateral ZAXW + ∆AYZ, and ∆ZWB = quadrilateral ZAXW + ∆AXB. Swap the equal triangles: the areas are equal. ✅

Answer: ∆AYZ ≅ ∆AXB, so the two figures have equal areas

📘 Try these · Areas in real life pages 170–171

1An A4 sheet is 21 cm × 29.7 cm. Find its area.
Show solution

21 × 29.7 = 623.7.

Answer: 623.7 cm²
2Express in cm: (i) 5 in (ii) 7.4 in. Express in inches: (iii) 5.08 cm (iv) 11.43 cm.
Show solution

Multiply by 2.54 to go from in to cm; divide by 2.54 to go back.

(i) 5 × 2.54 = 12.7 cm (ii) 7.4 × 2.54 = 18.796 cm (iii) 5.08 ÷ 2.54 = 2 in (iv) 11.43 ÷ 2.54 = 4.5 in

Answer: 12.7 cm, 18.796 cm, 2 in, 4.5 in
3How many cm² is 1 in²? 10 in²? Convert 161.29 cm² to in².
Show solution

1 in² = 2.54 × 2.54 = 6.4516 cm². 10 in² = 64.516 cm². 161.29 ÷ 6.4516 = 25.

Answer: 6.4516 cm²; 64.516 cm²; 25 in²
4How many in² is 1 ft²? How many m² is 1 km²?
Show solution

1 ft² = 12 in × 12 in = 144 in². 1 km² = 1000 m × 1000 m = 10,00,000 m² (one million). For land: 1 acre = 43,560 ft².

Answer: 144 in²; 10,00,000 m²
📐

✗ Parallelogram with sides 8 cm and 5 cm: area = 8 × 5 = 40 cm².

✓ Use base × height, the perpendicular distance between the parallel sides. The slanting 5 cm side is not the height (the height is shorter).

🔺

✗ Triangle with base 10 cm and height 6 cm: area = 10 × 6 = 60 cm².

✓ A triangle is half a rectangle: ½ × 10 × 6 = 30 cm².

🧵

✗ "This field has a longer boundary, so it must have more area."

✓ Perimeter does not measure area. A 9 × 1 rectangle has a bigger perimeter (20) but smaller area (9) than a 4 × 4 square (16, 16).

📏

✗ 1 in = 2.54 cm, so 1 in² = 2.54 cm².

✓ Area has two lengths: 1 in² = 2.54 × 2.54 = 6.4516 cm². Likewise 1 m² = 10,000 cm², not 100.

🪜

✗ Trapezium area = ½ × height × (the two slanting sides).

✓ Use the two parallel sides: ½ × h × (a + b).

🔶

✗ Rhombus with diagonals 10 cm and 8 cm: area = 10 × 8 = 80 cm².

✓ Half the product: ½ × 10 × 8 = 40 cm². (The rectangle in the dissection uses only HALF of one diagonal.)

↘️

✗ "This obtuse triangle has no height, because the altitude falls outside it."

✓ Extend the base: the altitude meets the extended line at 90°. ½ × base × height still works.

🔁

✗ Finding another altitude: using the old height with the new base.

✓ Each base goes with its own perpendicular height. Find the area first, then height = 2 × area ÷ base (triangle) or area ÷ base (parallelogram).
